optionExplanations.0: An individual has two alleles per trait, not one (a gamete has one).
optionExplanations.1: The two alleles need not be identical; heterozygotes have different alleles.
optionExplanations.3: Most traits are governed by two alleles per individual, not three.

shortExplanation: Crossing TT x tt gives all Tt offspring. Since T (tall) is dominant, 100% of the F1 are tall.
solutionSteps: TT produces only T gametes; tt produces only t gametes.
Every offspring is Tt (heterozygous).
Tall is dominant, so all Tt plants are tall.
Percentage tall = 100%.
keyConcept: A homozygous dominant x homozygous recessive cross yields uniformly heterozygous, dominant-phenotype offspring.
commonMistake: Applying the 3:1 or 1:2:1 ratios, which arise from a heterozygous x heterozygous cross, not this one.

optionExplanations.0: 0% would require tall to be recessive, which it is not.
optionExplanations.1: 25% is the recessive fraction of a Tt x Tt cross, not this cross.
optionExplanations.2: 50% would arise from a Tt x tt testcross, not TT x tt.

shortExplanation: A normal human somatic cell is diploid with 46 chromosomes (23 pairs).
solutionSteps: Somatic cells are diploid (2n).
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes.
2n = 2 x 23 = 46 chromosomes.
keyConcept: Diploid human somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes; gametes are haploid with 23.
commonMistake: Reporting 23, which is the haploid gamete number, not the somatic-cell number.

optionExplanations.0: 23 is the haploid number found in gametes, not somatic cells.
optionExplanations.2: 48 is characteristic of some great apes, not humans.
optionExplanations.3: 23 pairs of autosomes is inaccurate; humans have 22 pairs of autosomes plus one pair of sex chromosomes, totaling 46.

shortExplanation: Auxin promotes cell elongation and drives phototropism by redistributing to the shaded side of a shoot.
solutionSteps: Auxin is produced in shoot tips and transported down.
It loosens cell walls, allowing cells to elongate.
Uneven auxin distribution toward light causes bending (phototropism).
keyConcept: Auxin controls cell elongation and mediates directional growth toward light.
commonMistake: Confusing auxin with gibberellin, which chiefly promotes stem elongation and seed germination but not phototropic bending.

optionExplanations.0: Cytokinins promote cell division, not elongation-driven phototropism.
optionExplanations.1: Gibberellins drive stem elongation and germination, but auxin governs phototropism.
optionExplanations.2: Abscisic acid promotes dormancy and stomatal closure, inhibiting growth.

shortExplanation: Stomata are pores that allow gas exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) and release water vapor during transpiration.
solutionSteps: Stomata are adjustable pores in the leaf epidermis.
They admit CO2 for photosynthesis and release O2.
They also allow water vapor to escape (transpiration).
keyConcept: Stomata mediate both gas exchange and transpiration.
commonMistake: Thinking stomata absorb water; water uptake occurs at the roots, not the stomata.

optionExplanations.0: Water is absorbed by roots, not through stomata.
optionExplanations.2: Support and water transport are functions of xylem and other tissues, not stomata.
optionExplanations.3: Glucose production occurs in chloroplasts; storage is not a stomatal role.

shortExplanation: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, translating mRNA into polypeptide chains.
solutionSteps: Ribosomes read mRNA codons.
They assemble amino acids into polypeptides.
This translation process is protein synthesis.
keyConcept: Ribosomes carry out translation, the direct synthesis of proteins.
commonMistake: Attributing protein synthesis to the endoplasmic reticulum itself, when it is the ribosomes on the rough ER that build the proteins.

optionExplanations.0: Mitochondria produce ATP, not proteins as their primary role.
optionExplanations.2: The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins after they are made.
optionExplanations.3: The endoplasmic reticulum transports and folds proteins; ribosomes on it do the synthesis.

shortExplanation: Sunlight is the primary energy source; producers capture it via photosynthesis to power ecosystems.
solutionSteps: Producers convert light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.
This energy flows to consumers through food chains.
Thus sunlight is the ultimate energy source for most ecosystems.
keyConcept: Nearly all ecosystem energy originates from sunlight captured by photosynthesis.
commonMistake: Confusing a required material (water, soil nutrients) with the energy source itself.

optionExplanations.0: Wind is a physical force, not the base energy input for food chains.
optionExplanations.1: Water is essential but is not the energy source ecosystems run on.
optionExplanations.3: Soil nutrients supply minerals, not the primary energy for the food web.

shortExplanation: The vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium of the heart.
solutionSteps: Deoxygenated blood collects from body tissues.
It drains into the superior and inferior vena cava.
The vena cava empties into the right atrium of the heart.
keyConcept: The vena cava carries oxygen-poor blood from the body back to the heart.
commonMistake: Choosing the pulmonary artery, which carries deoxygenated blood but from the heart to the lungs, not from the body to the heart.

optionExplanations.0: The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the heart to the body.
optionExplanations.1: The pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
optionExplanations.2: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, but from the heart to the lungs.

shortExplanation: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
solutionSteps: Chloroplasts absorb light energy.
This energy drives the synthesis of glucose from CO2 and water.
The chemical energy is stored in the bonds of glucose.
keyConcept: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy (glucose).
commonMistake: Confusing photosynthesis with respiration, which releases stored chemical energy rather than capturing light energy.

optionExplanations.0: Respiration releases stored chemical energy; it does not capture light.
optionExplanations.2: Transpiration is the loss of water vapor, not energy conversion.
optionExplanations.3: Fermentation is anaerobic energy release, not light capture.

shortExplanation: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements and maintains balance and posture.
solutionSteps: The cerebellum sits below the cerebrum at the back of the brain.
It integrates sensory input to fine-tune motor activity.
This controls balance, posture, and coordination.
keyConcept: The cerebellum governs balance and motor coordination.
commonMistake: Assigning coordination to the cerebrum, which handles higher thought and voluntary initiation, not fine balance control.

optionExplanations.0: The cerebrum handles thought, sensation, and voluntary action, not balance fine-tuning.
optionExplanations.2: The medulla oblongata controls autonomic functions like breathing and heart rate.
optionExplanations.3: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis, hormones, and body temperature.

shortExplanation: Organic chemistry is defined by carbon-based molecules; carbon's four bonds let it form the vast chains and rings of all organic compounds.
solutionSteps: Organic molecules are, by definition, carbon-containing compounds.
Carbon forms four stable covalent bonds, enabling chains, rings, and branches.
Hence carbon is the element central to all organic molecules.
keyConcept: Carbon's tetravalency makes it the backbone element of all organic compounds.
commonMistake: Choosing hydrogen or oxygen because they are common, though carbon defines the class.

optionExplanations.0: Hydrogen is abundant in organics but does not define the class the way carbon does.
optionExplanations.1: Nitrogen is present in some organics (amines, proteins) but is not universal.
optionExplanations.2: Oxygen appears in many organics but is not the required central element.

shortExplanation: In an open container, faster-moving surface molecules escape into the air, so the liquid slowly evaporates.
solutionSteps: Liquid molecules have a range of kinetic energies.
The most energetic surface molecules escape into the vapor phase.
Over time in an open container the liquid level drops, i.e. it evaporates.
keyConcept: Evaporation is surface vaporization that occurs below the boiling point in open air.
commonMistake: Thinking the liquid cools or solidifies; it may cool slightly, but the net observable change is evaporation.

optionExplanations.0: Oxidation is a chemical reaction, not the general fate of a liquid left open.
optionExplanations.1: A liquid at room temperature does not spontaneously freeze in an open container.
optionExplanations.3: Some evaporative cooling occurs, but the defining slow change is loss of liquid by evaporation.

shortExplanation: Electronegativity is an atom's tendency to attract the shared electrons of a covalent bond toward itself.
solutionSteps: Consider two bonded atoms sharing electrons.
Electronegativity measures how strongly one atom pulls those shared electrons.
Thus it is the tendency to attract bonding electrons.
keyConcept: Electronegativity = attraction for shared electrons in a chemical bond.
commonMistake: Confusing electronegativity with ionization energy (removing an electron) or electron affinity (gaining one).

optionExplanations.0: Energy released when an atom gains an electron is electron affinity, not electronegativity.
optionExplanations.1: The tendency to lose electrons describes electropositivity, the opposite trend.
optionExplanations.4: Energy needed to remove an electron is ionization energy, a different property.

shortExplanation: Sulphuric acid has the formula H2SO4, with two hydrogens, one sulfur, and four oxygens.
solutionSteps: Sulphuric acid is a strong diprotic acid with two acidic hydrogens.
Sulfur is in the +6 state bonded to four oxygens as sulfate.
The formula is therefore H2SO4.
keyConcept: Sulphuric acid is H2SO4 (two H, one S, four O).
commonMistake: Confusing sulphuric acid (H2SO4) with sulphurous acid (H2SO3).

optionExplanations.0: H2S is hydrogen sulfide, a gas, not an oxoacid.
optionExplanations.2: H2S2O3 is thiosulfuric acid, a different compound.
optionExplanations.4: H2SO3 is sulphurous acid, with one fewer oxygen than sulphuric acid.

shortExplanation: Benzene (C6H6) is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, a single six-carbon ring with delocalized pi electrons.
solutionSteps: Aromatic hydrocarbons have a stable ring with delocalized (aromatic) electrons.
Benzene is the smallest such ring, C6H6.
Therefore benzene is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon.
keyConcept: Benzene, C6H6, is the archetypal simplest aromatic ring.
commonMistake: Choosing naphthalene, which is aromatic but larger (two fused rings), not the simplest.

optionExplanations.0: Methane is a simple alkane with no ring and no aromaticity.
optionExplanations.1: Naphthalene has two fused benzene rings, so it is more complex than benzene.
optionExplanations.4: Butene is an alkene, not an aromatic compound.

shortExplanation: The change from liquid to vapor (gas) is vaporization, listed here as evaporation.
solutionSteps: Identify the two phases: liquid to vapor.
The liquid-to-gas transition is vaporization/evaporation.
So evaporation is the correct term among the choices.
keyConcept: Liquid to gas is vaporization (evaporation); solid to gas is sublimation.
commonMistake: Confusing sublimation (solid to gas) with the liquid-to-vapor change.

optionExplanations.1: Deposition is gas-to-solid, the reverse direction and wrong phases.
optionExplanations.2: Fusion is melting, the solid-to-liquid transition.
optionExplanations.4: Sublimation is the solid-to-gas transition, not liquid-to-gas.

shortExplanation: Saturated open-chain hydrocarbons (alkanes) follow the general formula CnH2n+2.
solutionSteps: Alkanes are fully saturated, single-bonded hydrocarbons.
For each carbon count n, the hydrogen count is 2n+2.
Check: methane n=1 gives CH4 (2*1+2=4), consistent, so CnH2n+2.
keyConcept: Alkanes: CnH2n+2; alkenes CnH2n; alkynes CnH2n-2.
commonMistake: Using CnH2n (the alkene formula) instead of CnH2n+2 for alkanes.

optionExplanations.0: CnH2n is the general formula for alkenes (one double bond) or cycloalkanes.
optionExplanations.1: CnH2n-2 corresponds to alkynes or dienes, which are unsaturated.
optionExplanations.4: CnH2n+4 exceeds the maximum hydrogen count allowed for carbon.

shortExplanation: Group I (alkali metals) includes Na, K, Rb, and Cs. Calcium (Ca) is an alkaline-earth metal in group II, so it does not belong.
solutionSteps: Group I alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs.
Among the choices, Na, K, Rb, and Cs are all group I.
Ca is in group II (alkaline earth), so it is the odd one out.
keyConcept: Alkali metals (group I) have one valence electron; Ca in group II has two.
commonMistake: Grouping calcium with the alkali metals because it is also a reactive metal.

optionExplanations.1: K (potassium) is a group I alkali metal.
optionExplanations.2: Cs (cesium) is a group I alkali metal.
optionExplanations.4: Na (sodium) is a group I alkali metal.

shortExplanation: Mole fraction is defined as the moles of one component divided by the total moles of all components in the mixture.
solutionSteps: Write the ratio: moles of solute divided by total moles (solute + solvent).
This dimensionless ratio is the mole fraction.
So the described quantity is the mole fraction.
keyConcept: Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles in the mixture.
commonMistake: Confusing mole fraction with molarity (moles per liter of solution).

optionExplanations.1: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, based on mass, not moles.
optionExplanations.2: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution, not a ratio of moles to total moles.
optionExplanations.4: Normality is equivalents of solute per liter, unrelated to a mole ratio.

formulaNotes: Mole fraction of solute = n_solute / (n_solute + n_solvent).

shortExplanation: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons, so they share the same atomic number; all potassium isotopes have atomic number 19.
solutionSteps: Atomic number = number of protons in the nucleus.
Isotopes differ in neutron number (mass number), not proton number.
39K, 40K, and 41K all have 19 protons, so their atomic number is identical.
keyConcept: Isotopes share the same atomic number; only the mass number (neutrons) differs.
commonMistake: Confusing the mass number (superscript) with the atomic number, and picking 41K.

optionExplanations.1: 39K has the lowest mass but the same atomic number, 19, as the rest.
optionExplanations.2: 40K differs only in neutrons; its atomic number is still 19.
optionExplanations.3: 41K has the highest mass number, but its atomic number equals the others' (19).

shortExplanation: In methane (CH4) carbon shares all four valence electrons in four C-H bonds, leaving no lone pairs. The other molecules each have oxygen or nitrogen atoms bearing lone pairs.
solutionSteps: Count lone pairs on the central/heteroatoms of each molecule.
In CH4, carbon uses all four electrons in bonds, so zero lone pairs.
Water, ethers, pyridine, and ammonia all have O or N atoms carrying lone pairs.
Therefore methane is the molecule with no lone pairs.
keyConcept: Carbon in CH4 is fully bonded (four C-H bonds) with no non-bonding electron pairs.
commonMistake: Forgetting that nitrogen and oxygen atoms always carry lone pairs in these molecules.

optionExplanations.0: Water's oxygen carries two lone pairs.
optionExplanations.2: Pyridine's ring nitrogen has a lone pair in the plane of the ring.
optionExplanations.3: Ammonia's nitrogen carries one lone pair.

shortExplanation: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Cu + Zn2+, copper ions gain electrons (reduction) and zinc atoms lose electrons (oxidation).
solutionSteps: Track Zn: goes from 0 to +2, so it loses 2 electrons = oxidized.
Track Cu: goes from +2 to 0, so it gains 2 electrons = reduced.
Match to the option stating copper is reduced and zinc is oxidized.
keyConcept: Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number); reduction is gain of electrons (decrease).
commonMistake: Confusing the two by assuming the metal that dissolves is 'reduced' rather than oxidized.

optionExplanations.1: Zinc rises from 0 to +2, so it is oxidized, not reduced.
optionExplanations.2: Both zinc and copper change oxidation number, so a redox process clearly occurs.
optionExplanations.3: This reverses the roles; zinc is oxidized and copper is reduced.

shortExplanation: Electrolytes are substances that dissociate into ions when dissolved, allowing the solution to conduct electricity.
solutionSteps: Recall that conduction in solution requires mobile charged particles.
Identify that electrolytes provide these charges by forming ions.
Select the definition based on ion formation in solution.
keyConcept: An electrolyte is any species that produces ions in solution and thereby conducts current.
commonMistake: Restricting electrolytes to only acids or only bases, when salts and many other species qualify.

optionExplanations.1: Acids are electrolytes, but the term is broader and includes salts and bases too.
optionExplanations.2: Free electrons do not exist in aqueous solution; conduction is by ions.
optionExplanations.4: Bases are one class of electrolyte, not the general definition.

shortExplanation: Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules in both liquid water and ice, arising from H bonded to the highly electronegative O.
solutionSteps: Hydrogen bonding requires H attached to N, O, or F.
Water has O-H bonds, so it forms strong hydrogen bonds.
These persist in liquid water and in the ordered lattice of ice.
keyConcept: Hydrogen bonding occurs when H bonded to N, O, or F is attracted to a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
commonMistake: Calling hydrogen bonds covalent; they are strong intermolecular attractions, not shared-electron bonds.

optionExplanations.0: Methane has only C-H bonds and cannot hydrogen bond.
optionExplanations.1: Water is the classic example of hydrogen bonding, so this is false.
optionExplanations.2: Hydrogen bonds are intermolecular attractions, not covalent bonds.

shortExplanation: Pb2+ gains 2 electrons to become neutral Pb, which is a reduction (decrease in oxidation number).
solutionSteps: Read the half-reaction: Pb2+ + 2e- -> Pb.
Oxidation number of lead falls from +2 to 0.
Gaining electrons and lowering oxidation number defines reduction.
keyConcept: Reduction is the gain of electrons and a decrease in oxidation number.
commonMistake: Labeling any electron transfer as oxidation regardless of direction.

optionExplanations.0: No proton is added; electrons are gained.
optionExplanations.1: Oxidation number changes from +2 to 0, so redox does occur.
optionExplanations.2: Gaining electrons is reduction, not oxidation.

shortExplanation: Hydrogen sulphide is H2S, with two hydrogen atoms bonded to one sulfur atom.
solutionSteps: Sulfur is in group 16 and typically forms 2 bonds.
Two hydrogens satisfy sulfur's bonding, giving H2S.
Match to the H2S formula.
keyConcept: Hydrogen sulphide is the sulfur analog of water, formula H2S.
commonMistake: Confusing it with sulfur oxoacids such as sulfuric or sulfurous acid.

optionExplanations.1: HNO3 is nitric acid, a nitrogen compound.
optionExplanations.2: H2SO3 is sulfurous acid, not hydrogen sulphide.
optionExplanations.4: H2SO4 is sulfuric acid, containing oxygen.

shortExplanation: Covalent bonds share electron pairs between atoms, while ionic bonds involve transfer of electrons to form oppositely charged ions.
solutionSteps: Covalent bonding: atoms of similar electronegativity share electrons.
Ionic bonding: a large electronegativity gap causes electron transfer.
Select the option matching share vs transfer.
keyConcept: Covalent = shared electrons; ionic = transferred electrons producing cations and anions.
commonMistake: Swapping the definitions or tying bond type strictly to metals vs nonmetals labels.

optionExplanations.1: This reverses the definitions; covalent shares and ionic transfers.
optionExplanations.2: Ionic bonds typically form between a metal and a nonmetal, not this labeling.
optionExplanations.3: Relative strength is not the defining distinction between the bond types.

shortExplanation: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity of all elements on the Pauling scale.
solutionSteps: Electronegativity increases toward the top-right of the periodic table.
Fluorine sits at that extreme, above chlorine and beside oxygen.
Fluorine's value (about 4.0) exceeds oxygen, nitrogen, and chlorine.
keyConcept: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, with a Pauling value near 4.0.
commonMistake: Choosing oxygen, which is second-highest but below fluorine.

optionExplanations.1: Oxygen is highly electronegative (about 3.4) but lower than fluorine.
optionExplanations.3: Nitrogen (about 3.0) is below both oxygen and fluorine.
optionExplanations.4: Chlorine (about 3.2) is lower than fluorine, which is above it in the group.

shortExplanation: When a single element replaces another within a compound, the reaction is a single displacement (substitution).
solutionSteps: Pattern A + BC -> AC + B describes one element taking another's place.
This is the single displacement type.
Select single displacement.
keyConcept: Single displacement: one free element displaces another from a compound.
commonMistake: Confusing it with double displacement, where two compounds exchange ions.

optionExplanations.0: Synthesis combines simpler species into one product, not a replacement.
optionExplanations.1: Decomposition breaks one compound into simpler ones.
optionExplanations.3: Double displacement swaps partners between two compounds, not a single element.

shortExplanation: CO2 has molar mass 12 + 2(16) = 44 g/mol.
solutionSteps: Carbon contributes about 12 g/mol.
Two oxygens contribute 2 x 16 = 32 g/mol.
keyConcept: Molar mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in the formula.
commonMistake: Counting only one oxygen or forgetting the subscript of 2.

optionExplanations.0: 12 is only the carbon contribution.
optionExplanations.1: 28 would arise from mis-adding (e.g. C plus one O).
optionExplanations.3: 32 is the mass of the two oxygens alone (or O2).

shortExplanation: Combustion of gasoline releases heat to the surroundings, so it is exothermic.
solutionSteps: Exothermic processes release energy (negative enthalpy change).
Melting, evaporation, sublimation, and photosynthesis all absorb energy.
Only combustion releases heat, making it exothermic.
keyConcept: Exothermic reactions release energy; phase changes to higher-energy states and photosynthesis absorb it.
commonMistake: Assuming any physical change involving heat is exothermic, when melting and evaporation absorb heat.

optionExplanations.0: Melting ice absorbs heat (endothermic).
optionExplanations.1: Evaporating water absorbs heat to overcome intermolecular forces.
optionExplanations.3: Photosynthesis stores energy from light, so it is endothermic.

shortExplanation: At 25 C a neutral solution has equal H+ and OH- concentrations, giving pH = 7.
solutionSteps: Select pH 7.
keyConcept: Neutrality at 25 C corresponds to pH = 7, where [H+] equals [OH-].
commonMistake: Thinking neutral means pH 0 or the midpoint of any arbitrary scale.

optionExplanations.0: pH 0 corresponds to a strongly acidic 1 M H+ solution.
optionExplanations.2: pH 14 corresponds to a strongly basic solution.
optionExplanations.4: pH 5 is mildly acidic, not neutral.

formulaNotes: pH = -log[H+]; neutral at 25 C means [H+] = 10^-7 -> pH 7.

shortExplanation: Dalton's Law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of its components.
solutionSteps: Identify the law about partial pressures.
Dalton's Law: P_total = P1 + P2 + ...
Select Dalton's Law.
keyConcept: Dalton's Law of partial pressures: total pressure is the sum of component partial pressures.
commonMistake: Mixing it up with Boyle's or Avogadro's laws, which address different variables.

optionExplanations.0: Boyle's Law relates pressure and volume at constant temperature.
optionExplanations.1: Charles's Law relates volume and temperature at constant pressure.
optionExplanations.3: Avogadro's Law relates volume and amount of gas.

shortExplanation: Sodium has 11 electrons, giving the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.
solutionSteps: Sodium's atomic number is 11, so it has 11 electrons.
Result: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1.
keyConcept: Electron configurations fill orbitals in order of increasing energy up to the atomic number.
commonMistake: Stopping at neon's configuration or placing the last electron in 3p instead of 3s.

optionExplanations.1: 1s2 2s2 2p6 is neon (10 electrons), one short of sodium.
optionExplanations.2: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 has 12 electrons (magnesium).
optionExplanations.3: The 3s subshell fills before 3p, so 3p1 is incorrect.

shortExplanation: NaCl forms between a metal and a nonmetal with a large electronegativity difference, making it ionic.
solutionSteps: Ionic bonding arises from a large electronegativity gap (metal + nonmetal).
NaCl pairs sodium (metal) with chlorine (nonmetal).
The other compounds share electrons covalently among nonmetals.
keyConcept: Ionic compounds form between metals and nonmetals via electron transfer.
commonMistake: Assuming polar molecules like water are ionic; they are covalent with partial charges.

optionExplanations.0: H2O is a polar covalent molecule, not ionic.
optionExplanations.1: CO2 is covalent between two nonmetals.
optionExplanations.3: CH4 is nonpolar covalent.

shortExplanation: Moles = mass / molar mass = 22 / 44 = 0.5 mol.
solutionSteps: Use n = m / M.
n = 22 g / 44 g/mol.
n = 0.5 mol.
keyConcept: Number of moles equals mass divided by molar mass.
commonMistake: Multiplying instead of dividing, or misreading the molar mass.

optionExplanations.1: 1 mole would require 44 g of CO2.
optionExplanations.2: 2 moles would require 88 g.
optionExplanations.3: 0.25 moles would correspond to 11 g.

shortExplanation: HCl is a strong acid that dissociates completely in water into H+ and Cl-.
solutionSteps: Strong acids fully ionize in aqueous solution.
HCl dissociates completely, unlike weak acids.
Select HCl.
keyConcept: Strong acids (like HCl) ionize completely in water.
commonMistake: Calling acetic or carbonic acid strong; they are weak and only partly ionize.

optionExplanations.1: NaOH is a strong base, not an acid.
optionExplanations.3: CH3COOH (acetic acid) is a weak acid.
optionExplanations.4: H2CO3 (carbonic acid) is a weak acid.

shortExplanation: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass, at roughly 46%.
solutionSteps: Recall crustal abundance: oxygen about 46%, silicon about 28%.
Oxygen exceeds silicon and all metals.
Select oxygen.
keyConcept: Oxygen is the most abundant crustal element, mainly bound in silicates and oxides.
commonMistake: Choosing silicon, which is second, or a metal like aluminum or iron.

optionExplanations.0: Silicon is second most abundant, not first.
optionExplanations.2: Aluminum is the most abundant metal but ranks third overall.
optionExplanations.3: Iron is fourth by mass in the crust.

shortExplanation: Alkali metal reactivity increases down the group, so Rb > K > Na > Li.
solutionSteps: Reactivity of alkali metals rises down group 1 as the outer electron is lost more easily.
Order from most to least reactive: Rb, K, Na, Li.
Select Rb > K > Na > Li.
keyConcept: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group due to easier loss of the valence electron.
commonMistake: Reversing the trend and putting lithium as most reactive.

optionExplanations.0: This lists reactivity increasing upward, the reverse of the true trend.
optionExplanations.2: K is not more reactive than Rb, and Rb is misplaced last.
optionExplanations.4: The ordering of Na and K is wrong; K is more reactive than Na.

shortExplanation: N2 has a triple bond, sharing three electron pairs to give each nitrogen an octet.
solutionSteps: Each nitrogen has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more for an octet.
The two atoms share three electron pairs.
This is a triple bond (N#N).
keyConcept: N2 is held by a strong nitrogen-nitrogen triple bond.
commonMistake: Assuming diatomic gases have single bonds; N2 needs a triple bond for octets.

optionExplanations.0: A single bond leaves each nitrogen short of an octet.
optionExplanations.1: A double bond still leaves an unpaired electron deficiency.
optionExplanations.3: N2 is a covalent molecule, not ionic.

shortExplanation: CH4 (methane) contains only carbon and hydrogen, so it is a hydrocarbon.
solutionSteps: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen atoms.
CH4 fits this definition exactly.
The others contain oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur.
keyConcept: A hydrocarbon is a compound of only carbon and hydrogen.
commonMistake: Including oxygen- or nitrogen-containing molecules as hydrocarbons.

optionExplanations.1: H2O contains oxygen and no carbon.
optionExplanations.2: CO2 has carbon but also oxygen, so it is not a hydrocarbon.
optionExplanations.3: NH3 contains nitrogen and hydrogen, no carbon.

shortExplanation: Boyle's Law relates pressure and volume inversely at constant temperature.
solutionSteps: Identify the law linking P and V at fixed temperature.
Boyle's Law: P*V = constant.
Select Boyle's Law.
keyConcept: Boyle's Law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional.
commonMistake: Confusing it with Charles's Law (volume vs temperature).

optionExplanations.1: Charles's Law relates volume and temperature at constant pressure.
optionExplanations.2: Gay-Lussac's Law relates pressure and temperature at constant volume.
optionExplanations.3: Avogadro's Law relates volume and amount of gas.

formulaNotes: Boyle: P1*V1 = P2*V2 at constant T.

shortExplanation: Complete combustion of methane yields carbon dioxide and water: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O.
solutionSteps: Combustion of a hydrocarbon in ample oxygen gives CO2 and H2O.
Balance: CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O.
Select CO2 and H2O.
keyConcept: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water.
commonMistake: Choosing CO (incomplete combustion) or leaving hydrogen unoxidized.

optionExplanations.0: CO and H2O result from incomplete combustion, not the main complete-combustion products.
optionExplanations.3: H2 is not a product; hydrogen ends up as water.
optionExplanations.4: CO and H2 are not the products of methane combustion in oxygen.

shortExplanation: H2O is polar because its bent shape gives an uncancelled net dipole toward the oxygen.
solutionSteps: Polarity requires polar bonds and an asymmetric geometry.
Water is bent, so its O-H bond dipoles do not cancel.
The result is a net molecular dipole, making water polar.
keyConcept: Molecular polarity depends on bond dipoles and molecular geometry; bent water has a net dipole.
commonMistake: Assuming polar bonds always make a polar molecule; symmetric CO2 is nonpolar despite polar bonds.

optionExplanations.0: O2 has identical atoms and no bond dipole, so it is nonpolar.
optionExplanations.1: CO2 is linear, so its bond dipoles cancel, giving a nonpolar molecule.
optionExplanations.4: CH4 is tetrahedral and symmetric, so it is nonpolar.

shortExplanation: Electrons, especially valence electrons, determine an element's chemical properties and bonding behavior.
solutionSteps: Chemical behavior involves gaining, losing, or sharing electrons.
Valence electrons control bonding and reactivity.
Select electron.
keyConcept: Valence electrons govern chemical bonding and reactivity.
commonMistake: Choosing protons; protons fix identity but chemistry is driven by electrons.

optionExplanations.0: Protons determine which element it is but not its bonding behavior directly.
optionExplanations.1: Neutrons affect mass and isotopes, not chemical properties.
optionExplanations.3: The nucleus (protons plus neutrons) sets identity and mass, not bonding.

shortExplanation: Helium has the highest first ionization energy of these elements, due to its small size and full, stable 1s shell.
solutionSteps: Ionization energy increases across a period and up a group.
Helium sits at the top-right extreme with a filled 1s2 shell.
Its ionization energy exceeds neon, fluorine, oxygen, and hydrogen.
keyConcept: Helium has the highest first ionization energy of all elements because of its tiny radius and stable full shell.
commonMistake: Choosing fluorine or neon; among these, helium's compact filled shell wins.

optionExplanations.0: Fluorine has high ionization energy but less than the noble gases listed.
optionExplanations.2: Oxygen's ionization energy is lower than fluorine and the noble gases.
optionExplanations.3: Neon is very high but still below helium.

shortExplanation: Oxygen has 8 protons in its nucleus, so its atomic number is 8.
solutionSteps: The atomic number equals the number of protons.
Oxygen (O) occupies position 8 in the periodic table.
Therefore its atomic number is 8.
keyConcept: Atomic number = number of protons in the nucleus.
commonMistake: Confusing atomic number (8) with atomic mass (about 16).

optionExplanations.0: 6 is the atomic number of carbon, not oxygen.
optionExplanations.3: 16 is oxygen's approximate atomic mass, not its atomic number.
optionExplanations.4: 12 is the mass number of common carbon, unrelated to oxygen's proton count.

shortExplanation: Fluorine has 9 protons; subtracting from mass number 19 gives 10 neutrons.
solutionSteps: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Fluorine's atomic number is 9.
19 − 9 = 10 neutrons.
keyConcept: Neutron count = mass number minus proton (atomic) number.
commonMistake: Using 19 directly or confusing protons with neutrons.

optionExplanations.0: 8 would require an atomic number of 11, which is not fluorine.
optionExplanations.1: 9 is the number of protons (atomic number), not neutrons.
optionExplanations.4: 19 is the mass number (protons + neutrons), not the neutron count alone.

shortExplanation: O–H joins two different nonmetals with a large electronegativity difference but shared electrons, making it a polar covalent bond.
solutionSteps: A polar covalent bond forms between nonmetals of unequal electronegativity.
O (about 3.5) and H (about 2.1) differ significantly but still share electrons.
The unequal sharing gives partial charges, so O–H is polar covalent.
keyConcept: Polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally between nonmetals of different electronegativity.
commonMistake: Classifying Na–Cl as covalent; its large electronegativity gap makes it ionic.

optionExplanations.0: H–H joins identical atoms, so it is nonpolar covalent.
optionExplanations.1: Na–Cl is between a metal and nonmetal, forming an ionic bond, not covalent.
optionExplanations.3: C–H has only a small electronegativity difference, so it is essentially nonpolar.

shortExplanation: Magnesium sits in group 2 and period 3 of the periodic table.
solutionSteps: Group 2 contains the alkaline earth metals.
Period 3 is the third row.
The group-2 element in period 3 is magnesium (Mg).
keyConcept: Group gives the column; period gives the row.
commonMistake: Choosing calcium (group 2 but period 4) or beryllium (group 2 but period 2).

optionExplanations.0: Calcium is group 2 but period 4, not period 3.
optionExplanations.1: Sodium is period 3 but group 1, not group 2.
optionExplanations.3: Beryllium is group 2 but period 2, not period 3.

shortExplanation: O²⁻, Na⁺, and Mg²⁺ each have 10 electrons, matching neon, so all of them are isoelectronic with neon.
solutionSteps: Neon has 10 electrons.
O²⁻: 8 + 2 = 10 electrons.
Na⁺: 11 − 1 = 10 electrons.
Mg²⁺: 12 − 2 = 10 electrons.
All three match neon, so 'All of the above' is correct.
keyConcept: Isoelectronic species share the same total electron count.
commonMistake: Picking only one ion and missing that all three reach 10 electrons.

optionExplanations.0: O²⁻ is correct but not the only correct species listed.
optionExplanations.1: Na⁺ is correct but not the only correct species listed.
optionExplanations.4: F⁺ has 8 electrons (9 − 1), matching oxygen, not neon.

shortExplanation: An oxide contains oxygen bonded to another element; CO₂ is carbon dioxide, an oxide.
solutionSteps: An oxide is a binary compound of oxygen with another element.
CO₂ contains only carbon and oxygen.
Therefore CO₂ is an oxide.
keyConcept: Oxides are binary compounds of oxygen with one other element.
commonMistake: Counting NaOH or H₂SO₄ as oxides; they contain oxygen but are not binary oxides.

optionExplanations.0: NaCl is a chloride salt containing no oxygen.
optionExplanations.1: NaOH is a hydroxide, not a binary oxide.
optionExplanations.4: H₂SO₄ is an oxoacid, not a simple oxide.

shortExplanation: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) only partially dissociates in water, making it a weak acid.
solutionSteps: Weak acids ionize only partially in water.
HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, and HBr are strong acids that dissociate almost completely.
CH₃COOH dissociates only slightly, so it is the weak acid.
keyConcept: Weak acids establish an equilibrium and ionize only partially.
commonMistake: Assuming any acid with hydrogen fully dissociates.

optionExplanations.0: HCl is a classic strong acid, fully dissociated.
optionExplanations.1: H₂SO₄ is a strong acid (at least in its first dissociation).
optionExplanations.3: HNO₃ is a strong acid, fully dissociated in water.

shortExplanation: By Arrhenius theory a base releases OH⁻ ions in water; NaOH does exactly this.
solutionSteps: An Arrhenius base increases OH⁻ concentration in water.
NaOH dissociates into Na⁺ and OH⁻.
Therefore NaOH is the Arrhenius base.
keyConcept: Arrhenius bases release hydroxide (OH⁻) ions in aqueous solution.
commonMistake: Choosing NH₃; it is a base but by Brønsted–Lowry, not by the strict Arrhenius OH⁻ definition.

optionExplanations.0: NH₃ has no OH⁻ to release directly, so it is not an Arrhenius base.
optionExplanations.2: HCl releases H⁺, making it an acid, not a base.
optionExplanations.3: HNO₃ releases H⁺, making it an acid.

shortExplanation: HCl reacting with NaOH produces the salt NaCl and water.
solutionSteps: Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water.
The cation Na⁺ from NaOH pairs with the anion Cl⁻ from HCl.
The salt formed is NaCl.
keyConcept: The salt combines the base's cation with the acid's anion.
commonMistake: Introducing carbonate or sulfate ions that are not present in HCl or NaOH.

optionExplanations.1: Na₂CO₃ would require a carbonate source, which is absent here.
optionExplanations.3: Na₂SO₄ would require sulfuric acid, not hydrochloric acid.
optionExplanations.4: NaNO₃ would require nitric acid, not hydrochloric acid.

shortExplanation: With H as +1 and O as −2, sulfur must be +6 to balance the neutral H₂SO₄ molecule.
solutionSteps: Assign H = +1 (total +2) and O = −2 (total −8).
The molecule is neutral, so 2 + S + (−8) = 0.
Solve: S = +6.
keyConcept: Oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule sum to zero.
commonMistake: Forgetting there are four oxygens, giving too low a sulfur value.

optionExplanations.0: +2 is far too low to balance four −2 oxygens.
optionExplanations.1: +4 would be sulfur in H₂SO₃ or SO₂, not H₂SO₄.
optionExplanations.3: +8 exceeds sulfur's maximum oxidation state of +6.

shortExplanation: Cu²⁺ gains electrons to become Cu metal, so Cu²⁺ is reduced.
solutionSteps: Reduction is a gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number).
Cu²⁺ goes from +2 to 0, gaining two electrons.
Therefore Cu²⁺ is the species reduced.
keyConcept: Reduction = gain of electrons and a drop in oxidation state.
commonMistake: Confusing the reactant Cu²⁺ (reduced) with the product Cu, or reversing oxidation and reduction.

optionExplanations.0: Zn is oxidized (0 to +2), losing electrons, not reduced.
optionExplanations.2: Cu is the product of reduction, not the species being reduced.
optionExplanations.3: Zn²⁺ is the oxidation product of zinc, not reduced.

shortExplanation: Water's molar mass is 2(1) + 16 = 18 g/mol, so one mole weighs 18 g.
solutionSteps: Add atomic masses: 2 hydrogens = 2 g, 1 oxygen = 16 g.
Molar mass of H₂O = 18 g/mol.
One mole therefore weighs 18 g.
keyConcept: Molar mass is the sum of the atomic masses in the formula.
commonMistake: Forgetting oxygen's mass or miscounting the hydrogens.

optionExplanations.1: 10 g omits oxygen's contribution entirely.
optionExplanations.2: 12 g is closer to carbon's molar mass, not water's.
optionExplanations.3: 20 g overcounts the hydrogen or oxygen masses.

shortExplanation: Avogadro's number is 6.02×10²³, the count of particles in one mole.
solutionSteps: One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles.
That value is 6.02×10²³ per mole.
So the correct choice is 6.02×10²³.
keyConcept: One mole = 6.02×10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).
commonMistake: Choosing a negative exponent or confusing it with other physical constants.

optionExplanations.0: 6.02×10⁻²⁶ has the wrong sign on the exponent.
optionExplanations.3: 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg is roughly a proton's mass, not Avogadro's number.
optionExplanations.4: 2.18×10⁻¹⁸ J relates to hydrogen's ionization energy, unrelated here.

solutionSteps: Apply pH = −log[H⁺].
−log(10⁻⁵) = 5, so pH = 5.
keyConcept: pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of [H⁺].
commonMistake: Reporting the magnitude of the exponent with the wrong value or sign.

optionExplanations.1: 3 corresponds to [H⁺] = 10⁻³, far more concentrated.
optionExplanations.2: 4 corresponds to [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴, ten times more acidic.
optionExplanations.4: 6 corresponds to [H⁺] = 10⁻⁶, ten times less acidic.

shortExplanation: Higher pH means more basic, so pH 10 is the most basic of the listed values.
solutionSteps: The pH scale increases with basicity.
Among 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10, the largest is 10.
Therefore pH 10 is the most basic.
keyConcept: Basicity increases as pH rises above 7.
commonMistake: Thinking a lower pH number is more basic.

optionExplanations.0: pH 6 is slightly acidic, below neutral.
optionExplanations.1: pH 7 is neutral, not basic.
optionExplanations.3: pH 9 is basic but less so than pH 10.

shortExplanation: Sulfate is an inorganic ion, not an organic functional group like alcohol, ester, ketone, or amine.
solutionSteps: Organic functional groups are carbon-based reactive units.
Alcohol (−OH), ester, ketone (C=O), and amine (−NH₂) are all organic groups.
Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) is an inorganic polyatomic ion, not an organic functional group.
keyConcept: Organic functional groups are carbon-centered structural units.
commonMistake: Confusing the inorganic sulfate ion with organic sulfur-containing groups.

optionExplanations.0: Alcohol (−OH on carbon) is a standard organic functional group.
optionExplanations.1: Ester is a recognized organic functional group.
optionExplanations.3: Ketone (C=O between carbons) is an organic functional group.

shortExplanation: In NaClO, Na is +1 and O is −2, so Cl must be +1 for the neutral compound.
solutionSteps: Assign Na = +1 and O = −2.
The compound is neutral: +1 + Cl + (−2) = 0.
Solve: Cl = +1.
keyConcept: Oxidation numbers sum to zero in a neutral compound.
commonMistake: Assuming chlorine is always −1 as in chlorides.

optionExplanations.0: −1 is chlorine's state in NaCl, not in the hypochlorite NaClO.
optionExplanations.1: 0 applies to elemental Cl₂, not to Cl bonded in NaClO.
optionExplanations.3: +3 is chlorine's state in chlorites (ClO₂⁻), not hypochlorite.

shortExplanation: Aluminium hydroxide reacts with both acids and bases, so Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric.
solutionSteps: An amphoteric compound reacts as both an acid and a base.
Al(OH)₃ dissolves in acids (forming Al³⁺) and in strong bases (forming aluminate).
Therefore Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric.
keyConcept: Amphoteric substances react with both acids and bases.
commonMistake: Picking a purely acidic or purely basic species as amphoteric.

optionExplanations.0: NaOH is a strong base only, not amphoteric.
optionExplanations.1: HCl is a strong acid only.
optionExplanations.3: H₂SO₄ is a strong acid only.

shortExplanation: A ketone has a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to two carbon groups; CH₃COCH₃ (acetone) fits this.
solutionSteps: A ketone has C=O flanked by two carbon atoms.
CH₃COCH₃ places the carbonyl between two methyl groups.
Therefore CH₃COCH₃ is the ketone.
keyConcept: Ketones have a carbonyl carbon bonded to two other carbons.
commonMistake: Confusing the carbonyl of a ketone with the −COOH of a carboxylic acid.

optionExplanations.0: CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol (−OH group).
optionExplanations.1: CH₃COOH is a carboxylic acid (−COOH group).
optionExplanations.3: CH₃NH₂ is an amine (−NH₂ group).

shortExplanation: An alkyne has a carbon–carbon triple bond; C₂H₂ (acetylene) has one.
solutionSteps: Alkynes contain a C≡C triple bond with formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
For n = 2, that gives C₂H₂.
Therefore C₂H₂ is the alkyne.
keyConcept: Alkynes contain a carbon–carbon triple bond (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
commonMistake: Confusing the double-bonded alkene C₂H₄ with the triple-bonded alkyne.

optionExplanations.1: C₂H₄ (ethene) has a double bond, making it an alkene.
optionExplanations.2: CH₄ (methane) has only single bonds, an alkane.
optionExplanations.3: C₂H₆ (ethane) has only single bonds, an alkane.

formulaNotes: Alkyne general formula: CnH(2n−2); C2H2 fits

shortExplanation: A saturated hydrocarbon has only single bonds; ethane (C₂H₆) qualifies.
solutionSteps: Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) contain only C–C single bonds.
Ethane, C₂H₆, has only single bonds.
Therefore ethane is the saturated hydrocarbon.
keyConcept: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single carbon–carbon bonds.
commonMistake: Calling benzene saturated; its ring has delocalized unsaturation.

optionExplanations.0: Ethene has a C=C double bond, so it is unsaturated.
optionExplanations.1: Ethyne has a C≡C triple bond, so it is unsaturated.
optionExplanations.3: Benzene has delocalized double bonds and is unsaturated.

shortExplanation: A single compound breaking into two products, AB → A + B, is a decomposition reaction.
solutionSteps: Identify one reactant splitting into multiple products.
AB → A + B goes from one compound to two simpler substances.
This pattern defines a decomposition reaction.
keyConcept: Decomposition breaks one compound into two or more products.
commonMistake: Reversing it with synthesis, which combines substances into one.

optionExplanations.0: Synthesis is the opposite: A + B → AB.
optionExplanations.2: Combustion requires reaction with oxygen, producing oxides.
optionExplanations.3: Neutralization is an acid–base reaction forming salt and water.

shortExplanation: Isobutane shares butane's formula C₄H₁₀ but has a branched structure, making it a structural isomer.
solutionSteps: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity.
Isobutane also has the formula C₄H₁₀.
Its branched arrangement differs from straight-chain butane, so it is an isomer.
keyConcept: Structural isomers share a molecular formula but differ in atom arrangement.
commonMistake: Choosing propane or pentane, which have different molecular formulas.

optionExplanations.0: Propane is C₃H₈, a different formula.
optionExplanations.1: Cyclobutane is C₄H₈, so it is not an isomer of C₄H₁₀.
optionExplanations.3: Pentane is C₅H₁₂, a different formula.

shortExplanation: A carboxylic acid contains the −COOH group; CH₃COOH (acetic acid) has it.
solutionSteps: Carboxylic acids carry the −COOH (carboxyl) functional group.
CH₃COOH ends in −COOH.
Therefore CH₃COOH is the carboxylic acid.
keyConcept: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group −COOH.
commonMistake: Confusing the −OH of an alcohol or the C=O of a ketone with the carboxyl group.

optionExplanations.1: CH₄ is methane, a hydrocarbon with no functional group.
optionExplanations.2: CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol (−OH), not a carboxylic acid.
optionExplanations.3: CH₃COCH₃ is a ketone (C=O between carbons).

shortExplanation: Silver chloride (AgCl) is essentially insoluble in water, unlike the other listed compounds.
solutionSteps: Most chlorides are soluble, but silver chloride is a notable exception.
NaCl, HCl, and NaOH all dissolve readily in water.
AgCl precipitates and is insoluble, so it is the answer.
keyConcept: AgCl is an insoluble chloride (a classic solubility-rule exception).
commonMistake: Assuming all chlorides are soluble and overlooking the silver-halide exception.

optionExplanations.0: NaCl is highly soluble in water.
optionExplanations.2: HCl dissolves completely, forming a strong acid solution.
optionExplanations.3: NaOH is very soluble, giving a strongly basic solution.

shortExplanation: A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidized. H2 readily gives up electrons (its H is oxidized from 0 to +1), so it acts as a reducer.
solutionSteps: A reducing agent supplies electrons to another species and gets oxidized in the process.
H2 has hydrogen in oxidation state 0 and can be oxidized to +1, releasing electrons.
O2, Cl2 and CO2 tend to gain electrons (they oxidize others), so they are oxidizing agents.
keyConcept: Reducing agent = electron donor = the species that gets oxidized.
commonMistake: Confusing reducing agent with oxidizing agent (the reducer is oxidized, not reduced).

optionExplanations.0: O2 is a strong oxidizer that gains electrons; it oxidizes others rather than reducing them.
optionExplanations.1: Cl2 readily accepts electrons to form Cl-, making it an oxidizing agent.
optionExplanations.3: In CO2 carbon is already at its highest common oxidation state (+4), so it acts as an oxidizer, not a reducer.

shortExplanation: The cathode is where reduction occurs. Na+ ions gain electrons at the cathode and are reduced to sodium metal.
solutionSteps: In electrolysis, reduction happens at the cathode (negative electrode).
Molten NaCl provides free Na+ and Cl- ions.
Na+ + e- -> Na, so solid sodium metal deposits at the cathode.
Cl- is oxidized to Cl2 gas at the anode instead.
keyConcept: Cathode = reduction; cations are reduced there.
commonMistake: Placing chlorine at the cathode; chlorine forms at the anode by oxidation.

optionExplanations.0: Na+ is the ion that arrives at the cathode, but the product formed is the neutral metal, not the ion.
optionExplanations.2: Cl- migrates toward the anode, not the cathode.
optionExplanations.3: Cl2 gas is produced at the anode by oxidation of Cl-, not at the cathode.

formulaNotes: Cathode reduction: Na+ + e- -> Na. Anode oxidation: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-.

shortExplanation: A redox reaction involves changes in oxidation states. NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O is a simple acid-base neutralization with no change in any oxidation number.
solutionSteps: Check oxidation-state changes in each reaction.
NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O: Na stays +1, Cl stays -1, O stays -2, H stays +1 — no change.
The other three all show clear oxidation-state changes (metal oxidized, nonmetal reduced).
Therefore the neutralization is the non-redox reaction.
keyConcept: Redox requires a change in oxidation number; neutralization does not.
commonMistake: Assuming any reaction that forms water or a salt must be redox.

optionExplanations.0: Zn is oxidized (0 to +2) and Cu2+ is reduced (+2 to 0), so this is redox.
optionExplanations.2: Fe is oxidized (0 to +3) and O is reduced (0 to -2), so this is redox.
optionExplanations.3: H2 (0 to +1) and Cl2 (0 to -1) both change oxidation state, so this is redox.

shortExplanation: Carbon in methane forms four equivalent single bonds arranged tetrahedrally, which requires sp3 hybridization.
solutionSteps: Count electron domains around carbon: four bonding pairs (to four H), no lone pairs.
Four equivalent domains require mixing one s and three p orbitals.
This gives four sp3 hybrid orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron.
keyConcept: Four sigma bonds and no lone pairs -> sp3 hybridization.
commonMistake: Counting fewer domains and choosing sp or sp2.

optionExplanations.0: sp gives only two hybrid orbitals (linear), too few for four bonds.
optionExplanations.1: sp2 gives three hybrid orbitals (trigonal planar), too few for four bonds.
optionExplanations.3: sp2d is not the hybridization for a simple four-coordinate carbon; carbon does not use d orbitals here.

shortExplanation: Methane is tetrahedral with four equivalent C-H bonds, giving the characteristic tetrahedral bond angle of 109.5 degrees.
solutionSteps: CH4 has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs on carbon.
Four equal electron domains spread out maximally into a tetrahedron.
The ideal tetrahedral angle between bonds is 109.5 degrees.
keyConcept: Ideal tetrahedral geometry has 109.5 degree bond angles.
commonMistake: Guessing 90 degrees from a square-drawn structure instead of the real 3D tetrahedron.

optionExplanations.0: 90 degrees corresponds to octahedral or square-planar arrangements, not tetrahedral CH4.
optionExplanations.2: 120 degrees is the trigonal planar angle (sp2), not tetrahedral.
optionExplanations.3: 180 degrees is the linear angle (sp), not tetrahedral.

shortExplanation: Methane (CH4) has four C-H single bonds and nothing else. The other choices all contain at least one multiple bond.
solutionSteps: Examine bonding in each molecule.
CH4: only four single C-H bonds.
C2H4 has a C=C double bond, C2H2 has a C triple bond C, CO2 has two C=O double bonds.
Only CH4 is entirely single-bonded.
keyConcept: Saturated single-bonded molecules contain no double or triple bonds.
commonMistake: Overlooking the multiple bonds implied by low H:C ratios in C2H4 and C2H2.

optionExplanations.0: C2H4 (ethene) contains a carbon-carbon double bond.
optionExplanations.2: C2H2 (ethyne) contains a carbon-carbon triple bond.
optionExplanations.3: CO2 contains two carbon-oxygen double bonds.

shortExplanation: CO2 has two double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon, giving a linear O=C=O geometry with a 180 degree angle.
solutionSteps: Carbon in CO2 has two electron domains (two double bonds), no lone pairs.
Two domains arrange linearly at 180 degrees.
The other molecules have lone pairs or four bonds that bend or pyramidalize them.
keyConcept: Two electron domains with no lone pairs give linear geometry.
commonMistake: Assuming any small triatomic molecule (like H2O) is linear.

optionExplanations.0: CH4 is tetrahedral, not linear.
optionExplanations.1: H2O is bent (about 104.5 degrees) because oxygen has two lone pairs.
optionExplanations.3: NH3 is trigonal pyramidal due to nitrogen's lone pair.

shortExplanation: Dividing the subscripts of C6H12O6 by their greatest common factor (6) gives the simplest whole-number ratio CH2O.
solutionSteps: Take the ratio C:H:O = 6:12:6.
Divide each by the GCD, which is 6.
This yields 1:2:1, i.e., CH2O.
keyConcept: Empirical formula is the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms.
commonMistake: Dividing by a smaller factor and stopping at C3H6O3 or C2H4O2.

optionExplanations.0: CHO gives a 1:1:1 ratio, but glucose's H:C ratio is 2:1, so this is wrong.
optionExplanations.1: C3H6O3 comes from dividing by only 2 and is not the simplest ratio.
optionExplanations.2: C2H4O2 comes from dividing by only 3 and is not fully reduced.

shortExplanation: Nitrogen forms three N-H bonds in ammonia, so its valency (combining capacity) is 3.
solutionSteps: Count the bonds nitrogen forms in NH3: three, one to each hydrogen.
Valency equals the number of bonds an atom forms.
Therefore nitrogen's valency is 3 (it also keeps one lone pair).
keyConcept: Valency = number of bonds an atom forms with other atoms.
commonMistake: Confusing valency (3) with nitrogen's group number or its max oxidation state (5).

optionExplanations.0: A valency of 1 would mean only one N-H bond, but NH3 has three.
optionExplanations.1: A valency of 2 would give NH2, not NH3.
optionExplanations.3: 5 is nitrogen's maximum oxidation state (e.g., in HNO3), not its valency in NH3.

shortExplanation: CH4 is nonpolar with no hydrogen bonded to N, O or F, so its only intermolecular attraction is weak London dispersion forces.
solutionSteps: Determine polarity: CH4 is symmetric and nonpolar (no net dipole).
Hydrogen bonding needs H on N, O or F — methane has none.
Nonpolar molecules attract only through temporary induced dipoles: London dispersion forces.
keyConcept: Nonpolar molecules interact only via London dispersion forces.
commonMistake: Assuming any molecule with hydrogen can hydrogen bond.

optionExplanations.0: Hydrogen bonds require H attached to N, O or F, which CH4 lacks.
optionExplanations.1: Ionic bonds are intramolecular attractions in ionic compounds, not present in molecular CH4.
optionExplanations.2: Dipole-dipole forces require a permanent dipole, but CH4 is nonpolar.

shortExplanation: A Lewis base donates an electron pair. NH3 has a lone pair on nitrogen that it can donate, so it is a Lewis base.
solutionSteps: A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor; a Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor.
NH3 has a lone pair on nitrogen available for donation.
AlCl3 and BF3 have electron-deficient central atoms and accept pairs (Lewis acids); HCl donates H+ (Bronsted acid).
keyConcept: Lewis base = electron-pair donor (has an available lone pair).
commonMistake: Thinking NH3 must be an acid because it contains hydrogen.

optionExplanations.0: HCl donates a proton, acting as an acid, not an electron-pair donor.
optionExplanations.1: AlCl3 has an electron-deficient aluminum and accepts electron pairs (Lewis acid).
optionExplanations.3: BF3 has an electron-deficient boron and accepts electron pairs (Lewis acid).

shortExplanation: Ethene (C2H4) contains one carbon-carbon double bond; the other options have only single bonds or a triple bond.
solutionSteps: Compare the H:C ratios to infer bonding.
C2H4 has the formula of an alkene, requiring one C=C double bond.
CH4 and CH3CH3 are fully saturated (single bonds); C2H2 has a triple bond.
keyConcept: Alkenes (CnH2n) contain exactly one carbon-carbon double bond.
commonMistake: Confusing the double bond of C2H4 with the triple bond of C2H2.

optionExplanations.0: CH4 has only single C-H bonds.
optionExplanations.1: C2H2 (ethyne) has a carbon-carbon triple bond, not a double bond.
optionExplanations.3: CH3CH3 (ethane) is fully saturated with single bonds only.

shortExplanation: CH4 is nonpolar with only weak London dispersion forces, so it has the lowest boiling point; the others hydrogen bond.
solutionSteps: Identify intermolecular forces: H2O, CH3OH and NH3 all form hydrogen bonds.
CH4 is nonpolar and has only weak London dispersion forces.
Weaker intermolecular forces mean the lowest energy needed to boil, so CH4 boils lowest.
keyConcept: Weaker intermolecular forces give a lower boiling point.
commonMistake: Choosing by molar mass instead of by the strength of intermolecular forces.

optionExplanations.0: H2O has strong, extensive hydrogen bonding and a high boiling point (100 C).
optionExplanations.2: CH3OH hydrogen bonds through its -OH group, raising its boiling point well above CH4.
optionExplanations.3: NH3 hydrogen bonds through N-H, giving a higher boiling point than CH4.

shortExplanation: A trivalent ion carries a 3+ (or 3-) charge. Al3+ has a charge of 3+, making it trivalent.
solutionSteps: Trivalent means an ionic charge magnitude of 3.
Read the charges: Na+ is 1, Ca2+ is 2, Al3+ is 3, Fe2+ is 2.
Al3+ is the only ion with charge 3.
keyConcept: Valency of an ion equals the magnitude of its charge.
commonMistake: Confusing group number with ionic charge for transition metals like iron.

optionExplanations.0: Na+ is monovalent (charge 1+).
optionExplanations.1: Ca2+ is divalent (charge 2+).
optionExplanations.3: Fe2+ shown here is divalent (charge 2+); iron can be 3+ but this ion is written as 2+.

shortExplanation: Molarity is moles of solute divided by liters of solution: 2 mol / 1 L = 2 M.
solutionSteps: Write M = moles of solute / volume in liters.
Substitute: 2 mol / 1 L.
The result is 2 M.
keyConcept: Molarity (M) = moles of solute per liter of solution.
commonMistake: Dividing volume by moles instead of moles by volume.

optionExplanations.0: 0.5 M would require only 0.5 mol in 1 L (or 2 mol in 4 L).
optionExplanations.1: 1 M would require 1 mol in 1 L, but there are 2 mol.
optionExplanations.3: 3 M would require 3 mol in 1 L.

formulaNotes: M = n / V = 2 mol / 1 L = 2 mol/L.

shortExplanation: Alkyl halides have a polar C-X bond that makes the carbon electrophilic, so nucleophiles readily displace the leaving halide in nucleophilic substitution.
solutionSteps: Nucleophilic substitution needs a good leaving group and an electrophilic carbon.
In alkyl halides the electronegative halogen polarizes the C-X bond, leaving carbon partially positive.
A nucleophile attacks that carbon and displaces the halide ion.
keyConcept: Alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution via their polar C-X bond and halide leaving group.
commonMistake: Assuming alkenes (which undergo electrophilic addition) do nucleophilic substitution.

optionExplanations.0: Alkanes are unreactive toward nucleophiles (they undergo radical substitution, not nucleophilic).
optionExplanations.1: Aromatics typically undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution, not simple nucleophilic substitution.
optionExplanations.3: Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition across the double bond, not nucleophilic substitution.

shortExplanation: Nitrogen exists naturally as the diatomic molecule N2 under standard conditions.
solutionSteps: Recall which elements are diatomic gases: H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2 (plus Br2, I2).
N2 fits this list.
Na is a metallic solid, He is a monatomic noble gas, and C is a solid network/allotrope — none are diatomic.
keyConcept: Nitrogen is one of the diatomic elements (N2) at standard conditions.
commonMistake: Assuming metals or noble gases form diatomic molecules.

optionExplanations.1: Na is a metallic solid, not a diatomic molecule.
optionExplanations.2: He is a monatomic noble gas that does not form molecules.
optionExplanations.3: Carbon exists as solid allotropes (graphite, diamond), not as a diatomic gas.

shortExplanation: A reactive metal reacting with a dilute acid displaces hydrogen, producing hydrogen gas (H2).
solutionSteps: General reaction: metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen gas.
The metal reduces H+ from the acid to H2.
Example: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.
keyConcept: Metal + acid -> salt + H2 gas.
commonMistake: Confusing this with metal + acid producing CO2 (that is carbonate + acid).

optionExplanations.0: CO2 comes from acid reacting with a carbonate, not a metal.
optionExplanations.1: O2 is not released in acid-metal reactions.
optionExplanations.3: N2 is not a product of typical acid-metal reactions.

shortExplanation: A secondary alcohol has its -OH on a carbon bonded to two other carbons. In (CH3)2CHOH the OH-bearing carbon is attached to two methyl groups.
solutionSteps: Classify by counting carbons attached to the carbon bearing the -OH group.
(CH3)2CHOH: the OH carbon is bonded to two CH3 groups -> secondary.
CH3CH2OH and CH3CH2CH2OH are primary (OH carbon bonded to one carbon); CH3OH is methanol (no adjacent carbon).
keyConcept: Secondary alcohol: -OH on a carbon attached to two other carbons.
commonMistake: Classifying by total carbon count instead of by the carbons on the OH-bearing carbon.

optionExplanations.0: CH3CH2OH (ethanol) is primary; its OH carbon touches only one other carbon.
optionExplanations.2: CH3OH (methanol) has its OH carbon bonded to no other carbon.
optionExplanations.3: CH3CH2CH2OH (1-propanol) is primary; its OH carbon touches only one other carbon.

shortExplanation: Amines are characterized by the amino functional group, -NH2 (a nitrogen bearing hydrogens).
solutionSteps: Match each group to its class: -OH is alcohol, -NH2 is amine, -COOH is carboxylic acid, -CHO is aldehyde.
The defining group of amines is the nitrogen-containing amino group.
Therefore -NH2 is the amine functional group.
keyConcept: Amines contain the amino group -NH2.
commonMistake: Confusing the amine group with the amide (-CONH2) or other N-containing groups.

optionExplanations.0: -OH is the hydroxyl group of alcohols.
optionExplanations.2: -COOH is the carboxyl group of carboxylic acids.
optionExplanations.3: -CHO is the aldehyde group.

shortExplanation: Ethyne (C2H2) contains a carbon-carbon triple bond, as required by its formula CnH2n-2 with two carbons.
solutionSteps: Assess the degree of unsaturation from each formula.
C2H2 has only two hydrogens for two carbons, forcing a triple bond between the carbons.
CH4 is saturated, C2H4 has a double bond, and C6H6 (benzene) has delocalized/alternating bonds but no isolated triple bond.
keyConcept: Alkynes (CnH2n-2) contain a carbon-carbon triple bond.
commonMistake: Confusing the triple bond of C2H2 with the double bond of C2H4.

optionExplanations.0: CH4 is fully saturated with single bonds.
optionExplanations.2: C2H4 (ethene) has a double bond, not a triple bond.
optionExplanations.3: C6H6 (benzene) has aromatic delocalized bonding, not a triple bond.

shortExplanation: Stronger intermolecular attractions raise boiling point. Hydrogen bonding is a strong intermolecular force, so it increases boiling point.
solutionSteps: Boiling point rises when intermolecular forces are stronger.
Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole interaction that holds molecules together tightly.
Lower mass, more branching and shorter chains all reduce intermolecular contact and lower boiling point.
keyConcept: Stronger intermolecular forces (like hydrogen bonding) raise the boiling point.
commonMistake: Thinking branching raises boiling point; branching reduces surface contact and lowers it.

optionExplanations.0: Lower mass means weaker dispersion forces, lowering the boiling point.
optionExplanations.2: More branching reduces molecular surface contact and lowers the boiling point.
optionExplanations.3: Shorter chains have less surface area and weaker dispersion forces, lowering boiling point.

shortExplanation: A nucleophile is electron-rich and donates an electron pair. Cl- carries a negative charge and a lone pair, so it acts as a nucleophile.
solutionSteps: Nucleophiles are electron-rich species (often negative) that attack electron-poor centers.
Cl- has a full negative charge and available lone pairs.
H+, Na+ and Fe3+ are electron-poor cations (electrophiles/Lewis acids), not nucleophiles.
keyConcept: Nucleophile = electron-rich, electron-pair donor.
commonMistake: Treating positively charged ions as nucleophiles; positives are electrophiles.

optionExplanations.0: H+ is a bare proton with no electrons to donate; it is an electrophile.
optionExplanations.2: Na+ is a positive cation lacking available electron pairs to donate.
optionExplanations.3: Fe3+ is a highly positive cation that accepts electron pairs (a Lewis acid), not a nucleophile.

shortExplanation: Three bonding pairs plus one lone pair give four electron domains (tetrahedral electron geometry) but a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape, like NH3.
solutionSteps: Total electron domains = 3 bonding + 1 lone = 4, so electron geometry is tetrahedral.
The lone pair occupies one corner and is not counted in molecular shape.
The three bonded atoms form a pyramid: trigonal pyramidal (e.g., NH3).
keyConcept: AX3E (3 bonding, 1 lone pair) gives trigonal pyramidal shape.
commonMistake: Calling it trigonal planar and ignoring the lone pair's effect on shape.

optionExplanations.0: Linear corresponds to two domains, not four.
optionExplanations.1: Tetrahedral is the electron-domain geometry, but the molecular shape with one lone pair is pyramidal.
optionExplanations.3: Trigonal planar (AX3, no lone pair) would apply only if there were no lone pair.

shortExplanation: A diprotic acid can donate two protons. H2SO4 has two ionizable hydrogens, making it diprotic.
solutionSteps: Count ionizable (acidic) hydrogens per molecule.
H2SO4 releases two H+ ions (to HSO4- then SO4^2-), so it is diprotic.
HCl, HNO3 and CH3COOH each donate only one proton (monoprotic).
keyConcept: Diprotic acid donates two protons per molecule.
commonMistake: Counting all hydrogens in acetic acid; only the -COOH hydrogen is acidic, so it is monoprotic.

optionExplanations.0: HCl donates only one proton (monoprotic).
optionExplanations.1: HNO3 donates only one proton (monoprotic).
optionExplanations.3: CH3COOH has only one acidic (carboxyl) hydrogen, so it is monoprotic.

shortExplanation: Boiling water absorbs heat to break intermolecular attractions and convert liquid to vapor, so it is endothermic.
solutionSteps: Endothermic means the process absorbs heat from its surroundings.
Boiling requires continuous heat input to change liquid into gas, so it absorbs energy.
The other choices all release heat, making them exothermic.
keyConcept: Endothermic processes absorb heat; a phase change from liquid to gas requires energy input.
commonMistake: Assuming any reaction involving heat must be exothermic, ignoring the direction of heat flow.

optionExplanations.0: Combustion releases large amounts of heat and is strongly exothermic.
optionExplanations.2: Freezing releases heat as particles form an ordered solid, so it is exothermic.
optionExplanations.3: Condensation releases heat as vapor becomes liquid, so it is exothermic.

shortExplanation: Both colloids and true solutions have particles small enough to stay dispersed and never settle out, so both qualify.
solutionSteps: A suspension has large particles that settle under gravity over time.
A colloid has intermediate particles that remain dispersed and do not settle.
A solution has dissolved particles at the molecular level that never settle.
Since both colloids and solutions resist settling, the combined choice is correct.
keyConcept: Particle size determines settling: only suspensions settle, while colloids and solutions stay dispersed.
commonMistake: Picking only colloid and forgetting that true solutions also never settle.

optionExplanations.0: A suspension is exactly the mixture whose particles do settle out.
optionExplanations.1: Colloids do not settle, but this is incomplete because solutions also qualify.
optionExplanations.2: Solutions do not settle, but this alone omits colloids, which also qualify.

shortExplanation: Helium has 2 electrons that completely fill its only (first) shell, giving it a full outer shell like a noble gas.
solutionSteps: The first electron shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons.
Helium has exactly 2 electrons, filling that shell completely.
This full outer shell explains helium's chemical inertness.
keyConcept: A full outer shell (noble-gas configuration) makes an element stable and unreactive.
commonMistake: Assuming a full outer shell always needs 8 electrons, forgetting the first shell is complete at 2.

optionExplanations.1: Fluorine has 7 outer electrons and needs one more to complete its shell.
optionExplanations.2: Chlorine has 7 outer electrons and is one short of a full shell.
optionExplanations.3: Carbon has 4 outer electrons, only half-filling its outer shell.

shortExplanation: Hydrolysis of an ester cleaves the C-O bond, regenerating the parent alcohol and carboxylic acid.
solutionSteps: An ester is formed from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol with loss of water.
Hydrolysis reverses this by adding water across the ester linkage.
The products are the carboxylic acid and the alcohol that originally combined.
keyConcept: Ester hydrolysis is the reverse of esterification, yielding a carboxylic acid plus an alcohol.
commonMistake: Confusing ester hydrolysis with reduction or with amide chemistry.

optionExplanations.1: Ketone plus water is not produced; esters do not hydrolyze to ketones.
optionExplanations.2: No ketone forms in ester hydrolysis; the product is a carboxylic acid.
optionExplanations.3: Amides come from amines and acids, not from ester hydrolysis.

shortExplanation: Magnesium is in Group 2 of the periodic table, so it has 2 valence electrons.
solutionSteps: The group number for main-group elements gives the number of valence electrons.
Magnesium is in Group 2 (alkaline earth metals).
Therefore magnesium has 2 valence electrons.
keyConcept: For main-group elements, the group number equals the number of valence electrons.
commonMistake: Confusing total electrons with valence electrons, or misreading the element's group.

optionExplanations.0: Oxygen is in Group 16 and has 6 valence electrons.
optionExplanations.2: Nitrogen is in Group 15 and has 5 valence electrons.
optionExplanations.3: Chlorine is in Group 17 and has 7 valence electrons.

shortExplanation: Salt fully dissolves in water to give a single uniform phase, making salt water a homogeneous mixture.
solutionSteps: Homogeneous means uniform composition throughout with one visible phase.
Dissolved salt distributes evenly at the molecular level in water.
The result is one uniform solution, which is homogeneous.
keyConcept: Homogeneous mixtures (solutions) have uniform composition and a single phase throughout.
commonMistake: Assuming any liquid mixture is homogeneous, even when phases separate or particles remain visible.

optionExplanations.0: Oil and water separate into two distinct layers, so the mixture is heterogeneous.
optionExplanations.2: Sand and iron are visibly distinct solids, forming a heterogeneous mixture.
optionExplanations.3: Smoke contains suspended solid particles in gas, making it heterogeneous.

shortExplanation: Removing one proton from H2CO3 gives HCO3-, its conjugate base.
solutionSteps: A conjugate base is formed by removing one H+ from an acid.
H2CO3 loses one H+ to become HCO3-.
HCO3- is therefore the conjugate base of carbonic acid.
keyConcept: The conjugate base has exactly one fewer proton than its acid.
commonMistake: Removing two protons and choosing the carbonate ion instead of the bicarbonate ion.

optionExplanations.0: CO3^2- is the conjugate base of HCO3-, formed by losing a second proton.
optionExplanations.2: H2O is a product of neutralization, not the direct conjugate base of H2CO3.
optionExplanations.3: OH- is the conjugate base of water, unrelated to carbonic acid.

shortExplanation: Chlorine belongs to Group 17, the halogens.
solutionSteps: Halogens are the Group 17 elements: F, Cl, Br, I, At.
Chlorine (Cl) is in Group 17.
Therefore chlorine is the halogen among the choices.
keyConcept: Halogens are the Group 17 nonmetals with 7 valence electrons.
commonMistake: Confusing halogens with other reactive nonmetals such as oxygen or sulfur.

optionExplanations.0: Oxygen is in Group 16 (chalcogens), not a halogen.
optionExplanations.2: Sulfur is in Group 16, not a halogen.
optionExplanations.3: Potassium is a Group 1 alkali metal, not a halogen.

shortExplanation: A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular attraction, much weaker than the true chemical bonds listed.
solutionSteps: Covalent, ionic, and metallic bonds are strong primary chemical bonds.
A hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force between molecules.
It is far weaker than the primary bonds, so it is the weakest type here.
keyConcept: Intermolecular forces like hydrogen bonds are weaker than primary chemical bonds.
commonMistake: Treating a hydrogen bond as a strong chemical bond rather than an intermolecular attraction.

optionExplanations.0: Covalent bonds involve shared electron pairs and are strong.
optionExplanations.1: Ionic bonds arise from strong electrostatic attraction between ions.
optionExplanations.3: Metallic bonding gives strong cohesion in metals.

shortExplanation: Covalent bonds form when two nonmetals share electron pairs.
solutionSteps: Nonmetals have high electronegativity and tend to share electrons rather than transfer them.
Sharing electron pairs between nonmetal atoms creates a covalent bond.
Therefore covalent bonds form between nonmetals.
keyConcept: Covalent bonding is electron sharing, typically between two nonmetals.
commonMistake: Confusing electron sharing (covalent) with electron transfer between a metal and nonmetal (ionic).

optionExplanations.0: Metals bond to one another through metallic bonding, not covalent bonding.
optionExplanations.2: A metal and nonmetal typically form an ionic bond by electron transfer.
optionExplanations.3: Ions attract electrostatically in ionic bonds, not by covalent sharing.

shortExplanation: Copper is a d-block element, making it a transition metal.
solutionSteps: Transition metals occupy the d-block of the periodic table.
Copper (Cu) lies in the d-block with a partially filled d subshell.
Therefore copper is the transition metal.
keyConcept: Transition metals are d-block elements with characteristic variable oxidation states.
commonMistake: Assuming any metal is a transition metal, even main-group metals like Na, Mg, and Al.

optionExplanations.0: Sodium is a Group 1 alkali metal, not a transition metal.
optionExplanations.1: Aluminium is a Group 13 main-group metal, not a transition metal.
optionExplanations.3: Magnesium is a Group 2 alkaline earth metal, not a transition metal.

shortExplanation: CO2 has two double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon, giving a linear 180-degree geometry.
solutionSteps: Carbon in CO2 is bonded to two oxygen atoms and has no lone pairs.
Two electron domains arrange to minimize repulsion at 180 degrees.
This gives a linear molecular shape.
keyConcept: Two electron domains with no lone pairs on the central atom give a linear shape.
commonMistake: Assuming CO2 is bent like water; unlike O in water, carbon here has no lone pairs.

optionExplanations.0: A bent shape requires lone pairs on the central atom, which CO2 lacks.
optionExplanations.1: Tetrahedral geometry needs four electron domains, but CO2 has only two.
optionExplanations.3: Trigonal geometry needs three domains around the central atom.

shortExplanation: Losing one negative electron leaves sodium with a net charge of +1, forming Na+.
solutionSteps: A neutral sodium atom has equal protons and electrons.
Removing one electron leaves one more proton than electrons.
The resulting ion has a +1 charge, written Na+.
keyConcept: Losing an electron gives a cation with a positive charge equal to electrons lost.
commonMistake: Reversing the sign and writing Na- after loss of an electron.

optionExplanations.0: Na- would require gaining an electron, not losing one.
optionExplanations.2: Na2+ would require losing two electrons, but only one is lost.
optionExplanations.3: Losing an electron changes the charge, so the atom is no longer neutral.

shortExplanation: Freezing releases heat as particles arrange into an ordered solid, so it is exothermic.
solutionSteps: Exothermic means the process releases heat to its surroundings.
During freezing, particles lose energy and form an ordered solid, releasing heat.
Therefore freezing is exothermic.
keyConcept: Exothermic processes release heat; forming a more ordered state releases energy.
commonMistake: Assuming freezing absorbs energy because it happens at low temperature.

optionExplanations.0: Photosynthesis absorbs light energy and is endothermic.
optionExplanations.1: Boiling water absorbs heat and is endothermic.
optionExplanations.3: Electrolysis requires electrical energy input and is endothermic.

shortExplanation: Acetylene (C2H2) has a carbon-carbon triple bond, so each carbon is sp hybridized.
solutionSteps: Count electron domains on each carbon to assign hybridization.
In C2H2 each carbon bonds to one H and triple-bonds to the other carbon: two sigma domains.
Two sigma domains correspond to sp hybridization.
keyConcept: Two sigma-bond domains (a triple bond plus one single bond) give sp hybridization.
commonMistake: Counting the extra pi bonds as separate domains, which would misassign the hybridization.

optionExplanations.0: CH4 has four sigma bonds, giving sp3 hybridization.
