shortExplanation: A plane mirror always produces a virtual, upright, same-size image behind the mirror.
solutionSteps: Reflected rays only appear to diverge from behind the mirror, so the image is virtual.
The image is the same way up as the object, hence upright.
It is also the same size and laterally inverted, but among the options it is virtual and upright.
keyConcept: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright, same-size image.
commonMistake: Calling the image real or inverted; plane-mirror images are virtual and upright.

optionExplanations.0: A plane mirror image is not real and not vertically inverted.
optionExplanations.2: The image is not real; reflected rays do not actually converge.
optionExplanations.3: A plane mirror does not magnify; the image is the same size.

shortExplanation: Snell's law gives sin(θ2) = sin(40°)/1.33 = 0.483, so θ2 ≈ 28.9°.
solutionSteps: n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2).
keyConcept: Entering a denser medium bends light toward the normal.
commonMistake: Using the wrong index in the numerator or skipping the arcsine.

optionExplanations.1: 31.2° overestimates the refracted angle.
optionExplanations.2: 33.5° does not satisfy Snell's law for n = 1.33.
optionExplanations.4: 38.1° is close to the incident angle, implying too little bending.

shortExplanation: Using the 1D elastic-collision formula, the 2 kg mass finishes at v1 = (1/3)(4) + (2/3)(2) = 2.67 m/s.
solutionSteps: For elastic collision: v1' = ((m1-m2)/(m1+m2))*u1 + (2*m2/(m1+m2))*u2.
keyConcept: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy.
commonMistake: Assuming the masses simply swap or stick together.

optionExplanations.0: 2 m/s ignores that the 2 kg mass keeps some forward speed.
optionExplanations.2: 3.33 m/s overestimates the final speed of the heavier mass.
optionExplanations.3: 4 m/s would mean no interaction occurred.

shortExplanation: The splitting of white light into its component colors by a prism is called dispersion.
solutionSteps: Different wavelengths refract by different amounts in the glass.
This wavelength-dependent bending separates the colors, a process called dispersion.
keyConcept: Dispersion is the separation of light into colors by wavelength-dependent refraction.
commonMistake: Calling it plain refraction; dispersion is refraction that varies with wavelength.

optionExplanations.0: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, not splitting into colors.
optionExplanations.1: Diffraction is bending around obstacles, not the prism color split.
optionExplanations.2: Refraction is the underlying cause, but the color-splitting phenomenon is named dispersion.

shortExplanation: Frequency f = v/λ = 300/1.5 = 200 Hz.
solutionSteps: Use v = f*λ, so f = v/λ.
keyConcept: Frequency equals wave speed divided by wavelength.
commonMistake: Multiplying speed and wavelength instead of dividing.

optionExplanations.0: 100 Hz would need λ = 3 m.
optionExplanations.1: 150 Hz would need λ = 2 m.
optionExplanations.4: 300 Hz would need λ = 1 m.

shortExplanation: A real image twice the size means image distance v = 2u = 60 cm; then 1/f = 1/60 + 1/30 gives f = 20 cm.
solutionSteps: Real image magnitude 2 means v = 2*u = 2*30 = 60 cm.
Lens equation: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = 1/60 + 1/30.
keyConcept: Magnification |m| = v/u links image and object distances for a lens.
commonMistake: Setting v = u/2 instead of v = 2u for a magnified real image.

optionExplanations.0: 10 cm would come from mismatched distances.
optionExplanations.1: 15 cm results from using v = 30 cm rather than 60 cm.
optionExplanations.4: 30 cm equals the object distance, not the focal length.

shortExplanation: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J).
solutionSteps: Energy and work share the unit joule, defined as 1 N·m.
keyConcept: Energy is measured in joules.
commonMistake: Confusing energy (joule) with power (watt) or force (newton).

optionExplanations.0: The watt is the unit of power (energy per unit time).
optionExplanations.1: The newton is the unit of force.
optionExplanations.3: The volt is the unit of electric potential.

shortExplanation: Gamma rays have the highest frequency and shortest wavelength, so they carry the highest photon energy of the listed bands.
solutionSteps: Photon energy E = h*f increases with frequency.
Gamma rays have the highest frequency among these, hence the highest energy.
keyConcept: Higher frequency means higher photon energy (E = h*f).
commonMistake: Picking ultraviolet, which is energetic but far below gamma rays.

optionExplanations.0: Infrared is lower frequency than visible light, so low energy.
optionExplanations.1: Radio waves have the lowest frequency and least energy.
optionExplanations.2: Ultraviolet is energetic but lower than gamma rays.

shortExplanation: With object at 50 cm and f = 25 cm (object at 2f), the image forms at 50 cm and magnification = v/u = 1.0.
solutionSteps: Lens equation: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, so 1/25 = 1/v + 1/50.
Magnification |m| = v/u = 50/50 = 1.0.
keyConcept: An object at 2f of a convex lens forms an equal-size image at 2f.
commonMistake: Assuming an object beyond f is always magnified; at 2f the size is unchanged.

optionExplanations.0: 0.33 would require a much farther object.
optionExplanations.2: 1.5 does not match v = 50 cm.
optionExplanations.3: 2.0 would need the object at 1.5f.

shortExplanation: Equilibrium means no net force and no net torque, so the vector sum of all forces is zero and the object stays at rest or moves at constant velocity.
solutionSteps: Equilibrium is defined by the absence of acceleration.
By Newton's second law F = ma, zero acceleration requires zero net force.
Therefore the net force must be exactly zero.
keyConcept: In equilibrium the vector sum of all forces (the net force) is zero.
commonMistake: Confusing 'zero net force' with 'no forces at all' — individual forces exist but cancel.

optionExplanations.1: Weight is only one force; equilibrium requires it be balanced by an equal opposing force, not that the net equals the weight.
optionExplanations.2: A maximum net force would produce maximum acceleration, the opposite of equilibrium.
optionExplanations.3: A changing net force implies changing acceleration, which is not equilibrium.

shortExplanation: A derived unit is built from combinations of base units; the newton is kg*m/s^2, a combination of base units.
solutionSteps: Identify the SI base units: second, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela, metre.
Second, kilogram and ampere are all base units.
The newton equals kg*m/s^2, so it is derived from base units.
keyConcept: Derived units are products/quotients of the seven SI base units.
commonMistake: Assuming any named unit is fundamental; the newton is defined through kg, m and s.

optionExplanations.0: The second is one of the seven SI base units.
optionExplanations.1: The kilogram is an SI base unit.
optionExplanations.3: The ampere is an SI base unit.

shortExplanation: Newton's second law gives F = m*a = 3 kg * 5 m/s^2 = 15 N.
solutionSteps: Apply F = m*a.
Substitute m = 3 kg and a = 5 m/s^2.
keyConcept: Net force equals mass times acceleration.
commonMistake: Adding mass and acceleration instead of multiplying them.

optionExplanations.0: 10 N would require m*a = 10, not matching 3*5.
optionExplanations.2: 20 N does not equal 3*5.
optionExplanations.4: 30 N would double the correct product.

shortExplanation: Work is force times displacement along the force: W = F*d = 10 N * 5 m = 50 J.
solutionSteps: Use W = F*d for a force parallel to motion.
Substitute F = 10 N and d = 5 m.
keyConcept: Work done by a constant force along the displacement is force times distance.
commonMistake: Bringing in the 2 kg mass, which is irrelevant when force and distance are given directly.

optionExplanations.0: 20 J would come from multiplying mass by distance, not force by distance.
optionExplanations.2: 40 J does not equal 10*5.
optionExplanations.4: 60 J overshoots the correct product.

shortExplanation: Power in a resistor is P = V^2/R = 12^2/3 = 144/3 = 48 W.
solutionSteps: Use P = V^2/R since voltage and resistance are known.
Compute V^2 = 12^2 = 144.
keyConcept: Power dissipated in a resistor is V^2/R (equivalently I^2*R or V*I).
commonMistake: Using P = V*R (48 becomes 36) or forgetting to square the voltage.

optionExplanations.0: 12 W would ignore squaring the voltage.
optionExplanations.1: 24 W is not 144/3.
optionExplanations.4: 60 W does not match 144/3.

shortExplanation: Each branch carries I = V/R: 8/2 = 4 A and 8/4 = 2 A; total current is their sum, 6 A.
solutionSteps: In parallel, both resistors have the same 8 V across them.
Current in the 2 ohm branch: 8/2 = 4 A.
Current in the 4 ohm branch: 8/4 = 2 A.
Total supplied current = 4 + 2 = 6 A.
keyConcept: In a parallel circuit branch currents add to give the total supply current.
commonMistake: Adding the resistances first or using only one branch, missing the sum of branch currents.

optionExplanations.0: 2 A is only the smaller branch current.
optionExplanations.1: 4 A is only the larger branch current.
optionExplanations.3: 8 A double-counts or misuses the numbers.

shortExplanation: Capacitance is measured in farads (F), defined as one coulomb per volt.
solutionSteps: Capacitance relates charge to voltage: C = Q/V.
Its unit is coulomb per volt, named the farad.
Therefore the unit is the farad.
keyConcept: 1 farad = 1 coulomb/volt.
commonMistake: Confusing the unit of charge (coulomb) with the unit of capacitance (farad).

optionExplanations.0: The ampere is the unit of electric current.
optionExplanations.1: The coulomb is the unit of electric charge, not capacitance.
optionExplanations.3: The ohm is the unit of resistance.

shortExplanation: Frequency is speed divided by wavelength: f = 340/0.85 = 400 Hz.
solutionSteps: Use v = f*lambda, so f = v/lambda.
Substitute v = 340 m/s and lambda = 0.85 m.
keyConcept: Wave frequency equals wave speed divided by wavelength.
commonMistake: Multiplying speed by wavelength instead of dividing.

optionExplanations.0: 200 Hz would need lambda = 1.7 m.
optionExplanations.1: 300 Hz does not equal 340/0.85.
optionExplanations.3: 500 Hz does not equal 340/0.85.

shortExplanation: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: v = 4 * 2 = 8 m/s.
solutionSteps: Use v = f*lambda.
Substitute f = 4 Hz and lambda = 2 m.
keyConcept: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
commonMistake: Dividing frequency by wavelength instead of multiplying.

optionExplanations.0: 4 m/s ignores the wavelength factor.
optionExplanations.1: 6 m/s does not equal 4*2.
optionExplanations.3: 10 m/s does not equal 4*2.

shortExplanation: Using 1/f = 1/do + 1/di with f = 20 cm and do = 40 cm gives 1/di = 1/20 - 1/40 = 1/40, so di = 40 cm.
solutionSteps: Apply the thin lens equation 1/f = 1/do + 1/di.
di = 40 cm.
keyConcept: Thin lens equation relates focal length, object and image distances.
commonMistake: Adding the reciprocals instead of subtracting, or forgetting the common denominator.

optionExplanations.0: 13 cm would place the image inside the focal length, impossible for a real object here.
optionExplanations.1: 25 cm does not satisfy 1/20 = 1/40 + 1/di.
optionExplanations.2: 30 cm does not satisfy the lens equation.

shortExplanation: Violet has the shortest wavelength and highest refractive index in glass, so it bends most in a prism.
solutionSteps: Refractive index increases as wavelength decreases.
Violet has the shortest visible wavelength.
Higher index means greater bending, so violet bends most.
keyConcept: Shorter wavelength light refracts more strongly (violet bends most, red least).
commonMistake: Assuming red bends most because it appears at one edge of the spectrum.

optionExplanations.0: Red has the longest wavelength and bends least.
optionExplanations.1: Green bends less than blue and violet.
optionExplanations.2: Blue bends strongly but less than violet.

shortExplanation: Dispersion arises because different colors travel at different speeds in glass, so their refractive indices and bending angles differ.
solutionSteps: In glass the speed of light depends on wavelength (color).
Different speeds mean different refractive indices.
Different indices bend each color by a different angle, spreading the light.
keyConcept: Dispersion is wavelength-dependent refraction due to color-dependent wave speed in the medium.
commonMistake: Attributing the color spread to reflection or absorption rather than refraction differences.

optionExplanations.0: Absorption removes light but does not separate colors by angle.
optionExplanations.2: Reflection does not separate white light into a spectrum in a prism.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure has no role in prism dispersion.

shortExplanation: Power = energy/time; energy has dimensions ML^2 T^-2, so dividing by time (T) gives ML^2 T^-3.
solutionSteps: Work/energy = force x distance = (MLT^-2)(L) = ML^2 T^-2.
Power = energy / time = ML^2 T^-2 / T.
Result: ML^2 T^-3.
keyConcept: Dimensions of power are [M L^2 T^-3] because power is energy per unit time.
commonMistake: Stopping at the dimensions of energy (ML^2 T^-2) and forgetting to divide by time.

optionExplanations.0: MLT^-1 is the dimension of momentum, not power.
optionExplanations.1: ML^2 T^-2 is the dimension of energy or work, not power.
optionExplanations.3: MLT^-2 is the dimension of force, not power.

formulaNotes: Power = Work/time; [Work] = ML^2 T^-2, so [Power] = ML^2 T^-3.

shortExplanation: For KE = 1/2 m v^2, relative errors add with the power as a coefficient: error = %m + 2*%v = 2% + 2*3% = 8%.
solutionSteps: For a product/power relation, fractional errors add, each multiplied by its exponent.
KE depends on m to the first power and v to the second power.
keyConcept: For y = k*a^p*b^q, the maximum relative error is p*(error in a) + q*(error in b).
commonMistake: Forgetting the exponent 2 on velocity and simply adding 2% + 3% = 5%.

optionExplanations.0: 5% ignores the squaring of velocity and just adds 2% + 3%.
optionExplanations.2: 11% would come from doubling the mass error too (4% + 6%), which is incorrect.
optionExplanations.3: 6% is only the velocity contribution (2*3%) and omits the mass error.

shortExplanation: Velocity is the derivative v(t) = 6t - 12; setting it to zero gives t = 2 s.
solutionSteps: v(t) = dx/dt = 6t - 12.
t = 2 s.
keyConcept: A particle is momentarily at rest when its instantaneous velocity (the derivative of position) equals zero.
commonMistake: Setting the position x(t) equal to zero instead of the velocity v(t).

optionExplanations.0: At t = 1 s, v = 6 - 12 = -6 m/s, not zero.
optionExplanations.2: At t = 3 s, v = 18 - 12 = 6 m/s, not zero.
optionExplanations.3: At t = 4 s, v = 24 - 12 = 12 m/s, not zero.

formulaNotes: v(t) = dx/dt; rest occurs when v(t) = 0.

shortExplanation: Time to rise = v/g = 20/10 = 2 s; by symmetry the fall takes the same time, so total time in air = 4 s.
solutionSteps: Time to reach the top: t_up = v/g = 20/10 = 2 s.
The descent is symmetric, taking another 2 s.
Total time = 2 + 2 = 4 s.
keyConcept: For vertical projectile motion returning to launch height, total time = 2v/g.
commonMistake: Reporting only the time to reach maximum height (2 s) instead of the full up-and-down time.

optionExplanations.0: 2 s is only the time to rise to the highest point, not the full flight.
optionExplanations.2: 6 s overestimates; the total flight is 2v/g = 4 s.
optionExplanations.3: 8 s would require an initial speed of 40 m/s or g = 5 m/s^2.

shortExplanation: At constant volume no work is done (W = 0), so by the first law Q = ΔU: all heat supplied goes to changing internal energy.
solutionSteps: Isochoric means volume is constant, so W = P x ΔV = 0.
First law: ΔU = Q - W = Q - 0.
Therefore Q = ΔU.
keyConcept: In an isochoric process W = 0, so heat added equals the change in internal energy.
commonMistake: Assuming pressure stays constant; in an isochoric process pressure changes while volume is fixed.

optionExplanations.0: No work is done because the volume does not change (W = 0), so it cannot be positive.
optionExplanations.1: Adding heat raises internal energy (and temperature); it is not constant.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure generally changes during an isochoric process; volume, not pressure, is held constant.

shortExplanation: Carnot efficiency = 1 - T_cold/T_hot = 1 - 300/400 = 0.25 = 25%.
solutionSteps: Use absolute temperatures: T_hot = 400 K, T_cold = 300 K.
Efficiency = 1 - T_cold / T_hot = 1 - 300/400.
keyConcept: Maximum (Carnot) efficiency depends only on the ratio of absolute reservoir temperatures.
commonMistake: Using T_cold/T_hot alone (75%) instead of 1 - T_cold/T_hot.

optionExplanations.0: 75% is the ratio T_cold/T_hot, not the efficiency.
optionExplanations.1: 33% would arise from mis-using the temperature difference over the sink temperature.
optionExplanations.3: 100% efficiency is impossible; it would require T_cold = 0 K.

shortExplanation: By Bernoulli's principle in a horizontal pipe, faster fluid speed corresponds to lower pressure.
solutionSteps: Bernoulli (horizontal): P + (1/2)*rho*v^2 = constant.
If v increases, the (1/2)*rho*v^2 term increases.
To keep the sum constant, P must decrease.
keyConcept: In horizontal flow, higher fluid speed means lower pressure (Bernoulli's principle).
commonMistake: Assuming faster flow means higher pressure; the relationship is inverse.

optionExplanations.0: Pressure decreases, not increases, as speed rises.
optionExplanations.2: Pressure is not constant when speed changes in horizontal flow.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure depends on speed here, not solely on pipe diameter.

shortExplanation: Newton's law of gravitation gives F = G*m1*m2/r^2 = 6.67e-11 * 25 / 4 which is about 4.17e-10 N.
solutionSteps: Write F = G*m1*m2/r^2.
Insert values: F = 6.67e-11 * 5 * 5 / 2^2.
Divide by r^2 = 4: F = 4.17e-10 N.
keyConcept: Gravitational force scales with the product of the masses and inversely with the square of the separation.
commonMistake: Forgetting to square the distance (dividing by 2 instead of by 4).

optionExplanations.1: This is twice the correct value, obtained by dividing by r = 2 instead of r^2 = 4.
optionExplanations.2: An order of magnitude too large, from misplacing the power of ten.
optionExplanations.3: Combines both errors, giving a value far above the true force.

shortExplanation: Buoyant force depends only on the volume of liquid displaced, which is the same for both bodies since they have equal volume.
solutionSteps: Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = density_liquid * g * volume_displaced.
Both bodies are fully immersed and have the same volume, so they displace the same amount of liquid.
Mass and density of the bodies do not enter the buoyant-force formula.
Therefore the buoyant force on B equals that on A.
keyConcept: Buoyant force scales with displaced volume, not with the object's own mass or weight.
commonMistake: Assuming the heavier body (mB = 3mA) experiences a proportionally larger buoyant force.

optionExplanations.1: No physical basis; buoyancy does not scale with the square of any ratio.
optionExplanations.2: Confuses the object's weight ratio with the buoyant force, which ignores mass.
optionExplanations.4: Inverts the (irrelevant) mass ratio; buoyancy is independent of mass.

shortExplanation: After time t the speed is v = g*t, and the kinetic energy is (1/2)m*v^2 = (1/2)(P/g)(g*t)^2 = (1/2)P*g*t^2.
solutionSteps: Free fall from rest: v = g*t.
Kinetic energy KE = (1/2)*m*v^2.
The body's mass is m = P/g since weight P = m*g.
Substitute: KE = (1/2)(P/g)(g*t)^2 = (1/2)*P*g*t^2.
keyConcept: Use weight P = m*g to convert weight into mass before applying KE = (1/2)m*v^2.
commonMistake: Forgetting the square on t or dropping a factor of g when substituting m = P/g.

optionExplanations.0: (1/2)Pgt is missing the square on t, so its units are wrong (energy needs t^2).
optionExplanations.3: 2Pgt^2 has the wrong numerical coefficient; it should be 1/2, not 2.
optionExplanations.4: (1/2)Pg^2t^2 has an extra factor of g from not cancelling g in m = P/g.

shortExplanation: Efficiency = work out / heat absorbed, so Q_in = W / eff = 3.6 kJ / 0.75 = 4.8 kJ.
solutionSteps: Thermal efficiency eff = W / Q_absorbed.
Rearrange: Q_absorbed = W / eff.
Substitute: Q_absorbed = 3.6 kJ / 0.75.
Compute: Q_absorbed = 4.8 kJ.
keyConcept: Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to heat input, so heat input exceeds the work.
commonMistake: Multiplying work by efficiency instead of dividing, giving a value smaller than the work.

optionExplanations.0: 2.7 kJ = 0.75 * 3.6, which wrongly multiplies work by efficiency.
optionExplanations.2: 14.4 kJ divides by 0.25 instead of 0.75, using the rejected-heat fraction.
optionExplanations.4: 3.6 kJ just repeats the work; heat input must be larger than the work produced.

formulaNotes: eff = W / Q_in -> Q_in = W / eff = 3.6 / 0.75 = 4.8 kJ

shortExplanation: Sound is a mechanical (elastic) wave that needs a material medium, and its speed depends on the properties of that medium.
solutionSteps: Sound is produced by mechanical vibrations transmitted as compressions and rarefactions.
These require particles to interact, so a material (elastic) medium is necessary.
The propagation speed depends on the medium's elasticity and density (e.g. faster in solids than air).
Therefore sound is an elastic wave whose speed depends on the medium.
keyConcept: Sound is a mechanical wave; it cannot travel through vacuum and its speed is medium-dependent.
commonMistake: Treating 340 m/s as a universal sound speed, when that value applies only to air near room temperature.

optionExplanations.1: Sound cannot propagate in vacuum, so this is impossible.
optionExplanations.2: The speed of sound is not a single fixed value like the speed of light.
optionExplanations.3: 300,000 km/s is the speed of light, and sound does not travel in vacuum.

shortExplanation: The equilibrium temperature is the mass-weighted average: (60*20 + 20*60)/80 = 30 °C.
solutionSteps: Water volumes are proportional to masses, so use 60 and 20 as weights.
Heat balance: 60*(T - 20) = 20*(60 - T) with the same specific heat.
keyConcept: For the same substance, the final temperature is the mass-weighted mean of the initial temperatures.
commonMistake: Taking the plain average (40 °C) and ignoring that more water is at the lower temperature.

optionExplanations.0: 25 °C overweights the cold water beyond the actual 60:20 ratio.
optionExplanations.2: 40 °C is the simple midpoint, which ignores the 3:1 mass imbalance toward the colder water.
optionExplanations.4: 35 °C would require equal masses, but here the cold water dominates.

shortExplanation: A neutral or oppositely charged sphere is attracted to a charged rod, but repulsion only happens between like charges, so B must be positive.
solutionSteps: A positive rod attracts any neutral conductor (by induction) and any negative object.
So A being attracted means A is negative OR neutral (not determined).
Repulsion occurs only between charges of the same sign.
Since B is repelled by the positive rod, B must be positively charged.
keyConcept: Attraction is ambiguous (neutral or opposite charge), but repulsion certifies same-sign charge.
commonMistake: Concluding A is definitely negative, when an attracted sphere could simply be neutral.

optionExplanations.0: B is repelled, which a neutral sphere never is, so B cannot be neutral.
optionExplanations.3: It allows B to be neutral, but a repelled sphere must carry the same sign as the rod.
optionExplanations.4: It forces A to be negative, but an attracted sphere could instead be neutral.

shortExplanation: The scalar projection of a onto b equals the dot product a·b divided by the magnitude |b|.
solutionSteps: The projection length of a onto b is |a|*cos(theta), where theta is the angle between them.
The dot product gives a·b = |a|*|b|*cos(theta).
Divide by |b|: (a·b)/|b| = |a|*cos(theta).
This is exactly the (signed) magnitude of the projection of a on b.
keyConcept: Scalar projection of a on b = (a·b)/|b|.
commonMistake: Using the cross product, which measures the perpendicular component, not the projection along b.

optionExplanations.0: The cross product gives |a||b|sin(theta), related to the perpendicular component, not the projection.
optionExplanations.2: a·b alone has units of |a||b|cos(theta); it is not divided by |b|, so it is not the projection length.
optionExplanations.3: a + b is a vector sum, unrelated to projecting one vector onto another.

shortExplanation: At 40 m/s with a wheel circumference of about 2.51 m, the wheel turns roughly 40/2.51 ≈ 16 times per second.
solutionSteps: Convert speed: 144 km/h = 144/3.6 = 40 m/s.
Wheel circumference C = pi*d = pi*0.80 m ≈ 2.51 m.
Turns per second = distance per second / circumference = 40 / 2.51.
This gives about 15.9, i.e. roughly 16 turns per second.
keyConcept: Rolling without slipping means distance covered per revolution equals the wheel circumference pi*d.
commonMistake: Using the diameter instead of the circumference (pi*d) when computing distance per turn.

optionExplanations.0: 8 uses the wrong speed conversion, roughly halving the correct rate.
optionExplanations.1: 57 comes from dividing by the diameter without pi, overcounting revolutions.
optionExplanations.2: 32 results from using the radius or omitting pi, effectively halving the circumference.

shortExplanation: Imagine the unluckiest possible draw. You could pull every pen of the two most common colors before ever touching the rarest. So plan for that worst case, then add one more pen to force the missing color.
solutionSteps: You want a guarantee, so ask: what is the largest number of pens I could draw and STILL be missing a color?
The unluckiest run avoids the rarest color (blue, 5 pens) for as long as possible by drawing only the other two colors first.
Those two are red (7) and green (6): that is 7 + 6 = 13 pens, all drawn without a single blue.
At 13 pens you could still be missing blue, so 13 is not enough. But every pen left in the drawer is now blue.
So the very next pen, number 14, MUST be blue. With 14 pens you are guaranteed at least one of each color.
keyConcept: Worst-case (pigeonhole) reasoning: to guarantee one of every color, add up all pens of every color EXCEPT the rarest one, then add 1. That final pen is forced to be the color you were avoiding.
commonMistake: Adding the two SMALLEST groups, or forgetting the '+1'. The worst case fills up on the two LARGEST groups first, and the extra pen is what actually forces the last color to appear.

optionExplanations.0: 12 pens could still be all red and green (13 of those exist), so blue might be missing. Not a guarantee.
optionExplanations.2: 13 pens is exactly all 7 red plus all 6 green, so you could still have zero blue. One short.
optionExplanations.3: 11 pens leaves even more room to have dodged blue entirely, so it fails.
optionExplanations.4: 15 works but is more than needed; 14 already forces a blue, so 15 is not the minimum.

shortExplanation: The negation of 'all flowers are beautiful' is that at least one flower fails to be beautiful.
solutionSteps: The statement is a universal claim: for every flower, it is beautiful.
Its negation is an existential claim: there exists at least one flower that is not beautiful.
This is exactly 'at least one flower is not beautiful.'
keyConcept: The negation of 'all A are B' is 'at least one A is not B', not 'no A is B'.
commonMistake: Over-negating to 'no flowers are beautiful', which is stronger than the falsity of the universal claim.

optionExplanations.0: 'All flowers are not beautiful' claims none are beautiful, far stronger than required.
optionExplanations.2: 'No flowers are beautiful' is the same over-strong claim and need not follow.
optionExplanations.4: 'All beautiful things are flowers' is an unrelated converse-type statement.

shortExplanation: 'Every applicant must submit a letter' means no one can apply without submitting one, which is the stated equivalent.
solutionSteps: The rule says: applying implies submitting a recommendation letter.
Equivalently, there is no applicant who lacks a letter.
That is 'no candidate applies without submitting a recommendation letter.'
keyConcept: 'All A must do B' is equivalent to 'no A does without B' (universal restated as denial of a counterexample).
commonMistake: Reading a mandatory requirement as optional or as allowing exceptions.

optionExplanations.1: 'At least one candidate applies without a letter' is the negation, not an equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: Timing of letter submission is not addressed by the original rule.
optionExplanations.3: 'Submitting is optional' contradicts the mandatory requirement.

shortExplanation: N's statement forces a contradiction, so N is false and O is true; then M must be false, making P true. The truth-tellers are O and P, giving exactly two true statements.
solutionSteps: M and P contradict each other (each calls the other a liar), so exactly one of them is true.
Suppose N is true: then M and O are both true, but O says N is lying, contradiction. So N is false.
O says 'N is lying', which is now true, so O is true.
N being false means 'M and O both true' is false; since O is true, M must be false.
M false makes P ('M is lying') true.
Truth-tellers are O and P, exactly two true statements, matching the condition.
keyConcept: Chain the mutually dependent statements: resolve the self-contradictory one first, then propagate truth values.
commonMistake: Assuming N could be true without checking that it forces O both true and lying simultaneously.

optionExplanations.0: M and O both true fails because M is false in the consistent assignment.
optionExplanations.1: N and P true fails because N leads to contradiction.
optionExplanations.4: M and P cannot both be true since they directly contradict each other.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is 'if not Q then not P': if traffic is not diverted, the road is not closed.
solutionSteps: Identify P = 'the road is closed', Q = 'traffic is diverted'.
The contrapositive is 'if not Q then not P'.
That reads 'if traffic is not diverted, the road is not closed.'
keyConcept: Contrapositive of P -> Q is (not Q) -> (not P), and it is logically equivalent to the original.
commonMistake: Confusing the contrapositive with the converse ('if traffic is diverted, the road is closed').

optionExplanations.1: 'If the road is not closed, traffic is diverted' is the inverse's negation-mismatch, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If traffic is diverted, the road is closed' is the converse, not the contrapositive.
optionExplanations.3: 'If traffic is diverted, the road is open' is neither converse nor contrapositive.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'if the river is dry, the boat cannot sail' is 'if the boat can sail, the river is not dry.'
solutionSteps: Let P = 'river is dry', Q = 'boat cannot sail'.
Contrapositive is (not Q) -> (not P): 'if the boat can sail, then the river is not dry'.
This matches the stated equivalent.
keyConcept: P -> Q is equivalent to its contrapositive (not Q) -> (not P).
commonMistake: Choosing the converse ('if boat cannot sail, river is dry') instead of the contrapositive.

optionExplanations.1: 'If the river is dry, the boat sails' contradicts the original.
optionExplanations.2: 'If the boat cannot sail, the river is dry' is the converse.
optionExplanations.3: 'If the river is not dry, the boat cannot sail' is the inverse, not equivalent.

shortExplanation: The falsity of 'all daily-studying students pass' means at least one student who studies daily does not pass, i.e. some fail.
solutionSteps: The universal claim: every student who studies daily passes.
Its negation: there exists a daily-studying student who does not pass.
That is 'some students who study daily fail.'
keyConcept: Negation of 'all A are B' is 'some A are not B', keeping the same subject class A.
commonMistake: Drawing conclusions about students who do NOT study daily, who are outside the negated claim.

optionExplanations.1: Claims about students who don't study go beyond what the original statement covers.
optionExplanations.2: 'Some who don't study pass' concerns a different group entirely.
optionExplanations.3: 'No student passes' is far stronger than the negation requires.

shortExplanation: 'and' is the only word appearing in all three sentences, and 'pa' is the only code common to all three, so 'and' = 'pa'.
solutionSteps: List shared words: 'and' appears in every sentence; the code common to all three sets is 'pa'.
Cross-check: 'apple' (sentences 1 and 2) maps to 'go'; 'sweet' (1 and 3) maps to 'ti'; 'the' (2 and 3) maps to 'la'.
That leaves 'pa' consistently paired with 'and'.
keyConcept: Decode by matching words shared across phrases to codes shared across the corresponding code strings.
commonMistake: Assigning 'and' to a code that appears in only two of the phrases (e.g. 'go' or 'la').

optionExplanations.0: 'go' matches 'apple' (in sentences 1 and 2 only).
optionExplanations.1: 'la' matches 'the' (in sentences 2 and 3 only).
optionExplanations.3: 'ti' matches 'sweet' (in sentences 1 and 3 only).

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of "if X then not Y" negates and swaps the parts, giving "if Y then not X".
solutionSteps: Original: X implies (not Y).
Contrapositive swaps and negates both: negate the consequent (not Y becomes Y) and negate the antecedent (X becomes not X), then swap.
Result: Y implies (not X).
In words: If Y occurs, then X does not occur.
keyConcept: The contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', logically equivalent to the original.
commonMistake: Confusing the contrapositive with the converse or inverse.

optionExplanations.1: 'If X does not occur, then Y occurs' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If Y does not occur, then X occurs' reverses the truth incorrectly.
optionExplanations.3: 'If X occurs, then Y occurs' contradicts the original statement.

shortExplanation: Chaining the two 'all' statements: equilateral shapes are triangles, and triangles are polygons, so all equilateral shapes are polygons.
solutionSteps: Given: every equilateral shape is a triangle.
Given: every triangle is a polygon.
By transitivity of the subset relation, every equilateral shape is a polygon.
So 'All equilateral shapes are polygons' must be true.
keyConcept: Two nested universal ('all') statements chain transitively: A subset B and B subset C imply A subset C.
commonMistake: Reversing a universal statement (e.g., assuming all polygons are triangles).

optionExplanations.0: 'All polygons are triangles' reverses the given inclusion and is not implied.
optionExplanations.2: 'Some polygons are not triangles' is plausible in reality but not forced by the premises.
optionExplanations.3: 'All triangles are equilateral' reverses the second premise incorrectly.

shortExplanation: 'Every student must attend' means attendance is required of all, which is the same as saying no student is allowed to skip.
solutionSteps: 'Every student must attend' is a universal obligation: for all students, attendance is required.
The logical negation of skipping being permitted is that skipping is forbidden for all.
So the equivalent statement is that no student can skip the lecture.
keyConcept: A universal requirement 'all must do X' is equivalent to 'none may fail to do X'.
commonMistake: Weakening 'every' to 'some', which changes the meaning entirely.

optionExplanations.1: 'Some students can skip' contradicts the universal requirement.
optionExplanations.2: 'After registering' adds a condition not present in the original.
optionExplanations.3: 'Optional' directly contradicts 'must attend'.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive negates and swaps both parts: 'If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.'
solutionSteps: Original: raining implies ground wet.
Contrapositive: negate consequent and antecedent, then swap.
Result: (ground not wet) implies (not raining).
In words: If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.
keyConcept: Contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', which is logically equivalent.
commonMistake: Giving the inverse ('if not raining then not wet') or converse ('if wet then raining').

optionExplanations.1: 'If it is not raining, then the ground is not wet' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If the ground is wet, then it is raining' is the converse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'If it is raining, then the ground is not raining/wet' contradicts the original.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'clear implies not raining' is 'raining implies not clear', i.e. 'If it is raining, then the sky is not clear.'
solutionSteps: Original: sky clear implies not raining.
Contrapositive: negate consequent (not raining becomes raining) and antecedent (clear becomes not clear), then swap.
Result: raining implies sky not clear.
In words: If it is raining, then the sky is not clear.
keyConcept: Contrapositive of 'P implies not Q' is 'Q implies not P', logically equivalent.
commonMistake: Confusing the equivalent contrapositive with the inverse or converse.

optionExplanations.1: 'If the sky is not clear, then it is raining' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If it is not raining, then the sky is clear' is the converse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'The sky is clear only if it is raining' misstates the direction of implication.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'frozen implies skating allowed' is 'skating not allowed implies not frozen'.
solutionSteps: Original: lake frozen implies skating allowed.
Contrapositive: negate both parts and swap.
Result: (skating not allowed) implies (lake not frozen).
In words: If skating is not allowed, the lake is not frozen.
keyConcept: Contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', the logically equivalent form.
commonMistake: Choosing the inverse ('if not frozen, no skating') which is not equivalent.

optionExplanations.1: 'If the lake is not frozen, skating is not allowed' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If skating is allowed, the lake is frozen' is the converse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.4: 'Skating is allowed only if the lake is not frozen' reverses the original meaning.

shortExplanation: The negation of a universal 'all are' statement is an existential 'at least one is not', so some artists are not talented.
solutionSteps: 'All artists are talented' asserts every artist has the property.
Its logical negation is: there exists at least one artist who is not talented.
In words: Some artists are not talented.
This is the only statement forced by the falsehood of the universal claim.
keyConcept: The negation of 'all A are B' is 'some A are not B', not 'no A are B'.
commonMistake: Over-negating to 'no artists are talented', which is stronger than required.

optionExplanations.1: 'All artists are not talented' claims none are talented, far stronger than needed.
optionExplanations.2: 'No artists are talented' is the contrary, not the negation.
optionExplanations.3: 'Some non-artists are talented' concerns non-artists, irrelevant to the claim.

shortExplanation: The word 'and' appears in all three phrases, and only the code word 'ka' appears in all three translations, so 'and' is 'ka'.
solutionSteps: Phrase 1 'sky and blue' = 'mi ka lo'; Phrase 2 'the sky and clear' = 'ta mi ka pu'; Phrase 3 'the sea and blue' = 'ta se ka lo'.
'and' is the only English word common to all three phrases.
Compare code words: 'ka' is the only token present in all three translations.
Therefore 'and' corresponds to 'ka'.
keyConcept: A word common to every phrase must map to the code token common to every translation.
commonMistake: Matching by position rather than by which token recurs across all phrases.

optionExplanations.0: 'mi' appears only where 'sky' appears (phrases 1 and 2), so it maps to 'sky'.
optionExplanations.2: 'lo' appears where 'blue' appears (phrases 1 and 3), so it maps to 'blue'.
optionExplanations.3: 'ta' appears where 'the' appears (phrases 2 and 3), so it maps to 'the'.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'if A then not B' negates and swaps to 'if B then not A'.
solutionSteps: Original: A implies (not B).
Contrapositive: negate the consequent (not B becomes B) and antecedent (A becomes not A), then swap.
Result: B implies (not A).
In words: If B happens, then A does not happen.
keyConcept: Contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', logically equivalent to the original.
commonMistake: Confusing the contrapositive with the converse or inverse.

optionExplanations.1: 'If A does not happen, then B happens' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If B does not happen, then A happens' does not follow from the original.
optionExplanations.3: 'If A happens, then B happens' contradicts the original statement.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'train late implies meeting canceled' is 'meeting not canceled implies train not late'.
solutionSteps: Original: train late implies meeting canceled.
Contrapositive: negate both parts and swap.
Result: (meeting not canceled) implies (train not late).
In words: If the meeting is not canceled, the train is not late.
keyConcept: Contrapositive of 'P implies Q' is 'not Q implies not P', logically equivalent.
commonMistake: Giving the inverse ('if train not late, meeting canceled') instead.

optionExplanations.1: 'If the train is not late, the meeting is canceled' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If the meeting is canceled, the train is late' is the converse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'If the train is late, the meeting is not canceled' contradicts the original.

shortExplanation: The negation of 'all doctors are compassionate' is 'at least one doctor is not compassionate', i.e. some doctors are not compassionate.
solutionSteps: 'All doctors are compassionate' asserts the property holds for every doctor.
Its negation is: there exists at least one doctor who is not compassionate.
In words: Some doctors are not compassionate.
This is exactly what must follow from the statement being false.
keyConcept: The negation of 'all A are B' is 'some A are not B', not 'no A are B'.
commonMistake: Over-negating to 'no doctors are compassionate', which is too strong.

optionExplanations.0: 'All doctors are not compassionate' claims none are, stronger than required.
optionExplanations.2: 'No doctors are compassionate' is the contrary, not the negation.
optionExplanations.3: 'Some nurses are compassionate' concerns nurses, irrelevant to the claim.

shortExplanation: The word 'and' is common to all three phrases, and only the token 'ta' appears in all three translations, so 'and' is 'ta'.
solutionSteps: Phrase 1 'sun and bright' = 'mo ta ki'; Phrase 2 'the sun and warm' = 'la mo ta su'; Phrase 3 'the moon and bright' = 'la ni ta ki'.
'and' is the only English word appearing in all three phrases.
Among code tokens, 'ta' is the only one present in all three translations.
Therefore 'and' corresponds to 'ta'.
keyConcept: The word common to all phrases maps to the token common to all translations.
commonMistake: Matching tokens by position instead of by recurrence across all phrases.

optionExplanations.0: 'mo' appears only with 'sun' (phrases 1 and 2), so it maps to 'sun'.
optionExplanations.2: 'ki' appears with 'bright' (phrases 1 and 3), so it maps to 'bright'.
optionExplanations.3: 'la' appears with 'the' (phrases 2 and 3), so it maps to 'the'.

shortExplanation: The equivalent statement is the contrapositive: 'If roads are not icy, it doesn't snow.'
solutionSteps: Original: snows implies roads icy.
Contrapositive: negate both parts and swap.
Result: (roads not icy) implies (does not snow).
In words: If roads are not icy, it doesn't snow.
keyConcept: Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to a conditional statement.
commonMistake: Choosing the converse ('if roads icy, it snows') or inverse.

optionExplanations.1: 'If it doesn't snow, roads are not icy' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'If roads are icy, it snows' is the converse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'If it snows, roads are not icy' contradicts the original.

shortExplanation: Add and subtract the two conditions: the larger number is (200+50)/2 = 125 and the smaller is (200-50)/2 = 75.
solutionSteps: Let the numbers be x and y with x + y = 200 and x - y = 50.
Add the equations: 2x = 250, so x = 125.
Subtract or substitute: y = 200 - 125 = 75.
keyConcept: A sum and a difference of two unknowns are solved by adding/subtracting the equations.
commonMistake: Splitting 200 into equal halves (100 and 100) and ignoring the difference of 50.

optionExplanations.1: 130 and 70 sum to 200 but differ by 60, not 50.
optionExplanations.2: 140 and 60 sum to 200 but differ by 80, not 50.
optionExplanations.4: 120 and 80 sum to 200 but differ by 40, not 50.

shortExplanation: By inclusion-exclusion, 80 + 60 - 40 = 100 students play at least one sport, so 120 - 100 = 20 play neither.
solutionSteps: Players of at least one sport = soccer + basketball - both.
Neither = total - at least one = 120 - 100 = 20.
keyConcept: Inclusion-exclusion: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|.
commonMistake: Adding 80 + 60 = 140 without subtracting the 40 counted twice.

optionExplanations.0: 10 would require 110 to play at least one sport, but only 100 do.
optionExplanations.2: 30 would require just 90 players of a sport, undercounting.
optionExplanations.3: 40 is the overlap value, not the number who play neither.

shortExplanation: The sequence doubles each term (geometric, ratio 2), so the nth term is 2^n; the 6th term is 2^6 = 64.
solutionSteps: Term 1 = 2, term 2 = 4, term 3 = 8, term 4 = 16 (each is double the previous).
keyConcept: In a geometric sequence, each term equals the previous term times a constant ratio.
commonMistake: Stopping at term 5 (32) instead of continuing to the 6th term.

optionExplanations.0: 32 is the 5th term, not the 6th.
optionExplanations.2: 128 is the 7th term (2^7).
optionExplanations.3: 256 is the 8th term.

shortExplanation: The negation of 'if P then Q' is 'P and not Q': it is raining yet you do not stay home.
solutionSteps: The statement is P -> Q with P = 'it is raining', Q = 'I will stay home'.
P -> Q is logically equivalent to 'not P or Q'.
Its negation is 'P and not Q'.
That is: it is raining and I will not stay home.
keyConcept: The negation of a conditional keeps the hypothesis true and makes the conclusion false.
commonMistake: Negating the conditional into another conditional (e.g., 'if not raining then not home') instead of P and not Q.

optionExplanations.1: 'Not raining and staying home' does not falsify the original conditional.
optionExplanations.2: 'Raining and staying home' is a case where the original statement holds true.
optionExplanations.4: 'Raining or staying home' is a disjunction, not the negation of the implication.

shortExplanation: Since 30 take neither, 270 take at least one language; by inclusion-exclusion 180 + 150 - 270 = 60 take both.
solutionSteps: Students taking at least one language = 300 - 30 = 270.
Inclusion-exclusion: French + German - both = at least one.
keyConcept: Inclusion-exclusion links the two-set total to the individual counts and the overlap.
commonMistake: Forgetting to remove the 30 'neither' students before applying inclusion-exclusion.

optionExplanations.1: 90 would make 'at least one' = 240, contradicting the 270 who take a language.
optionExplanations.2: 120 would leave only 210 taking at least one language.
optionExplanations.3: 150 is the German count, not the overlap.

shortExplanation: R&D holds 100 engineers plus 50 non-engineers = 150 people; 150/500 = 30%.
solutionSteps: R&D staff = engineers in R&D + non-engineers in R&D = 100 + 50 = 150.
Percentage = 150 / 500 = 0.30.
keyConcept: A percentage is the part divided by the whole, times 100.
commonMistake: Using only the 100 engineers in R&D and ignoring the 50 non-engineers.

optionExplanations.0: 20% (100/500) counts only engineers in R&D.
optionExplanations.1: 25% corresponds to 125 people, not the actual 150.
optionExplanations.4: 40% corresponds to 200 people, overcounting R&D.

shortExplanation: Sum equals average times count: 42 * 6 = 252.
solutionSteps: Average = sum / count, so sum = average * count.
keyConcept: The sum of a set equals its mean multiplied by the number of values.
commonMistake: Dividing instead of multiplying, or using the wrong count.

optionExplanations.0: 240 = 40 * 6, using the wrong average.
optionExplanations.3: 270 = 45 * 6, an inflated average.
optionExplanations.4: 280 does not equal 42 * 6.

shortExplanation: Depreciating 20% per year multiplies the value by 0.8 each year: 5000 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 3200.
solutionSteps: Value after 2 years = $3200.
keyConcept: Repeated percentage decrease is multiplicative: value = start x (0.8)^n.
commonMistake: Subtracting a flat 20% of the original twice (5000 - 2000 = 3000) instead of compounding.

optionExplanations.0: $3000 comes from subtracting 20% of 5000 twice, ignoring the shrinking base.
optionExplanations.2: $3500 does not match the compounded 0.8 x 0.8 factor.
optionExplanations.3: $4000 is only the value after one year, not two.

shortExplanation: Girls = 60 - 36 = 24; as a percentage, 24/60 = 40%.
solutionSteps: Number of girls = 60 - 36 = 24.
Percentage = (24/60) x 100.
keyConcept: Percentage = (part/whole) x 100.
commonMistake: Reporting the boys' percentage (60%) instead of the girls'.

optionExplanations.0: 30% would need 18 girls, but there are 24.
optionExplanations.2: 50% would need 30 girls, not 24.
optionExplanations.3: 60% is the percentage of boys, not girls.

shortExplanation: The discounted price is 90% of the original, so original = 900/0.9 = 1000.
solutionSteps: After a 10% discount, price = 90% of original.
0.90 x original = 900.
keyConcept: A discounted price equals (1 - discount rate) times the original price.
commonMistake: Adding 10% of 900 (=$990) instead of dividing by 0.90.

optionExplanations.0: $950 would give a discounted price of 855, not 900.
optionExplanations.1: $975 does not divide correctly by 0.90 to give 900.
optionExplanations.3: $1025 would give a discounted price above 900.

shortExplanation: From x - y = 2 we get x = y + 2; substituting into 5x + 4y = 19 gives 9y = 9, so y = 1 and x = 3.
solutionSteps: From x - y = 2, solve for x: x = y + 2.
Substitute into 5x + 4y = 19: 5(y + 2) + 4y = 19.
Expand: 5y + 10 + 4y = 19, so 9y = 9 and y = 1.
Back-substitute: x = 1 + 2 = 3.
Check: 5(3) + 4(1) = 19 and 3 - 1 = 2, both hold.
keyConcept: Solve a linear system by substitution, then verify the result in both original equations.
commonMistake: Expanding 5(y + 2) incorrectly (e.g. forgetting to multiply the 2), giving a wrong value of y.

optionExplanations.0: x = 5, y = 3 satisfies x - y = 2 but gives 5(5) + 4(3) = 37, not 19.
optionExplanations.1: x = 4, y = 2 satisfies x - y = 2 but gives 5(4) + 4(2) = 28, not 19.
optionExplanations.3: x = 6, y = 4 satisfies x - y = 2 but gives 5(6) + 4(4) = 46, not 19.
optionExplanations.4: x = 7, y = 5 satisfies x - y = 2 but gives 5(7) + 4(5) = 55, not 19.

formulaNotes: Substituting x = y + 2 into 5x + 4y = 19 yields 9y = 9, so y = 1, x = 3.

shortExplanation: 15% off means paying 85% of $80: 0.85 x 80 = $68.
solutionSteps: Discount = 15% of 80 = 12.
Price after discount = 80 - 12 = 68.
keyConcept: Final price = original x (1 - discount rate).
commonMistake: Subtracting 15 dollars instead of 15% of the price.

optionExplanations.0: $60 would be a 25% discount, not 15%.
optionExplanations.1: $64 corresponds to a 20% discount.
optionExplanations.4: $72 corresponds to only a 10% discount.

shortExplanation: The larger share is 9 parts = $450, so one part = $50; the smaller share is 4 parts = $200.
solutionSteps: Ratio is 4:9; the larger amount corresponds to 9 parts.
Smaller amount = 4 parts = 4 x 50 = 200.
keyConcept: In a ratio, find the value of one part, then scale to the required number of parts.
commonMistake: Assigning the $450 to the 4-part share instead of the 9-part share.

optionExplanations.0: $150 would be 3 parts, not 4.
optionExplanations.2: $250 would be 5 parts, not 4.
optionExplanations.3: $300 would be 6 parts, not 4.

shortExplanation: Perimeter 40 gives side 40/4 = 10 cm, so area = 10^2 = 100 cm^2.
solutionSteps: Side = perimeter/4 = 40/4 = 10 cm.
Area = side^2 = 10^2.
keyConcept: For a square, side = perimeter/4 and area = side^2.
commonMistake: Using the perimeter directly as the side, or forgetting to square the side.

optionExplanations.0: 80 cm^2 does not correspond to any square with integer side from this perimeter.
optionExplanations.2: 120 cm^2 is not the square of the side length 10.
optionExplanations.4: 160 cm^2 would require a side of about 12.6 cm, not 10.

shortExplanation: Alcohol is 80% of 200 mL: 0.80 x 200 = 160 mL.
solutionSteps: Alcohol fraction = 80% = 0.80.
Alcohol volume = 0.80 x 200 mL.
keyConcept: Component volume = percentage x total volume.
commonMistake: Computing the water amount (20% = 40 mL) instead of the alcohol.

optionExplanations.0: 140 mL would be 70% of the total, not 80%.
optionExplanations.1: 150 mL would be 75% of the total.
optionExplanations.4: 180 mL would be 90% of the total, not 80%.

shortExplanation: Three consecutive numbers centered on the middle value give a sum equal to three times that middle value, so the middle number is 78/3 = 26. The numbers are 25, 26, 27.
solutionSteps: Let the numbers be n, n+1, n+2.
The numbers are 25, 26, 27.
keyConcept: For an odd count of consecutive integers, the sum divided by the count gives the middle term.
commonMistake: Dividing 78 by 3 and using 26 as the smallest rather than the middle number.

shortExplanation: Swimming downstream, the current adds to the swimmer's speed: 10 + 2 = 12 km/h. Time = 24/12 = 2 hours.
solutionSteps: Downstream effective speed = still-water speed + current = 10 + 2 = 12 km/h.
Time = distance / speed = 24 / 12.
Time = 2 h.
keyConcept: Downstream speed = swimmer speed + current speed; upstream would subtract.
commonMistake: Using only the 10 km/h still-water speed (24/10 = 2.4 h) and ignoring the current.

optionExplanations.0: 1 h would require a speed of 24 km/h.
optionExplanations.2: 3 h corresponds to 8 km/h, which is the upstream speed, not downstream.
optionExplanations.3: 4 h corresponds to 6 km/h, far below the actual speed.

shortExplanation: Average speed = total distance / total time = 150 km / 2.5 h = 60 km/h.
solutionSteps: Average speed = distance / time.
keyConcept: Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
commonMistake: Dividing by 2 instead of 2.5, giving 75 km/h.

optionExplanations.0: 50 km/h would cover only 125 km in 2.5 h.
optionExplanations.2: 70 km/h would cover 175 km in 2.5 h.
optionExplanations.3: 80 km/h would cover 200 km in 2.5 h.

shortExplanation: Area = length x width, so width = area / length = 48 / 8 = 6 cm.
solutionSteps: Area = length x width = 48 cm^2.
width = 48 / 8.
width = 6 cm.
keyConcept: Rectangle area equals length times width; divide to recover a missing side.
commonMistake: Confusing area with perimeter and using P = 2(l+w).

optionExplanations.0: 4 cm would give an area of 32 cm^2.
optionExplanations.2: 8 cm would give an area of 64 cm^2.
optionExplanations.4: 12 cm would give an area of 96 cm^2.

shortExplanation: Since 5^2 + 12^2 = 13^2, the triangle is right-angled with the two shorter sides as legs. Area = (1/2)(5)(12) = 30 cm^2.
solutionSteps: Check: 5^2 + 12^2 = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13^2, so it is a right triangle.
The legs are 5 cm and 12 cm; the hypotenuse is 13 cm.
Area = (1/2) x base x height = (1/2)(5)(12).
Area = 30 cm^2.
keyConcept: A 5-12-13 triangle is a right triangle, so the legs serve as base and height.
commonMistake: Treating 13 cm as a height and multiplying by a wrong base instead of recognizing the right angle.

optionExplanations.0: 20 cm^2 does not match (1/2)(5)(12).
optionExplanations.2: 40 cm^2 is too large for these legs.
optionExplanations.4: 60 cm^2 forgets the factor of 1/2 (that is base x height).

formulaNotes: For a right triangle, Area = (1/2) x leg1 x leg2

shortExplanation: The three odd numbers fill the three odd positions in 3! = 6 ways and the two even numbers fill the two even positions in 2! = 2 ways, giving 6*2 = 12.
solutionSteps: Odd numbers: 29, 43, 55 (three of them); even numbers: 28, 36 (two).
Odd positions are 1, 3, 5 (three); even positions are 2, 4 (two).
Arrange the odd numbers in odd positions: 3! = 6.
Arrange the even numbers in even positions: 2! = 2.
Multiply: 6 * 2 = 12.
keyConcept: Independent arrangements multiply: count each parity group's permutations separately.
commonMistake: Adding 3! + 2! or forgetting that the two groups combine multiplicatively.

optionExplanations.0: 3 counts only one group's arrangements.
optionExplanations.1: 24 would treat all five as freely arrangeable in some slots.
optionExplanations.4: 6 is only the odd-number arrangements, missing the factor 2.

shortExplanation: Playing is banned only on Sundays and within 1-4 p.m.; at noon on a non-Sunday neither ban applies, so it is not forbidden.
solutionSteps: The rule forbids football on Sundays and during 1-4 p.m.
Playing is allowed whenever it is not Sunday and not within 1-4 p.m.
Noon on a non-Sunday falls outside both bans.
Therefore playing at noon on a non-Sunday is not forbidden.
keyConcept: An exception clause bans exactly the listed cases; everything else stays permitted.
commonMistake: Reading '1-4 p.m.' as including noon (12 p.m.), which is actually before the banned window.

optionExplanations.1: Sundays are banned all day, so playing on Sunday after 4 p.m. is still forbidden.
optionExplanations.3: 2 p.m. lies inside the 1-4 p.m. ban, so it is forbidden regardless of the day.
optionExplanations.4: 2 p.m. on a Sunday is doubly forbidden, not permitted.

shortExplanation: Only the fourth digit = 6 (so third = 3) yields valid ascending combinations with digits from {0,1,2}; the three such combinations mean at most 3 attempts are needed.
solutionSteps: Fourth digit must be even (third is its half) and not 4, so it is 2, 6, or 8.
If fourth = 8 then third = 4, forbidden.
If fourth = 2 then third = 1, leaving no room for two smaller ascending digits.
If fourth = 6 then third = 3, and the first two come from {0,1,2}: pairs (0,1), (0,2), (1,2).
That gives exactly 3 valid combinations, so 3 attempts guarantee success.
keyConcept: Systematically enumerate under all constraints simultaneously to bound the number of possibilities.
commonMistake: Overlooking that third = 4 (from fourth = 8) is excluded by the 'no 4' rule.

optionExplanations.1: 4 overcounts by admitting an invalid combination such as one with third digit 4.
optionExplanations.2: 5 includes cases that break the ascending or half-value constraints.
optionExplanations.4: 2 undercounts the three valid combinations ending in 3, 6.

shortExplanation: The contrapositive of 'no gas oven implies raw inside or burnt outside' is: well cooked inside AND not burnt outside implies a gas oven was used.
solutionSteps: Given: not gas oven implies (raw inside OR burnt outside).
Contrapositive: NOT(raw inside OR burnt outside) implies gas oven.
Negate the disjunction: (not raw inside) AND (not burnt outside).
That is: well cooked inside AND not burnt outside implies gas oven.
keyConcept: The contrapositive of 'if P then Q' is 'if not Q then not P', and not(A or B) = (not A) and (not B).
commonMistake: Turning the OR into an OR in the conclusion instead of an AND (De Morgan error).

optionExplanations.0: Well cooked inside alone does not rule out being burnt outside, so it does not force a gas oven.
optionExplanations.1: Using OR keeps cases (e.g. burnt but cooked inside) that a non-gas oven can still produce.
optionExplanations.3: Raw inside is consistent with a non-gas oven, so it cannot imply not-gas-oven directly this way.

shortExplanation: Two bacteria are what one bacterium becomes after a single day, so starting with two saves exactly one day: 29 days.
solutionSteps: One bacterium doubles daily and covers the pond in 30 days.
After day 1, that single bacterium has become two.
Starting with two is the same as being one day into the single-bacterium process.
So the pond is covered in 30 - 1 = 29 days.
keyConcept: Doubling each period means starting with twice as many advances the timeline by exactly one period.
commonMistake: Assuming double the starting count halves the time (15 days) rather than saving one doubling.

optionExplanations.0: 30 days ignores that starting with two skips the first doubling.
optionExplanations.1: 28 days removes two days, but only one doubling is saved.
optionExplanations.4: 15 days wrongly treats the growth as linear rather than exponential.

shortExplanation: By inclusion-exclusion, TV or fridge = 40% + 25% - 15% = 50%, so exactly 50% of the over-55 group own neither.
solutionSteps: Owners of TV or fridge = 40% + 25% - 15% (both) = 50%.
Those owning neither = 100% - 50% = 50%.
Only conclusions about the surveyed over-55 group are supported.
So 50% own neither a TV nor a fridge.
keyConcept: Inclusion-exclusion: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|.
commonMistake: Forgetting to subtract the 15% overlap, which would give 65% for the union.

optionExplanations.0: The survey covers only people older than 55, so nothing follows about younger people.
optionExplanations.1: The union is exactly 50%, not less than 45%.
optionExplanations.4: The union is exactly 50%, so 'more than 50%' is false.

shortExplanation: The top row is the sequence of triangular numbers and the bottom row is the sequence of factorials, so x = 15 and y = 720.
solutionSteps: Read the top row: 1, 3, 6, 10, ?, 21, 28. Differences are 2, 3, 4, ... so these are triangular numbers.
The missing triangular number after 10 is 10 + 5 = 15, so x = 15.
Read the bottom row: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ?, 5040. These are factorials 1!, 2!, 3!, 4!, 5!, 6!, 7!.
The missing value is 6! = 720, so y = 720.
keyConcept: Recognize standard number families: triangular numbers n(n+1)/2 and factorials n!.
commonMistake: Filling y as 240 by guessing a multiplication pattern instead of identifying the factorial sequence.

optionExplanations.0: x = 14 does not fit the triangular sequence, whose next term after 10 is 15.
optionExplanations.1: Both x = 14 and y = 240 break the triangular and factorial patterns.
optionExplanations.4: y = 240 is not 6! = 720, so it breaks the factorial sequence.

shortExplanation: Julia claims everyone except Paula likes coffee and Paula does not; the negation of that conjunction is that Paula likes coffee OR some non-Paula friend does not.
solutionSteps: Julia's statement is a conjunction: (all friends except Paula like coffee) AND (Paula does not like coffee).
Caroline says Julia is wrong, i.e. the whole conjunction is false.
Negating a conjunction gives a disjunction: at least one part is false.
So either Paula actually likes coffee, or someone other than Paula does not like coffee.
keyConcept: The negation of (A and B) is (not A) or (not B), not the negation of every part at once.
commonMistake: Assuming Julia is wrong on both points, when being wrong requires only one part to fail.

optionExplanations.0: This describes Paula liking coffee only, ignoring the other possibility.
optionExplanations.1: This is only one of the two ways Julia could be wrong, so stating it alone is too strong.
optionExplanations.2: This is the other single way Julia could be wrong, again too specific to be guaranteed.

shortExplanation: Disagreeing with 'all Tony's numbers are even' means asserting its negation: at least one Tony's number is not even.
solutionSteps: The claim under dispute is the universal statement: all Tony's numbers are even.
Hiyam disagrees, so she asserts the negation of that universal statement.
The negation of 'all are even' is 'there exists at least one that is not even'.
Therefore Hiyam believes at least one Tony's number is not even.
keyConcept: The negation of a universal ('all are P') is an existential ('at least one is not P').
commonMistake: Over-negating to 'all Tony's numbers are odd', which is far stronger than mere disagreement.

optionExplanations.1: This talks about non-Tony numbers, which is irrelevant to negating the original claim.
optionExplanations.2: 'All are odd' is the contrary, not the negation; disagreeing needs only one exception.
optionExplanations.4: This makes an extra claim about even numbers that disagreement does not require.

shortExplanation: Some students showing up means at least one attended, and 'not all present' means at least one was absent, matching exactly the last option.
solutionSteps: 'Some students showed up' guarantees at least one student took the test.
'Not all were present' guarantees at least one student was absent.
So it is false that all failed to show up (at least one did show up)...
...and true that at least one did not show up, which is the stated conclusion.
keyConcept: 'Some' guarantees existence; 'not all' guarantees at least one exception.
commonMistake: Inflating 'some' into 'the majority', which the data does not support.

optionExplanations.0: 'All took the test' contradicts 'not all were present'.
optionExplanations.1: 'No student showed up' contradicts 'some showed up'.
optionExplanations.3: The majority attending is not implied; 'some' can be just one.

shortExplanation: Lewis likes to swim and everyone who likes to swim is absent-minded, so Lewis is absent-minded.
solutionSteps: Premise: all people who like to swim are absent-minded.
Premise: Lewis likes to swim.
Apply the universal to the specific case of Lewis.
Conclusion: Lewis is absent-minded.
keyConcept: A valid syllogism applies a universal rule ('all swimmers are absent-minded') to a specific instance.
commonMistake: Reversing the rule (assuming absent-minded implies swimming or being a mathematician).

optionExplanations.0: The converse ('all absent-minded like to swim') is not given.
optionExplanations.1: Nothing links Lewis to being a mathematician; he only likes to swim.
optionExplanations.4: No premise connects mathematicians to swimming.

shortExplanation: The rule says a house is not habitable if it fails the standards, so meeting the standards is a necessary condition for being habitable.
solutionSteps: The regulation: if the house does not meet the standards, it is not habitable.
Contrapositive: if a house is habitable, then it meets the standards.
So meeting the standards is required for habitability, i.e. a necessary condition.
It is not stated to be sufficient, since other codes might also apply.
keyConcept: 'Not P implies not habitable' means P (meeting standards) is necessary for habitability.
commonMistake: Reading the rule as sufficient ('meets standards -> habitable'), which the wording does not guarantee.

optionExplanations.1: Being certainly habitable requires sufficiency, but only necessity is given.
optionExplanations.3: 'Sufficient' would mean meeting the standards guarantees habitability, which is not stated.
optionExplanations.4: A habitable house without water-saving standards would violate the stated rule.

shortExplanation: If one of the ten is younger than 20, the other nine sum to more than 361, which is impossible if all nine are 40 or under, so at least one must be over 40.
solutionSteps: Total age is 380 for ten people, average 38.
Suppose one person is younger than 20, so at most 19.
The remaining nine then sum to at least 380 - 19 = 361.
If all nine were at most 40, their sum would be at most 360, less than 361 — contradiction.
Hence at least one of the others must be older than 40.
keyConcept: Fixing one value low forces the remaining sum high, pushing at least one other value above the average bound.
commonMistake: Assuming the symmetric claim (one over 40 forces one under 20), which does not follow.

optionExplanations.0: Ages could exceed 40 (e.g. balanced by younger ones), so not all are under 40.
optionExplanations.2: Ten people averaging 38 can all be near 38, so one person over 40 need not force anyone under 20.
optionExplanations.3: All ten could be exactly 38 (sum 380), so no one need reach 39.

shortExplanation: To be sure of a white scarf he may draw all 10 non-white scarfs first, needing 11; the same holds for caps, so 11 + 11 = 22.
solutionSteps: In the dark, plan for the worst case for each drawer separately.
Scarfs: 5 red + 5 green = 10 non-white, so 11 scarfs guarantee at least one white scarf.
Caps: likewise 10 non-white, so 11 caps guarantee at least one white cap.
Total needed = 11 + 11 = 22.
keyConcept: Worst-case (pigeonhole) reasoning: draw all unwanted items plus one, done independently for each drawer.
commonMistake: Adding the drawers together and taking 11 total, forgetting each drawer needs its own guarantee.

optionExplanations.0: 20 leaves the possibility of drawing all 10 non-white in one drawer plus fewer than needed in the other.
optionExplanations.1: 21 could still miss a white item if the non-white draws fall unluckily across both drawers.
optionExplanations.2: 16 is far too few to force a white item out of a drawer of 15 with 10 non-white.

shortExplanation: From 2W + R = 2R + G we get G = 2W − R, so the left plate weighs 3W and the right 2W; adding one white sphere to the right makes both 3W.
solutionSteps: First balance: 2W + R = 2R + G, so G = 2W − R.
Left plate now: W + R + G = W + R + (2W − R) = 3W.
Right plate now: 2W.
Left exceeds right by exactly one white sphere weight (3W vs 2W).
Adding one white sphere to the right plate makes both sides equal to 3W.
keyConcept: Translate the balance into an equation for the unknown weights, then compare plate totals.
commonMistake: Adding to the heavier (left) plate, which increases the imbalance instead of correcting it.

optionExplanations.1: Adding white to the left gives 4W vs 2W, worsening the imbalance.
optionExplanations.3: The plates differ by W, not zero, so it is not already balanced.
optionExplanations.4: Adding green to the right gives 4W − R, which equals 3W only if W = R, not guaranteed.

formulaNotes: 2W + R = 2R + G => G = 2W - R; left = 3W, right = 2W

shortExplanation: One third plus three quarters of the members exceeds the whole board by 1/12, so at least that fraction voted for both measures.
solutionSteps: Let N be the number of members. In favor of restructuring: N/3; in favor of budget: 3N/4.
Maximum possible union of the two groups is N.
Since N/12 > 0, at least one member voted for both.
keyConcept: When two subset sizes sum to more than the whole, their overlap is at least that excess (inclusion-exclusion).
commonMistake: Concluding one group is contained in the other, when only a nonzero overlap is guaranteed.

optionExplanations.1: Containment is not forced; only a partial overlap of at least N/12 is guaranteed.
optionExplanations.2: Some members could oppose both; the data does not exclude that.
optionExplanations.3: Similarly, budget supporters need not all support restructuring.

shortExplanation: Two equivalent answers share the same truth value, and since only one answer can be correct, they cannot both be correct, so both must be wrong.
solutionSteps: Exactly one of the five answers is correct (true); the other four are wrong.
Two 'equivalent' answers are true together or false together.
If both were correct, there would be two correct answers, contradicting uniqueness.
Therefore two equivalent answers must both be wrong.
keyConcept: Uniqueness of the correct answer forces any two logically equivalent options to both be incorrect.
commonMistake: Thinking equivalence makes one of the pair correct, which would violate the single-correct-answer rule.

optionExplanations.0: A statement and its negation include one true option, which could be the single correct answer, so 'both wrong' is not guaranteed.
optionExplanations.1: If one equivalent answer were correct, so would the other, giving two correct answers — impossible.
optionExplanations.4: The correct answer could be the true member of the negated pair, not necessarily among the other three.

shortExplanation: A majority answered and all who answered support the park, so some contacted people definitely support it, making 'no-one contacted supports it' certainly false.
solutionSteps: The majority of contacted people answered the survey (so at least some answered).
Everyone who answered supports the park.
Those answerers were contacted and support the park.
Hence at least some contacted people support the park, so 'no-one contacted supports it' cannot be true.
keyConcept: Existence of even one supporter among the contacted makes a universal-negative ('no-one supports') false.
commonMistake: Looking for a statement that is merely uncertain instead of one that is provably false.

optionExplanations.0: This could be true if all contacted people happen to support the park; not certainly false.
optionExplanations.1: This could be true if some non-answerers oppose the park; not certainly false.
optionExplanations.3: Whether all supporters were contacted is unknown; it is not certainly false.

shortExplanation: By point P the cell has completed S phase, so its DNA is 4C. Replication does not change chromosome number: it still has 46 chromosomes, but each now consists of two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids in total.
solutionSteps: G1 cell: 46 chromosomes, 2C DNA, each chromosome a single chromatid.
S phase replicates the DNA to 4C; each chromosome now has two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere.
Replication copies DNA but does not separate centromeres, so chromosome count stays 46.
Total chromatids = 46 chromosomes * 2 = 92 sister chromatids at point P (just before mitosis).
keyConcept: Chromosome number is counted by centromeres, so DNA replication doubles chromatids (and DNA content) without changing chromosome number.
commonMistake: Believing DNA replication doubles the chromosome number to 92, when it only doubles the chromatids per chromosome.

optionExplanations.0: 46 chromatids describes a G1 cell before replication, not the post-S state at P where each chromosome is doubled.
optionExplanations.2: Chromosome number stays 46 through S and G2; it does not become 92 until anaphase separation.
optionExplanations.4: 184 chromatids would require 4C to have doubled again; the cell only reaches 4C (92 chromatids) before mitosis.

figureExplanation: The DNA-content graph shows the level rising from 2C to 4C during S phase and remaining at 4C at point P before mitosis, confirming doubled chromatids but unchanged chromosome count.

shortExplanation: The sequence is intact and, once cooled, the enzyme spontaneously refolds to 95% activity with no help added. This shows that the amino-acid sequence itself encodes the native 3-D fold, which re-forms as weak interactions re-establish.
solutionSteps: Peptide bonds and sequence are unchanged, so only the folded (tertiary) structure was disrupted by heat.
On cooling with nothing added, activity returns to about 95%.
Spontaneous recovery of function implies the polypeptide re-forms its native shape unaided.
Therefore the folding information resides in the primary sequence (Anfinsen's principle).
keyConcept: Anfinsen's principle: a protein's native 3-D conformation is dictated by its amino-acid sequence.
commonMistake: Believing chaperones are always required, or that refolding means denaturation never occurred.

optionExplanations.1: The enzyme genuinely denatured (heat broke weak bonds); the substrate is not the cause.
optionExplanations.2: Hydrogen bonds are not covalent; the reasoning is chemically false.
optionExplanations.3: Refolding occurred with no proteins added, disproving obligatory chaperone dependence.

shortExplanation: Water moves by osmosis toward the more concentrated (higher solute) side; since sucrose cannot cross, water flows from the 0.2 M left arm to the 0.5 M right arm, raising the right level.
solutionSteps: The membrane is permeable to water but not sucrose, so only osmosis can occur.
Osmosis moves water from lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration.
Left arm 0.2 M is more dilute than right arm 0.5 M.
Water therefore flows left to right, so the right-arm liquid level rises.
keyConcept: Osmosis is net water movement across a semipermeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration.
commonMistake: Thinking sucrose diffuses to equalize concentrations, but the membrane blocks sucrose entirely.

optionExplanations.0: Sucrose cannot diffuse because the membrane is impermeable to it.
optionExplanations.2: Water moving toward the dilute left arm reverses the correct osmotic direction.
optionExplanations.3: The membrane does pass water, so there is net movement, not none.

figureExplanation: The diagram shows the 0.2 M arm on the left, the 0.5 M arm on the right, equal starting levels, and the water-only membrane at the base, so water flows toward the right (higher concentration) arm.

shortExplanation: The bond count gives 1800 G-C pairs, so the duplex holds 1800 guanines total; strand 1 has 35% of 3000 = 1050 G, leaving 750 G in strand 2, which is 25%.
solutionSteps: Let AT pairs = a, GC pairs = g: a + g = 3000 and 2a + 3g = 7800.
Subtract to get g = 1800 (GC pairs) and a = 1200 (AT pairs).
Each GC pair has one guanine per strand, so total guanine across both strands = 1800.
Strand 1 guanine = 0.35 * 3000 = 1050, so strand 2 guanine = 1800 - 1050 = 750.
Strand 2 guanine percentage = 750 / 3000 = 25%.
keyConcept: Guanine on one strand pairs with cytosine on the other, so the two strands' G counts sum to the total G-C pair count.
commonMistake: Assuming each strand has the same guanine percentage; base composition is symmetric across the duplex, not within a strand.

optionExplanations.1: 35% just repeats strand 1's value, ignoring the antiparallel pairing that shifts G to C.
optionExplanations.2: 30% would be the whole-duplex average G (1800/6000), not strand 2's value.
optionExplanations.4: 65% confuses guanine with the sum of G and C on strand 1.

formulaNotes: GC pairs = total H-bonds - 2*(bp) = 7800 - 6000 = 1800; G(strand2) = GC_total - G(strand1).

shortExplanation: Uphill glucose uptake in intestinal cells uses a Na+-glucose symporter driven by the sodium gradient that the Na+/K+ ATPase maintains - classic secondary active transport.
solutionSteps: Glucose moving against its concentration gradient requires energy input.
The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps Na+ out, creating a steep inward Na+ gradient (uses ATP).
A Na+-glucose symporter couples Na+ moving down its gradient to glucose moving up its gradient.
The energy for glucose uptake comes indirectly from the ATP-maintained Na+ gradient, i.e. secondary active transport.
keyConcept: Secondary active transport uses an ion gradient (set up by a primary ATP-driven pump) to move a solute uphill.
commonMistake: Assuming the glucose carrier itself hydrolyses ATP; the ATP is spent by the Na+/K+ pump, not the symporter.

optionExplanations.0: The glucose carrier does not hydrolyse ATP; it is powered by the Na+ gradient.
optionExplanations.3: Facilitated diffusion (GLUT) only moves glucose down its gradient, not uphill.
optionExplanations.4: Osmosis moves water, not glucose against its gradient.

shortExplanation: Among black offspring, P(BB) = 1/3; among short-haired offspring, P(SS) = 1/3. Independent, so P(true-breeding for both) = 1/3 * 1/3 = 1/9.
solutionSteps: For each gene Bb x Bb gives genotypes 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb.
Among the dominant (black) offspring, the ratio BB:Bb is 1:2, so P(BB | black) = 1/3.
Similarly P(SS | short) = 1/3.
Genes assort independently, so multiply: (1/3)*(1/3) = 1/9.
