keyConcept: Given a dominant phenotype from a monohybrid cross, the homozygous-dominant fraction is 1/3, not 1/4.
commonMistake: Using 1/4 for each gene (unconditional homozygous fraction) instead of conditioning on the dominant phenotype, giving 1/16.

optionExplanations.0: 1/16 uses unconditional 1/4 per gene, ignoring that we already selected black and short.
optionExplanations.2: 1/4 answers only one gene, not both simultaneously.
optionExplanations.4: 9/16 is the fraction of all offspring that are black and short, not the true-breeding fraction among them.

formulaNotes: P(homozygous dominant | dominant phenotype) = 1/3 per gene; combined = (1/3)^2 = 1/9.

shortExplanation: The man is I^B i (his O mother gave him i); the woman is I^A I^B. Children are 1/4 AB, 1/2 B, 1/4 A. Only type A differs from both parents (B and AB), so probability = 1/4.
solutionSteps: Man is type B with an O (ii) mother, so he inherited i: genotype I^B i.
Woman is type AB: genotype I^A I^B.
Cross I^B i x I^A I^B: offspring I^A I^B (AB), I^B I^B (B), I^A i (A), I^B i (B).
Parents are B and AB; a child different from both must be type A.
P(type A) = 1/4.
keyConcept: Deduce the recessive allele from the parent's phenotype, then use a Punnett square for ABO ratios.
commonMistake: Assuming the man is I^B I^B; his type-O mother forces one i allele, so he is I^B i.

optionExplanations.0: A type differing from both parents does exist (type A), so it is not 0.
optionExplanations.3: 1/2 counts type B children, which match the father, not a new type.
optionExplanations.4: 3/4 overcounts; only the 1/4 that are type A differ from both parents.

formulaNotes: Man I^B i x woman I^A I^B -> 1 AB : 1 B : 1 A : 1 B; different-from-both = A = 1/4.

shortExplanation: Statement I is true (purines A+G = 35%, so pyrimidines = 65%) and II is true (complementary T pairs with this strand's 20% A). Statement III cannot be fixed because the strand's own C fraction is unknown, so the duplex C percentage is undetermined.
solutionSteps: Strand has A = 20%, G = 15%, so purines = 35% and pyrimidines (C + T) = 65%: I is true.
Complementary strand's thymine pairs with this strand's adenine; A = 20% here, so complement T = 20%: II is true.
Duplex %C equals %G overall, but that overall G = (G1 + C1)/2 depends on this strand's unknown C1.
Since C1 is not given (only that C+T = 65%), the whole-molecule C fraction is not fixed: III is not determinable.
keyConcept: Single-strand base percentages fix complement bases position-by-position, but duplex-wide C/G percentages need both strands' composition.
commonMistake: Applying Chargaff's whole-duplex rule (%G = %C = 15%) to a single strand's G value to force III.

optionExplanations.2: III is not determinable, so any option including III fails.
optionExplanations.3: III fails, so 'I, II, and III' is wrong even though I and II hold.
optionExplanations.4: III alone cannot be determined and I and II are actually valid.

formulaNotes: Complement base X count equals this strand's complementary base count; duplex %C = %G but its value needs C1.

shortExplanation: The drug travels arm vein -> right atrium -> right ventricle -> lungs -> pulmonary vein -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> aorta -> coronary arteries. The last of the listed chambers before the coronary arteries is the left ventricle.
solutionSteps: Venous drug enters the right atrium, then the right ventricle.
It is pumped to the lungs, returns via the pulmonary vein to the left atrium.
From the left atrium it passes to the left ventricle.
The left ventricle ejects into the aorta, from which the coronary arteries branch.
So among the listed structures, the left ventricle is passed LAST.
keyConcept: Coronary arteries arise from the base of the aorta, just after the left ventricle.
commonMistake: Thinking the coronary arteries branch from the right side of the heart; they come off the aorta after the left ventricle.

optionExplanations.0: The right atrium is one of the first structures reached, not the last.
optionExplanations.2: The left atrium precedes the left ventricle in the sequence.
optionExplanations.4: The pulmonary vein comes before both the left atrium and left ventricle.

shortExplanation: The dominant ventilation drive is a rise in blood CO2, which lowers blood/CSF pH; central chemoreceptors detect this and increase breathing.
solutionSteps: During exercise, muscles produce more CO2.
Rising CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering blood and cerebrospinal-fluid pH.
Central (and peripheral) chemoreceptors are most sensitive to this rise in CO2 / fall in pH.
They signal the respiratory centre to increase ventilation.
keyConcept: CO2 (via pH change) is the primary chemical driver of ventilation, not oxygen under normal conditions.
commonMistake: Assuming low oxygen is the main trigger; oxygen becomes a strong driver only at very low levels.

optionExplanations.0: A fall in oxygen is only a weak, secondary stimulus except at very low O2 levels.
optionExplanations.2: This is the reverse of what happens; CO2 rises during exercise, it does not fall.
optionExplanations.3: CO2 rises during exercise rather than falling, so a fall in CO2 is not the stimulus.

shortExplanation: With the electron transport chain blocked, only glycolysis (fermentation) yields net 2 ATP per glucose; the Krebs cycle stops because NADH cannot be reoxidised to NAD+, which the cycle requires.
solutionSteps: The electron transport chain is blocked, so oxidative phosphorylation produces no ATP.
Glycolysis still runs, giving a net 2 ATP per glucose.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ only in the cytoplasm, keeping glycolysis going.
The Krebs cycle needs NAD+/FAD, normally regenerated by the ETC; in the mitochondria NADH now accumulates and NAD+ is not restored.
Lacking NAD+, the Krebs cycle enzymes stall, so net yield is just 2 ATP.
keyConcept: Without the ETC, the Krebs cycle halts because its NAD+/FAD electron carriers cannot be reoxidised.
commonMistake: Thinking the poison directly inhibits Krebs-cycle enzymes; the enzymes are intact but starved of NAD+.

optionExplanations.2: Glycolysis does not depend on the ETC and still yields 2 ATP, so it is not 0.
optionExplanations.3: 36 ATP requires a working ETC, which is blocked here.
optionExplanations.4: The Krebs enzymes are stated to be intact; they stop due to lack of NAD+, not direct inhibition.

formulaNotes: Net glycolytic ATP = 2 per glucose; Krebs requires NAD+ regenerated by the ETC.

shortExplanation: The drug binds the 30S subunit of the bacterial 70S ribosome, so it halts E. coli translation. Viral proteins are synthesized on the host's 80S ribosomes, which the drug cannot bind, so virus production continues.
solutionSteps: The target is the 30S subunit of the prokaryotic 70S ribosome, present in E. coli.
E. coli translation is therefore blocked and growth halts.
Viruses have no ribosomes; they hijack the host cell's 80S ribosomes to make viral proteins.
The drug cannot bind 80S ribosomes, so viral particle assembly proceeds and uninfected human cells are spared.
keyConcept: Antibiotics targeting the 70S/30S ribosome are selective for bacteria; eukaryotic 80S ribosomes and virus-directed host translation are unaffected.
commonMistake: Assuming viruses carry their own 70S ribosomes or that all ribosomes are identical.

optionExplanations.1: Viruses lack 70S ribosomes; they use the host's 80S, so viral production is not blocked.
optionExplanations.2: Structural simplicity is irrelevant; the mechanism depends on ribosome type, and the drug does not affect 80S.
optionExplanations.4: Uninfected human cells use 80S ribosomes the drug cannot bind, so they are not the most damaged.

shortExplanation: With q^2 = 0.09, q = 0.3 and p = 0.7, carriers are 2pq = 0.42 and normals are p^2 + 2pq = 0.91; among tested (symptom-free) people the carrier fraction is 0.42/0.91 = 0.46.
solutionSteps: aa frequency = q^2 = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 1 - q = 0.7.
Carrier frequency (Aa) = 2pq = 2*0.7*0.3 = 0.42.
Phenotypically normal fraction = p^2 + 2pq = 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91.
Fraction of tested (normal) people who are carriers = 0.42 / 0.91 = 0.46.
keyConcept: Conditioning on phenotype: divide the carrier frequency by the total unaffected frequency, excluding aa.
commonMistake: Reporting 2pq = 0.42 directly, forgetting that affected (aa) individuals are excluded from the tested group.

optionExplanations.1: 0.42 is the unconditional carrier frequency in the whole population, not among the tested subset.
optionExplanations.3: 0.49 is the AA (homozygous normal) frequency, not the carrier fraction.
optionExplanations.4: 0.33 uses a wrong allele frequency or denominator.

shortExplanation: The action-potential peak is driven by Na+ rushing in toward its equilibrium potential; lowering external Na+ lowers that potential, so the overshoot is smaller and less positive.
solutionSteps: Depolarisation (the rising phase and peak) is produced by Na+ influx.
The peak approaches the Na+ equilibrium potential, set by the Na+ concentration gradient.
Reducing external Na+ to one-third weakens the inward gradient and lowers E(Na).
The spike therefore reaches a lower, less positive peak.
Resting potential (set mainly by K+) and repolarisation are essentially unchanged.
keyConcept: The action-potential peak tracks the Na+ equilibrium potential, which depends on external Na+.
commonMistake: Assuming external Na+ affects resting potential; the resting value is governed mainly by K+.

optionExplanations.1: Resting potential depends on K+, which is unchanged, so it does not become more negative.
optionExplanations.2: A larger peak would require more Na+ outside, not less.
optionExplanations.3: Repolarisation (K+ efflux) is unaffected, so depolarisation is not prolonged.

shortExplanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ from NADH; blocking it lets NAD+ run out, and glycolysis (the only ATP source) needs NAD+ at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate step, so ATP production collapses.
solutionSteps: In alcoholic fermentation, glycolysis makes ATP but consumes NAD+, producing NADH.
Reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol oxidizes NADH back to NAD+, recycling the coenzyme.
Inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase stops NAD+ regeneration, so NAD+ becomes depleted.
Glycolysis halts at the NAD+-dependent step, and with no other ATP route, ATP production falls to near zero.
keyConcept: Fermentation's role is to regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
commonMistake: Thinking that because no ATP is made at the ethanol step, blocking it is harmless; the step is essential for coenzyme recycling.

optionExplanations.1: It ignores that glycolysis stalls once NAD+ cannot be regenerated, so ATP is not sustained.
optionExplanations.3: The block does not selectively disable 'the second half of glycolysis'; it stops NAD+ recycling, halting all of glycolysis.
optionExplanations.4: The cells are strictly anaerobic with no respiratory route, so switching to aerobic respiration is impossible.

shortExplanation: Removing the phloem ring blocks downward sugar transport, so sugars accumulate and swell the trunk just above the ring while roots starve; the xylem stays intact so leaves remain hydrated.
solutionSteps: Phloem carries sugars from leaves downward; xylem carries water upward.
Girdling removes only the phloem, cutting the downward sugar path.
Sugars back up and accumulate above the ring, producing a swelling there.
Roots below the ring are cut off from sugar and are gradually starved.
Because the xylem is intact, water still rises and the leaves stay hydrated.
keyConcept: Phloem (sugars, downward) versus xylem (water, upward); girdling blocks only phloem.
commonMistake: Thinking the leaves wilt, which would only happen if the xylem (water path) were cut.

optionExplanations.1: Leaves do not wilt because water transport through the xylem is unaffected.
optionExplanations.2: The swelling forms above the ring where sugars accumulate, not below it.
optionExplanations.3: No effect is wrong; xylem and phloem transport different substances.

shortExplanation: Water moves from higher to lower water potential. Cell A has water potential -0.4 MPa and cell B has -0.7 MPa, so water flows from A to B.
solutionSteps: Water potential of A = solute + pressure = -0.9 + 0.5 = -0.4 MPa.
Water potential of B = -0.7 + 0.0 = -0.7 MPa.
Water always moves down the water-potential gradient, from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative).
Since -0.4 MPa (A) is higher than -0.7 MPa (B), net water flow is from A to B.
keyConcept: Net water movement is set by total water potential (solute + pressure), not by solute potential alone.
commonMistake: Judging the direction from the solute potential only, forgetting that turgor pressure raises A's total water potential.

optionExplanations.1: It uses solute potential alone; adding A's +0.5 MPa turgor makes A's total water potential the higher one, so water leaves A.
optionExplanations.3: Turgor pressure raises A's own water potential, which pushes water out of A, not into it.
optionExplanations.4: A's water potential is -0.4 MPa, not -1.4 MPa; the two components are added, not compounded.

figureExplanation: The diagram of the two adjacent cells simply labels their solute and pressure potentials; adding each pair gives A = -0.4 MPa and B = -0.7 MPa, which drives flow from A to B.
formulaNotes: Water potential = solute (osmotic) potential + pressure (turgor) potential.

shortExplanation: Alkaline phosphatase removes the plasmid's 5' phosphates, so it cannot re-seal to itself, but the insert still supplies phosphates allowing insert-containing plasmids to ligate.
solutionSteps: Ligation requires a 5' phosphate to join to a 3' hydroxyl.
Self-ligation of the plasmid uses its own two 5' phosphates.
Alkaline phosphatase strips those 5' phosphates from the cut plasmid.
Now the plasmid alone cannot re-close, but the insert's 5' phosphates let insert+plasmid ligate.
This selectively suppresses empty re-circularisation.
keyConcept: Dephosphorylating the vector prevents self-ligation while insert phosphates enable recombinants.
commonMistake: Cutting with a different enzyme, which would destroy the compatible sticky ends needed for the insert too.

optionExplanations.1: A different enzyme would make ends incompatible with the insert, preventing correct ligation.
optionExplanations.2: More ligase speeds both self- and insert-ligation, not selective against self-closure.
optionExplanations.4: Excess plasmid over insert increases self-ligation rather than reducing it.

shortExplanation: Woese built the three-domain system on comparisons of small-subunit (16S) ribosomal RNA sequences, which is the fundamental criterion that revealed Archaea as a separate deep branch.
solutionSteps: The domain system was constructed from molecular phylogenetics, specifically small-subunit ribosomal RNA sequence comparisons.
16S rRNA is universal, functionally conserved, and slowly evolving, making it an ideal molecular clock.
Woese's rRNA trees placed Archaea on a branch as distinct from Bacteria as from Eukarya.
So the rRNA sequence divergence is the actual, fundamental basis for the separate domain.
keyConcept: The three-domain tree is a molecular phylogeny rooted in ribosomal RNA sequence comparison.
commonMistake: Choosing a striking biochemical trait (membrane lipids or cell walls) as the defining criterion; these corroborate but are not the basis Woese used.

optionExplanations.1: Ether-linked branched lipids are a genuine archaeal trait but a supporting feature, not the phylogenetic basis of the domains.
optionExplanations.2: Lack of peptidoglycan is diagnostic but descriptive, not the sequence-based criterion the tree was built on.
optionExplanations.3: Eukaryote-like transcription machinery is real and interesting but was not the founding evidence for the domain split.

shortExplanation: A positive Benedict's test with negative iodine and negative Biuret points to a reducing sugar such as glucose, with no starch and no protein present.
solutionSteps: Brick-red Benedict's precipitate indicates a reducing sugar.
No colour change with iodine rules out starch.
Blue (no violet) with Biuret rules out protein.
The only conclusion consistent with all three is a reducing sugar like glucose.
keyConcept: Benedict's = reducing sugar; iodine = starch; Biuret = protein.
commonMistake: Assuming sucrose, which is non-reducing and would give a negative (blue) Benedict's result.

optionExplanations.1: Starch would turn iodine blue-black, but iodine stayed orange-brown.
optionExplanations.2: Protein would give a violet Biuret result, but it stayed blue.
optionExplanations.4: Sucrose is non-reducing and would not give a brick-red Benedict's precipitate.

shortExplanation: Removing the parathyroids removes PTH, so bone releases less calcium (I) and kidneys lose more calcium (II). Calcitonin only lowers calcium when it is high, so it does not rise here (IV correct, III wrong).
solutionSteps: Parathyroidectomy eliminates PTH, the main hormone that raises blood calcium.
I is correct: without PTH, osteoclast-driven bone resorption drops, so bone releases too little calcium.
II is correct: PTH normally promotes renal calcium reabsorption; without it, more calcium is lost in urine.
III is wrong: calcitonin lowers calcium when it is high, so it would not rise to fix low calcium.
IV is correct: with calcium already low, calcitonin stays low or falls. So I, II and IV are correct.
keyConcept: PTH raises blood calcium via bone, kidney and gut; calcitonin only opposes high calcium, so it cannot rescue hypocalcemia.
commonMistake: Assuming calcitonin rises reflexively to 'correct' any calcium abnormality, when it only acts against high calcium.

optionExplanations.1: It endorses statement III, but calcitonin does not rise to correct low calcium.
optionExplanations.2: It omits the kidney effect (II) and keeps the wrong calcitonin rise (III).
optionExplanations.3: It drops the renal calcium-loss statement (II), which is a genuine PTH effect.

shortExplanation: The autonomous tumour floods the blood with T3/T4, so the intact hypothalamus-pituitary axis senses excess hormone and suppresses TSH via negative feedback. With little TSH stimulation, the normal thyroid tissue becomes underactive and tends to atrophy.
solutionSteps: The tumour secretes T3/T4 independently of feedback, raising circulating thyroid hormone.
High T3/T4 acts on the intact hypothalamus and pituitary, which respond by cutting TSH release (negative feedback).
Low TSH means the normal (non-tumour) thyroid receives little trophic stimulation.
Without TSH drive, the normal follicular tissue reduces its activity and tends to shrink.
keyConcept: Thyroid hormone exerts negative feedback on the pituitary; TSH falls and unstimulated normal thyroid tissue atrophies.
commonMistake: Assuming high hormone stimulates more TSH (positive feedback) or that a tumour bypasses the feedback loop entirely.

optionExplanations.1: TSH does not rise; high thyroid hormone suppresses it, and there is no positive-feedback amplification of TSH.
optionExplanations.3: TSH falls correctly, but low TSH causes the normal tissue to shrink, not enlarge.
optionExplanations.4: The feedback still senses the circulating hormone, so TSH is driven down, not unchanged.

shortExplanation: Deleting the first G of GGC shifts the frame to ATG-AAT-GCA-AAT-TGA. The new codon 5 is TGA (stop), so four amino acids (Met-Asn-Ala-Asn) are made before termination.
solutionSteps: Original coding sequence: ATG AAT GGC AAA TTG ACA CTG TGG CAA.
Delete the first G of GGC: the string becomes ATGAAT GC AAATTGACACTGTGGCAA.
Re-read in triplets: ATG / AAT / GCA / AAT / TGA / ...
Translate: ATG=Met, AAT=Asn, GCA=Ala, AAT=Asn, then TGA=Stop.
Four amino acids are incorporated before the frameshift-created TGA stops translation at codon 5.
keyConcept: A single-base deletion causes a frameshift that re-reads all downstream codons, often generating a premature stop.
commonMistake: Assuming a deletion just alters the sequence without shifting the frame, or terminating immediately at the deletion site.

optionExplanations.1: The stop appears at codon 5 (TGA), not codon 4; three amino acids is one short.
optionExplanations.3: Codon 5 is already TGA (stop), so translation cannot reach a fifth amino acid.
optionExplanations.4: A frameshift does not stop the ribosome at the deletion; it keeps reading in the new frame until a stop codon.

shortExplanation: A test cross giving 1 red : 1 pink : 2 white means the red parent is heterozygous at both genes, PpRr.
solutionSteps: The white tester is pprr, so offspring phenotypes reveal the red parent's gametes directly.
Half the offspring are white (pp): this requires the red parent to pass p half the time, so it is Pp for gene P.
Among the colored (P-carrying) offspring, red and pink appear equally, so the R locus segregates 1 Rr : 1 rr, meaning the parent is Rr.
Combining gives PpRr, which yields 1 PpRr (red) : 1 Pprr (pink) : 1 ppRr : 1 pprr (both white) = 1:1:2.
keyConcept: In a test cross the heterozygous partner's genotype is read straight off the offspring ratio.
commonMistake: Assuming any red parent works, ignoring that white offspring force a Pp (not PP) genotype.

optionExplanations.1: PPRr would give no white offspring, since every offspring inherits P.
optionExplanations.2: PpRR would give only red and white, never pink, because RR cannot yield rr offspring.
optionExplanations.3: PPRR is homozygous for both and would produce only red offspring.

formulaNotes: Test cross PpRr x pprr -> 1 red : 1 pink : 2 white.

shortExplanation: The affected grandfather makes his daughter (II-2) an obligate carrier, so III-1 is a carrier with probability 1/2. An affected boy requires a son (1/2) who inherits the disease allele, giving 1/2 * 1/2 * 1/2 = 1/8.
solutionSteps: Let X^A be the normal allele and X^a the recessive disease allele.
I-1 is affected (X^a Y); he passes X^a to every daughter, so II-2 is an obligate carrier X^A X^a (probability 1).
II-1 marries in and carries no disease allele: X^A Y.
III-1 receives X^A from her father (a father gives his X to daughters) and, from her carrier mother, is a carrier X^A X^a with probability 1/2.
III-2 marries in and is X^A Y.
For an affected boy: the child must be a boy (father gives Y, probability 1/2) AND inherit X^a from the mother.
P(mother III-1 is a carrier) = 1/2, and if so she transmits X^a with probability 1/2.
Combine: 1/2 (boy) * 1/2 (mother carrier) * 1/2 (transmits X^a) = 1/8.
keyConcept: For X-linked recessive traits, condition on the mother's carrier probability before applying transmission probabilities.
commonMistake: Forgetting that III-1's carrier status is only 1/2 (not certain) and computing 1/4 by treating her as a definite carrier.

optionExplanations.1: 1/4 ignores the 1/2 chance that III-1 is actually a carrier and treats her as a certain carrier.
optionExplanations.2: 1/2 only accounts for the child being a boy and ignores both carrier and transmission probabilities.
optionExplanations.4: 0 is wrong because the disease allele genuinely survives through the obligate carrier II-2 into the next generation.

figureExplanation: The filled square I-1 is the only affected individual; being an affected male grandfather forces his daughter II-2 to be a carrier, which is the anchor of the whole calculation, while all other symbols are open (unaffected) and the diamond marks the unknown-sex first child.
formulaNotes: P(affected boy) = P(boy) * P(mother carrier) * P(transmit X^a) = 1/2 * 1/2 * 1/2 = 1/8.

shortExplanation: All five ions share 18 electrons, so radius is set by nuclear charge: as Z rises from 16 (S) to 20 (Ca), the pull on the electron cloud increases and the radius shrinks. Hence S2- > Cl- > Ar > K+ > Ca2+.
solutionSteps: Each species has exactly 18 electrons (isoelectronic), so electron-electron repulsion is roughly the same.
Nuclear charge rises: S = 16, Cl = 17, Ar = 18, K = 19, Ca = 20.
Higher effective nuclear charge pulls the fixed 18 electrons inward, decreasing radius.
Order of decreasing radius: S2- > Cl- > Ar > K+ > Ca2+.
keyConcept: Among isoelectronic species, radius decreases as nuclear charge (atomic number) increases.
commonMistake: Thinking a higher positive charge means more shells/larger size, or that identical configurations mean identical radii.

optionExplanations.1: The order is reversed; more nuclear charge shrinks, not enlarges, the radius.
optionExplanations.2: Identical electron configuration does not mean identical size; nuclear charge differs.
optionExplanations.3: Neutral Ar is not the largest; the anions with the same electron count are larger.

formulaNotes: Isoelectronic radius trend: radius decreases as Z increases (Zeff up).

shortExplanation: CO2 is linear (180 degrees), CH4 tetrahedral (109.5), NH3 has one lone pair (~107), and H2O has two lone pairs (~104.5). Increasing lone-pair repulsion progressively narrows the angle: CO2 > CH4 > NH3 > H2O.
solutionSteps: CO2: two bonding regions, no lone pairs on C, linear -> 180 degrees.
CH4: four bonding pairs, tetrahedral -> 109.5 degrees.
NH3: three bonds + one lone pair -> ~107 degrees.
H2O: two bonds + two lone pairs -> ~104.5 degrees.
Rank largest to smallest: CO2 > CH4 > NH3 > H2O.
keyConcept: Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles below the ideal geometry value.
commonMistake: Placing CH4 above CO2 or treating NH3 and CH4 as equal despite NH3's lone pair.

optionExplanations.1: CH4 (109.5) is below linear CO2 (180), so CH4 cannot be first.
optionExplanations.2: The order is inverted; CO2 has the largest angle, not H2O.
optionExplanations.3: CH4 (109.5) and NH3 (107) differ, so they are not equal.

formulaNotes: Ideal angles: linear 180, tetrahedral 109.5; lone pairs reduce these (NH3 ~107, H2O ~104.5).

shortExplanation: 28 g of N2 is 1 mol and 9.0 g of H2 is 4.5 mol; since 1 mol N2 needs only 3 mol H2, nitrogen is limiting and yields 2 mol of NH3 (34 g).
solutionSteps: Moles N2 = 28 / 28 = 1.0 mol.
Moles H2 = 9.0 / 2 = 4.5 mol.
Ratio requires 3 mol H2 per mol N2, so 1 mol N2 needs 3 mol H2; H2 (4.5 mol) is in excess and N2 is limiting.
NH3 formed = 2 x moles N2 = 2.0 mol.
Mass NH3 = 2.0 x 17 = 34 g.
keyConcept: Identify the limiting reagent, then scale product by the mole ratio.
commonMistake: Assuming H2 is limiting because it is heavier per gram, ignoring the 3:1 mole requirement.

optionExplanations.1: 17 g is only 1 mol of NH3, half the amount the mole ratio actually gives.
optionExplanations.2: 51 g (3 mol) would need 1.5 mol N2, more nitrogen than is present.
optionExplanations.4: 68 g (4 mol) assumes all 4.5 mol H2 reacts, but N2 runs out first.

formulaNotes: moles = mass / molar mass; product = (limiting moles) x (product coefficient / reactant coefficient).

shortExplanation: AgNO3 provides 0.0200 mol and CaCl2 provides 0.0150 mol; AgNO3 is limiting, giving 0.0200 mol AgCl = 2.87 g.
solutionSteps: Molar mass CaCl2 = 40 + 71 = 111; moles = 1.665 / 111 = 0.0150 mol.
The 2:1 ratio means 0.0200 mol AgNO3 needs only 0.0100 mol CaCl2, so CaCl2 is in excess and AgNO3 is limiting.
AgCl formed = moles AgNO3 = 0.0200 mol (2 AgNO3 -> 2 AgCl).
keyConcept: Limiting-reagent stoichiometry in a precipitation reaction with a 2:1 ratio.
commonMistake: Treating CaCl2 (which has more Cl atoms) as limiting instead of checking mole ratios.

optionExplanations.1: 4.31 g (0.0300 mol) assumes CaCl2 sets the amount, but AgNO3 runs out first.
optionExplanations.3: 2.16 g corresponds to using 1.5x too little AgNO3.
optionExplanations.4: 5.74 g doubles the correct answer, implying 0.0400 mol AgNO3.

shortExplanation: Going C -> N -> O the central atom has 0, then 1, then 2 lone pairs, and because lone-pair/bond-pair repulsion exceeds bond-pair/bond-pair repulsion, each added lone pair squeezes the H-X-H angle further.
solutionSteps: All three molecules have four electron domains, giving a tetrahedral base geometry near 109.5 degrees.
CH4 has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the angle is the ideal 109.5 degrees.
NH3 has one lone pair whose stronger repulsion compresses the bond angle to about 107 degrees.
H2O has two lone pairs, compressing it further to about 104.5 degrees.
The ordering of repulsion strength (lone-lone > lone-bond > bond-bond) explains the decreasing trend.
keyConcept: VSEPR: lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs and shrink bond angles.
commonMistake: Attributing the angle change to electronegativity or atomic size rather than lone-pair count.

optionExplanations.1: Electronegativity is a secondary effect; the dominant cause is the increasing number of lone pairs.
optionExplanations.2: Atomic size actually decreases across the period, so 'larger atoms' is factually wrong.
optionExplanations.3: Hydrogen-hydrogen repulsion does not drive the trend; lone pairs do.

shortExplanation: The combined mixture has 90 mmol NaCl in 600 mL (0.15 M). Removing half discards half the moles, leaving 45 mmol; diluting back to 600 mL gives 45/600 = 0.075 M.
solutionSteps: Discarding half removes half the NaCl: 45 mmol remain in 300 mL.
Add water to 600 mL: concentration = 45 mmol / 600 mL = 0.075 M.
keyConcept: Removing a fraction of a homogeneous solution removes the same fraction of solute; dilution then divides moles by the new volume.
commonMistake: Ignoring that half the moles are discarded and keeping 90 mmol, or forgetting the pure-water portion.

optionExplanations.1: 0.15 M is the mixture before discarding half; the final dilution halves it.
optionExplanations.2: 0.20 M ignores both the water added and the discard step.
optionExplanations.3: 0.30 M is only the first NaCl portion's concentration, not the mixture.

formulaNotes: M = mol / V; discarding half removes half the mol.

shortExplanation: Only 0.50 ppm of fluoride must be added over 38.0 L, which is 19.0 mg = 1.0 mmol F-. From a 0.0500 mol/L NaF stock that requires 20.0 mL.
solutionSteps: Fluoride to add: target 1.0 - background 0.50 = 0.50 ppm = 0.50 mg/L.
Total added mass over 38.0 L: 0.50 mg/L * 38.0 L = 19.0 mg F-.
Moles F- = 19.0 mg / 19.0 mg per mmol = 1.0 mmol; NaF gives 1 F- each, so 1.0 mmol NaF.
Stock is 0.0500 mol/L = 0.0500 mmol/mL.
Volume = 1.0 mmol / 0.0500 mmol/mL = 20.0 mL.
keyConcept: Only the deficit above the natural background must be dosed; convert the required mass to moles and divide by stock concentration.
commonMistake: Dosing for the full 1.0 ppm instead of the 0.50 ppm increment needed above the existing background.

optionExplanations.0: 10.0 mL would dose only 0.25 ppm, half of what is needed.
optionExplanations.2: 40.0 mL doses the full 1.0 ppm as if the water were fluoride-free, overshooting the target.
optionExplanations.4: 2.0 x 10^4 mL is absurdly large; a 0.0500 M stock is far more concentrated than that.

formulaNotes: V(stock) = (delta ppm * volume / molar mass F) / stock molarity

shortExplanation: NaOH converts half the acetic acid to acetate, leaving equal moles of acid (0.005 mol) and conjugate base (0.005 mol), so by Henderson-Hasselbalch pH = pKa = 4.74.
solutionSteps: Moles acetic acid = 0.100 L * 0.10 M = 0.010 mol; moles NaOH = 0.050 L * 0.10 M = 0.005 mol.
NaOH neutralizes 0.005 mol acid, forming 0.005 mol acetate and leaving 0.005 mol acid.
This is a buffer with equal acid and conjugate base concentrations.
pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log(1) = 4.74.
keyConcept: At the half-neutralization point of a weak acid, pH equals the pKa.
commonMistake: Treating the mixture as pure leftover strong acid or assuming complete neutralization to a neutral solution.

optionExplanations.0: 2.87 treats the leftover acetic acid as a strong acid, ignoring the buffering acetate.
optionExplanations.2: 7.00 wrongly assumes full neutralization; only half the acid is neutralized.
optionExplanations.4: 11.52 assumes excess OH-, but NaOH is the limiting reagent here.

formulaNotes: Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); equal moles give log(1) = 0.

shortExplanation: Moles: O2 = 8/32 = 0.25, CH4 = 8/16 = 0.50; O2 mole fraction = 0.25/0.75 = 1/3, so its partial pressure = 1.50/3 = 0.500 atm.
solutionSteps: Moles of CH4 = 8.00/16.0 = 0.500 mol.
Partial pressure of O2 = (1/3)*1.50 atm = 0.500 atm.
keyConcept: Dalton's law: each gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times the total pressure.
commonMistake: Splitting the pressure by equal mass rather than by moles; equal masses give unequal mole counts here.

optionExplanations.0: 0.250 atm would need an O2 mole fraction of 1/6, not 1/3.
optionExplanations.2: 0.750 atm assumes equal moles of the two gases, which is false.
optionExplanations.3: 1.00 atm gives O2 the larger share, but CH4 actually has twice the moles.

shortExplanation: At fixed V, heating 300 K to 400 K raises pressure to 4/3 atm. Venting back to 1.0 atm at 400 K leaves n2/n1 = 300/400 = 0.75 of the molecules, so 25% were released.
solutionSteps: Before venting: n1 at 300 K, 1.0 atm; after heating (valve closed) n1 stays, P = 400/300 atm.
After venting at 400 K to 1.0 atm, remaining n2 = PV/(R*400) with P = 1.0 atm.
Fraction released = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 = 25%.
keyConcept: At fixed V and P, amount of gas is inversely proportional to absolute temperature (n proportional to 1/T).
commonMistake: Using the pressure ratio 4/3 directly as the vented fraction, or thinking the vessel volume is needed.

optionExplanations.1: 33% comes from 100/300 (an incorrect ratio); the correct fraction is 25%.
optionExplanations.2: 50% overstates the loss; only a quarter of molecules leave.
optionExplanations.4: The vessel volume cancels out, so it is not required.

formulaNotes: At fixed V, P: n proportional to 1/T; n2/n1 = T1/T2 = 300/400.

shortExplanation: Boiling occurs when a liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure; at altitude the external pressure is lower, so that equality is reached at a lower temperature.
solutionSteps: Boiling is defined as the temperature at which vapour pressure equals the surrounding atmospheric pressure.
At high altitude the atmospheric pressure is lower.
Therefore a lower vapour pressure, reached at a lower temperature, suffices for boiling.
So water boils below 100 degrees C on a mountain.
keyConcept: Boiling point is set by where vapour pressure meets external pressure.
commonMistake: Blaming colder mountain air; boiling depends on pressure, not on the surrounding air temperature.

optionExplanations.0: Colder air is irrelevant; the liquid must still be heated to its boiling point, which pressure lowers.
optionExplanations.2: Vapour pressure is an intrinsic property of the liquid at a given temperature; pressure does not raise it.
optionExplanations.3: Kinetic energy at a given temperature is unchanged by air thinness.

shortExplanation: In Cr2O7^2- each chromium is +6; reduction to Cr^3+ is a gain of 3 electrons per Cr, and there are two Cr atoms, so one dichromate gains 6 electrons.
solutionSteps: Assign Cr oxidation state in Cr2O7^2-: with O = -2, 2*Cr + 7*(-2) = -2 gives Cr = +6.
Reduction to Cr^3+ changes each Cr from +6 to +3, a gain of 3 electrons per atom.
Two Cr atoms per dichromate: total electrons gained = 2 * 3 = 6.
keyConcept: Electrons transferred = change in oxidation state per atom multiplied by the number of atoms.
commonMistake: Counting only one chromium (3 electrons) instead of both atoms in the dimeric ion.

optionExplanations.1: 3 counts only a single Cr; the ion has two Cr atoms.
optionExplanations.3: 12 doubles the correct count, perhaps confusing charge with electron number.
optionExplanations.4: 14 has no basis in the +6 to +3 change for two chromium atoms.

formulaNotes: Cr: +6 -> +3 is 3 e- each; 2 Cr per Cr2O7^2- gives 6 e-.

shortExplanation: Fe3+ is reduced (cathode) and Zn is oxidized (anode); E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode = 0.77 - (-0.76) = 1.53 V > 0, so the reaction is spontaneous.
solutionSteps: In the given reaction Zn is oxidized (Zn -> Zn2+) and Fe3+ is reduced (Fe3+ -> Fe2+).
Reduction occurs at the cathode, so the Fe3+/Fe2+ electrode is the cathode.
E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode = (+0.77) - (-0.76) = +1.53 V.
A positive E_cell means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
keyConcept: The electrode with the higher reduction potential is the cathode; E_cell = E_cathode - E_anode.
commonMistake: Adding the two potentials or subtracting in the wrong order, giving 0.01 V instead of 1.53 V.

optionExplanations.1: Zn is oxidized, so the Zn electrode is the anode, not the cathode.
optionExplanations.2: 0.01 V comes from adding the reduction potentials incorrectly rather than subtracting.
optionExplanations.3: The E_cell is +1.53 V and positive, so the reaction is spontaneous, not merely 0.01 V.

shortExplanation: N2 (1 mol) is limiting versus H2 (4.5 mol), giving a theoretical 34.0 g NH3; the 27.2 g collected is 27.2/34.0 = 80.0% yield.
solutionSteps: N2 needs 3 mol H2 per mol, so 1.00 mol N2 needs 3.00 mol H2; N2 is limiting.
Theoretical NH3 = 2 x 1.00 = 2.00 mol = 34.0 g.
keyConcept: Percent yield = actual mass / theoretical mass (from the limiting reagent) x 100.
commonMistake: Computing theoretical yield from H2 instead of the limiting N2, distorting the percentage.

optionExplanations.0: 35.6% would come from an inflated theoretical amount based on H2.
optionExplanations.1: 53.3% mis-scales the theoretical value.
optionExplanations.2: 97.1% divides by an incorrectly small theoretical mass.

formulaNotes: percent yield = (actual / theoretical) x 100; theoretical NH3 = 34.0 g.

shortExplanation: The mass lost on heating is the CO2 released: 12.5 - 8.1 = 4.4 g = 0.1 mol CO2, which came from 0.1 mol CaCO3 = 10 g, so 10/12.5 = 80%.
solutionSteps: Mass loss = mass of CO2 released = 12.5 - 8.1 = 4.4 g.
Moles CO2 = 4.4 / 44 = 0.10 mol (molar mass CO2 = 44 g/mol).
Each mole CaCO3 releases one mole CO2, so moles CaCO3 = 0.10 mol.
keyConcept: The mass lost during carbonate decomposition equals the mass of CO2 evolved, which back-calculates the carbonate.
commonMistake: Using the residue mass (8.1 g of CaO) as the carbonate, or forgetting the inert impurity does not lose mass.

optionExplanations.1: 44.8% might arise from using 8.1 g or 4.4 g directly as CaCO3 without the mole conversion.
optionExplanations.2: 64.8% comes from equating residue mass to CaCO3 mass incorrectly.
optionExplanations.4: 20.0% inverts the ratio, using the impurity mass instead of the CaCO3 mass.

formulaNotes: n(CO2) = (m_initial - m_final)/M(CO2); m(CaCO3) = n * 100; molar mass CaCO3 = 100 g/mol.

shortExplanation: Both acids supply 2.5 mmol of acid, but H2SO4 is diprotic so it needs twice the moles of NaOH. HCl needs 12.5 mL and H2SO4 needs 25.0 mL of the 0.200 M base.
solutionSteps: Moles of each acid: 0.0250 L * 0.100 M = 2.5 mmol.
HCl is monoprotic: needs 2.5 mmol NaOH; volume = 2.5 mmol / 0.200 M = 12.5 mL.
H2SO4 is diprotic: needs 2 * 2.5 = 5.0 mmol NaOH; volume = 5.0 mmol / 0.200 M = 25.0 mL.
So Flask 2 (H2SO4) requires exactly twice the NaOH volume of Flask 1 (HCl).
keyConcept: Neutralization depends on moles of replaceable H+, not just concentration; a diprotic acid supplies twice the protons per mole.
commonMistake: Assuming equal concentrations mean equal titrant volumes, ignoring that H2SO4 releases two protons per molecule.

optionExplanations.1: Equal molarity does not mean equal titrant; H2SO4's second proton doubles its base demand.
optionExplanations.2: It reverses the roles: the diprotic acid needs more base, not less.
optionExplanations.4: The volumes are doubled incorrectly; 2.5 mmol acid at 0.200 M base gives 12.5 and 25.0 mL, not 25.0 and 50.0 mL.

formulaNotes: V(base) = (protons per acid * moles acid) / molarity(base)

shortExplanation: O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+ are isoelectronic (10 electrons each), so radius shrinks as nuclear charge rises: Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2-. Cl- has 18 electrons and a much larger radius, so it is biggest.
solutionSteps: Note O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+ all have 10 electrons (isoelectronic with Ne).
Within an isoelectronic set, higher nuclear charge pulls electrons in tighter: Mg2+ (12p) < Na+ (11p) < F- (9p) < O2- (8p).
Cl- has 18 electrons and an extra occupied shell, so it is larger than any of the 10-electron ions.
Increasing radius: Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2- < Cl-.
keyConcept: For isoelectronic ions, ionic radius decreases as nuclear charge increases; adding an electron shell increases radius overall.
commonMistake: Placing Cl- among the small ions or ranking purely by charge sign, ignoring that Cl- has an additional electron shell.

optionExplanations.1: It wrongly makes Cl- the smallest; Cl- has an extra shell and is actually the largest.
optionExplanations.3: It puts Cl- below O2-, but Cl- (18 electrons, extra shell) exceeds the 10-electron O2-.
optionExplanations.4: The whole trend is reversed: cations here are the smallest, not the largest.

shortExplanation: Zn is 0.100 mol but only 0.150 mol HCl is available; HCl is limiting, giving 0.0750 mol H2 = 1.68 L at STP.
solutionSteps: Moles HCl = 0.1000 L x 1.50 M = 0.150 mol.
Zn needs 2 HCl per Zn: 0.100 mol Zn would need 0.200 mol HCl, but only 0.150 mol is present, so HCl is limiting.
Volume at STP = 0.0750 x 22.4 = 1.68 L.
keyConcept: Find the limiting reagent (HCl here), then convert to gas volume via molar volume.
commonMistake: Assuming all the zinc reacts and getting 0.100 mol H2 (2.24 L), ignoring that HCl runs out.

optionExplanations.0: 3.36 L (0.150 mol H2) wrongly equates moles H2 to moles HCl.
optionExplanations.1: 2.24 L assumes Zn is limiting, but HCl runs out first.
optionExplanations.2: 1.12 L halves the correct amount.

formulaNotes: V = n x 22.4 L/mol at STP; H2 moles = HCl moles / 2.

shortExplanation: AgNO3 gives 0.00500 mol and CaCl2 gives 0.00300 mol; AgNO3 is limiting, so 0.00500 mol AgCl = 0.718 g precipitates.
solutionSteps: Moles AgNO3 = 0.0500 L x 0.100 M = 0.00500 mol.
Moles CaCl2 = 0.0300 L x 0.100 M = 0.00300 mol.
2 AgNO3 : 1 CaCl2, so 0.00500 mol AgNO3 needs only 0.00250 mol CaCl2; AgNO3 is limiting.
AgCl formed = moles AgNO3 = 0.00500 mol.
keyConcept: Compare mole ratio to find the limiting reagent, then convert to precipitate mass.
commonMistake: Treating CaCl2 as limiting because it supplies two chlorides, ignoring the 2:1 stoichiometry.

optionExplanations.1: 0.861 g (0.00600 mol) assumes CaCl2 sets the amount via its two Cl atoms.
optionExplanations.2: 0.431 g uses only 0.00300 mol, undercounting AgCl.
optionExplanations.3: 1.44 g roughly doubles the correct value.

formulaNotes: Molar mass AgCl = 143.5 g/mol; moles = volume(L) x molarity.

shortExplanation: Al (0.10 mol) is the limiting reactant since it needs only 0.075 mol O2 and 0.10 mol O2 is available. The theoretical Al2O3 is 0.050 mol = 5.10 g, so 4.08 g gives a yield of 80%.
solutionSteps: O2 required for 0.10 mol Al = 0.10 * 3/4 = 0.075 mol; O2 is in excess, so Al limits.
Al2O3 formed = 0.10 * 2/4 = 0.050 mol; theoretical mass = 0.050 * 102.0 = 5.10 g.
keyConcept: Percent yield = actual mass / theoretical mass from the limiting reactant.
commonMistake: Treating O2 as limiting or forgetting the 4:2 mole ratio between Al and Al2O3.

optionExplanations.0: 40% would result from using twice the correct theoretical mass, e.g. a wrong mole ratio.
optionExplanations.3: 100% ignores that the actual 4.08 g is below the 5.10 g theoretical amount.
optionExplanations.4: 125% exceeds 100%, impossible; it comes from dividing theoretical by actual by mistake.

formulaNotes: percent yield = (actual / theoretical) * 100; theoretical = mol(limiting) * ratio * molar mass.

shortExplanation: The sample contains 11.25 g CaCO3 (0.1125 mol), releasing 0.1125 mol CO2. Using PV=nRT at 320 K and 0.960 atm gives about 3.08 L.
solutionSteps: Moles CaCO3 = 11.25 / 100.0 = 0.1125 mol; each mole gives 1 mol CO2, so n(CO2) = 0.1125 mol.
Convert temperature: T = 47 + 273 = 320 K.
Numerator = 2.956 L*atm; divide by 0.960 atm = 3.08 L.
keyConcept: Stoichiometry converts limestone mass to moles of CO2, then the ideal gas law gives its volume at the stated conditions.
commonMistake: Forgetting the 75% purity factor or leaving the temperature in Celsius instead of converting to Kelvin.

optionExplanations.1: 1.03 L results from omitting the 3x factor or misusing conditions; the mole count gives about 3 L.
optionExplanations.2: 2.52 L would use the full 15.0 g as CaCO3 at STP-like assumptions, not the 47 C, 0.960 atm state with 75% purity.
optionExplanations.4: 4.11 L overestimates; it ignores that only 11.25 g is CaCO3.

shortExplanation: Kc = [NO2]^2/[N2O4] = 0.20^2/0.10 = 0.40. After doubling the volume both concentrations halve, giving Q = 0.10^2/0.05 = 0.20, which is less than Kc, so the system shifts forward toward NO2.
solutionSteps: Compute Kc at equilibrium: 0.20^2 / 0.10 = 0.040 / 0.10 = 0.40.
Expansion to 2.0 L halves every concentration: [N2O4] = 0.05 M, [NO2] = 0.10 M.
Compute Q immediately after: 0.10^2 / 0.05 = 0.010 / 0.05 = 0.20.
Q (0.20) < Kc (0.40), so the reaction proceeds forward to increase the product.
keyConcept: Compare the reaction quotient Q with Kc; Q < Kc drives the forward direction.
commonMistake: Computing Q with un-halved concentrations, or blindly citing 'more moles of gas side' without checking Q.

optionExplanations.1: The direction (reverse) and the Q value (0.80) are both wrong; Q is 0.20, not 0.80.
optionExplanations.2: Although expansion does favour the side with more gas moles, the stated reverse direction contradicts Q < Kc.
optionExplanations.4: Q < Kc drives the forward, not the reverse, direction.

formulaNotes: Q = [NO2]^2 / [N2O4]; concentrations scale by 1/2 when volume doubles.

shortExplanation: HCl is the limiting reagent, producing 0.0375 mol H2, which occupies 0.924 L at 300 K and 1.00 atm.
solutionSteps: Zn needs 2 HCl each; 0.0500 mol Zn would need 0.100 mol HCl, but only 0.0750 mol is available, so HCl limits.
H2 formed = 0.0750 / 2 = 0.0375 mol (1 H2 per 2 HCl).
keyConcept: Identify the limiting reagent by comparing available moles to the stoichiometric requirement before applying PV = nRT.
commonMistake: Treating zinc as limiting, which gives 0.0500 mol H2 (about 1.23 L) instead of the correct 0.0375 mol.

optionExplanations.0: 0.0831 L uses far too few moles of gas.
optionExplanations.1: 0.840 L slightly undercounts the moles of H2.
optionExplanations.3: 1.23 L wrongly assumes zinc is limiting, giving 0.0500 mol H2.

shortExplanation: HCl supplies 6.0 mmol H+ and NaOH supplies 3.0 mmol OH-, leaving 3.0 mmol excess H+ in 50.0 mL, so [H+] = 0.06 M and pH = -log(0.06) = 1.22.
solutionSteps: moles H+ = 30.0 mL * 0.20 M = 6.0 mmol; moles OH- = 20.0 mL * 0.15 M = 3.0 mmol.
Neutralization leaves 6.0 - 3.0 = 3.0 mmol excess H+.
keyConcept: Strong acid in excess of strong base sets pH from the leftover [H+].
commonMistake: Forgetting to add the two volumes, or concluding pH 7 as if neutralization were complete.

optionExplanations.1: 0.92 corresponds to [H+] = 0.12 M, ignoring the volume dilution to 50 mL.
optionExplanations.3: pH 7.00 assumes full neutralization, but acid is in excess.
optionExplanations.4: 12.78 is basic, which would require excess base, not excess acid.

formulaNotes: pH = -log[H+]; [H+] = excess mol H+ / total volume.

shortExplanation: The digit-sum-divisible-by-6 rule really tests divisibility by 3, not 6. For 258 the digit sum is 15 (not divisible by 6) so the function returns false, yet 258 = 6*43 is actually divisible by 6.
solutionSteps: The shortcut returns true iff the digit sum is divisible by 6.
258: digit sum 2+5+8=15, not divisible by 6 -> function says false. But 258/6=43, truly divisible by 6. WRONG.
132: digit sum 6 -> says true; 132/6=22 -> truly true. Correct.
153: digit sum 9 -> says false; 153/6 not integer -> truly false. Correct.
246: digit sum 12 -> says true; 246/6=41 -> truly true. Correct.
508: digit sum 13 -> says false; 508/6 not integer -> truly false. Correct.
keyConcept: Digit-sum divisibility detects multiples of 3 (and 9), not multiples of 6, which also require the number to be even.
commonMistake: Believing digit-sum tests extend to 6; a number can be divisible by 6 while its digit sum is not divisible by 6.

optionExplanations.1: 132 has digit sum 6 and is divisible by 6, so the outputs agree.
optionExplanations.3: 246 has digit sum 12 and is divisible by 6, so the outputs agree.
optionExplanations.4: 508 has digit sum 13 and is not divisible by 6, so the false output is correct.

shortExplanation: The first 24 batches sum to 11520 mg and all 30 sum to 15000 mg, so the last 6 sum to 3480 mg, giving a mean of 580 mg.
solutionSteps: Sum of first 24 = 24 * 480 = 11520 mg.
Mean of last 6 = 3480 / 6 = 580 mg.
keyConcept: A group mean equals its subtotal divided by its count; totals are additive across subgroups.
commonMistake: Averaging the two given means (480 and 500) instead of working with the actual sums.

optionExplanations.1: 520 mg would follow only if the last 6 sum were 3120, which is not the case.
optionExplanations.2: 500 mg is the overall mean, not the last-6 mean, which must be higher to pull the average up.
optionExplanations.4: 540 mg does not match the required subtotal of 3480 mg.

shortExplanation: The sides are 4k and 3k, so the area is 12k^2 = 300, giving k = 5. The sides are 20 cm and 15 cm, so the perimeter is 2(20+15) = 70 cm.
solutionSteps: Read the side lengths from the figure: base OA = 4k, height OC = 3k.
Solve k^2 = 25, so k = 5.
Sides: 4k = 20 cm and 3k = 15 cm.
Perimeter = 2(20 + 15) = 70 cm.
keyConcept: For a rectangle, area = length x width and perimeter = 2(length + width).
commonMistake: Solving 12k^2 = 300 and stopping at k = 5 instead of converting back to actual side lengths.

optionExplanations.1: 35 cm is half the true perimeter, as if only one length plus one width were counted.
optionExplanations.3: 350 cm treats the area value itself as a length instead of solving for k first.
optionExplanations.4: 60 cm comes from adding 4k + 3k + k mismatched factors rather than the actual 20 and 15.

figureExplanation: The base is labelled 4k and the vertical side 3k; these are the two dimensions whose product is the given area.

shortExplanation: The x-intercepts are -1, 2, 3, so P(x) = a(x+1)(x-2)(x-3). The y-intercept 12 forces a = 2.
solutionSteps: Read the three roots from the graph: x = -1, x = 2, x = 3.
Write P(x) = a(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 3).
Use the y-intercept (0, 12): P(0) = a(1)(-2)(-3) = 6a.
Set 6a = 12, so a = 2.
Therefore P(x) = 2(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 3).
keyConcept: A polynomial is determined up to a leading scale factor by its roots; one extra point fixes that factor.
commonMistake: Forgetting the leading coefficient and choosing the version with a = 1 despite the y-intercept being 12, not 6.

optionExplanations.0: With a = 1 the y-intercept would be 6, not the 12 shown.
optionExplanations.2: The negative leading coefficient would send the graph down on the right, but the curve rises there.
optionExplanations.4: These factors give roots at 1, -2, -3, which do not match the marked intercepts.

figureExplanation: The curve crosses the x-axis at -1, 2 and 3 and passes through (0, 12) on the y-axis; both facts are needed to pin down the scale factor.

shortExplanation: Total arrangements are 7!/(3!2!) = 420, and those with red and blue adjacent are 120. Subtracting gives 300 valid patterns.
solutionSteps: Total distinct arrangements of 3 green, 2 yellow, red, blue: 7!/(3!2!) = 5040/12 = 420.
Count adjacent red-blue: glue them into one block, leaving 6 units (block, 3 green, 2 yellow).
Arrangements of these 6 units: 6!/(3!2!) = 720/12 = 60.
The block has 2 internal orders (red-blue or blue-red): 60 * 2 = 120 adjacent cases.
Valid patterns = 420 - 120 = 300.
keyConcept: Use total minus the glued-block count to enforce a non-adjacency constraint with repeated identical items.
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide by 3! and 2! for identical bulbs, or omitting the factor of 2 for red-blue order in the block.

optionExplanations.1: 360 does not subtract the correct 120 adjacent cases from 420.
optionExplanations.2: 150 would halve the answer, likely from mishandling the identical-bulb divisions.
optionExplanations.4: 420 is the unrestricted total, before removing adjacent red-blue arrangements.

shortExplanation: A = (-4, 5) and B = (6, -1) give slope -3/5, and the line simplifies to 3x + 5y = 13.
solutionSteps: Read coordinates: A = (-4, 5), B = (6, -1).
Use point A: y - 5 = (-3/5)(x + 4).
Multiply by 5: 5y - 25 = -3x - 12, so 3x + 5y = 13.
keyConcept: A line through two known points is fixed by its slope and either point.
commonMistake: Misreading B as (6, 1) or swapping the run and rise, which flips the slope sign.

optionExplanations.1: 3x - 5y = -37 uses the wrong sign on the y-term and fails both points.
optionExplanations.3: 3x + 5y = 0 passes through the origin, but neither A nor B lies on it.
optionExplanations.4: 3x + 5y = 37 has the correct left side but wrong constant; A gives 13, not 37.

figureExplanation: A sits at (-4, 5) in the upper left and B at (6, -1) in the lower right; these two lattice points fix the line.

shortExplanation: The five values are about 0.477, 0.592, 0.955, 1.047, 1.273, sitting left to right at R, P, T, Q, S. Only 3/pi ~ 0.955 lies strictly between 3/5 = 0.6 and 1, and it is marked T.
solutionSteps: Match the increasing values to the left-to-right points in the figure: R ~ 0.477, P ~ 0.592, T ~ 0.955, Q ~ 1.047, S ~ 1.273.
Test the interval (0.6, 1): 0.477 no, 0.592 no, 0.955 yes, 1.047 no, 1.273 no.
The only value strictly between 3/5 and 1 is 3/pi ~ 0.955.
That value sits at the point labelled T, just to the left of the 1 mark.
keyConcept: Estimating each expression numerically lets you order irrational quantities on a scaled number line and test an interval.
commonMistake: Reading 5/pi - 1 ~ 0.592 as being above 0.6 and choosing point P instead of T.

optionExplanations.0: Point P marks 5/pi - 1 ~ 0.592, which is below 3/5 = 0.6, so it is outside the interval.
optionExplanations.1: Point Q marks pi/3 ~ 1.047, which is above 1, so it is outside the interval.
optionExplanations.2: Point R marks 3/(2pi) ~ 0.477, well below 0.6.
optionExplanations.3: Point S marks 4/pi ~ 1.273, well above 1.

figureExplanation: The points appear left to right as R, P (near 1/2), then T, Q (near 1), then S (between 1 and 3/2); T is drawn just left of the 1 mark, matching 3/pi ~ 0.955.
formulaNotes: 3/pi ~ 0.955 is the only listed number satisfying 0.6 < value < 1.

shortExplanation: O1 = (2,2) with R = 6 and O2 = (5,6) with r = 1; the centre distance is 5 = R - r, so the circles are internally tangent with the small one inside.
solutionSteps: Read the larger circle: centre O1 = (2, 2), radius R = 6 (from (2,2) to (8,2)).
Read the smaller circle: centre O2 = (5, 6), radius r = 1.
Distance between centres = sqrt((5-2)^2 + (6-2)^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5.
Compare with R - r = 6 - 1 = 5; they are equal.
Since d = R - r, the circles touch at one point with the smaller inside the larger: internal tangency.
keyConcept: Two circles are internally tangent when the distance between centres equals the difference of radii.
commonMistake: Comparing d with R + r (external test) instead of R - r, wrongly concluding no contact.

optionExplanations.1: External tangency needs d = R + r = 7, but d = 5.
optionExplanations.2: Two intersection points need R - r < d < R + r; here d exactly equals R - r, so they only touch.
optionExplanations.3: A gap inside needs d < R - r, but d equals R - r exactly, so they touch.

figureExplanation: The single contact point sits on the line through both centres (near (5.6, 6.8)) on the far side of the small circle, the hallmark of internal tangency.
formulaNotes: Internal tangency condition: d(O1,O2) = R - r, here 5 = 6 - 1.

shortExplanation: The 7 cm side QR is adjacent to theta, and cos theta = 7/25, so QR/QP = 7/25 gives QP = 25 cm.
solutionSteps: The right angle is at R, so QP is the hypotenuse and QR is the side adjacent to theta.
From sin theta = 24/25, cos theta = sqrt(1 - (24/25)^2) = sqrt(49/625) = 7/25.
cos theta = adjacent/hypotenuse = QR/QP = 7/QP.
Set 7/QP = 7/25, giving QP = 25 cm.
keyConcept: In a right triangle, the cosine of an angle equals the adjacent side over the hypotenuse.
commonMistake: Treating the 7 cm side as opposite theta and dividing by sin theta instead of cos theta.

optionExplanations.0: 1.96 cm comes from multiplying 7 by cos theta (7*(7/25) = 49/25 = 1.96) instead of dividing by it.
optionExplanations.1: 7.29 cm comes from wrongly treating 7 as the side opposite theta: 7/sin theta = 7/(24/25) = 175/24 ~ 7.29.
optionExplanations.2: 24 cm is the numerator of sin theta (the side opposite theta in a 7-24-25 triangle), not the hypotenuse.
optionExplanations.4: 175 cm results from computing 7*25 instead of 7 divided by (7/25).

figureExplanation: The 7 cm side QR lies along the base next to angle theta at Q, making it the adjacent side; QP rising to P is the hypotenuse, and the right angle is marked at R.
formulaNotes: cos theta = 7/25 = QR/QP, so QP = QR/cos theta = 7/(7/25) = 25.

shortExplanation: Pages 4^6 = 2^12 and cells per page 8^4 = 2^12 give 2^24 total cells; dividing by 2^3 cells per word gives 2^21 words.
solutionSteps: Cells per page: 8^4 = (2^3)^4 = 2^12.
Cells per word: 2^3. Words = 2^24 / 2^3 = 2^21.
keyConcept: Rewrite every quantity as a power of 2 and combine exponents by multiplication (add) and division (subtract).
commonMistake: Adding the base exponents (6, 4, 3) directly instead of converting each to a power of 2 first.

optionExplanations.0: 2^24 is the total number of cells, before dividing into words of 2^3 cells.
optionExplanations.1: 2^7 comes from naively summing exponents rather than converting bases to 2.
optionExplanations.3: 2^12 is only the page count or per-page cell count, not the final word total.

shortExplanation: Line ell through (-1, 1) and (2, 3) has slope 2/3, so a perpendicular line has slope -3/2; through P(1, 4) this gives 3x + 2y - 11 = 0.
solutionSteps: Read two lattice points on ell from the graph: (-1, 1) and (2, 3).
Perpendicular slope = -1/(2/3) = -3/2.
Read P = (1, 4); use point-slope: y - 4 = (-3/2)(x - 1).
Multiply by 2: 2y - 8 = -3x + 3, which rearranges to 3x + 2y - 11 = 0.
keyConcept: Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals; then fit the line through the given point.
commonMistake: Using the slope 2/3 (parallel) instead of its negative reciprocal -3/2, or picking a line with the right slope that misses P.

optionExplanations.1: 2x - 3y + 10 = 0 has slope 2/3, so it is parallel to ell rather than perpendicular.
optionExplanations.2: 3x - 2y + 5 = 0 has slope 3/2, the wrong sign for the perpendicular direction.
optionExplanations.3: 2x + 3y - 14 = 0 has slope -2/3, still not the required -3/2.
optionExplanations.4: 3x + 2y - 14 = 0 has the correct slope -3/2 but does not pass through P: 3(1) + 2(4) - 14 = -3, not 0.

figureExplanation: Line ell passes through the lattice points (-1, 1) and (2, 3), giving slope 2/3; the target line must be perpendicular to it and pass through P at (1, 4).

shortExplanation: P(x) = (x-5)Q(x) and Q(5) = 0 means (x-5) also divides Q, so P(x) = (x-5)^2 R(x). Hence P is divisible by (x-5)^2.
solutionSteps: P divisible by (x-5) means P(x) = (x-5) Q(x).
Q(5) = 0 means (x-5) divides Q(x), so Q(x) = (x-5) R(x).
Substitute: P(x) = (x-5)*(x-5) R(x) = (x-5)^2 R(x).
Therefore P(x) is divisible by (x-5)^2.
keyConcept: A root shared by a polynomial and its quotient after removing (x-a) means (x-a) appears with multiplicity at least 2.
commonMistake: Thinking that dividing by (x-5) removes the root permanently, when Q(5)=0 shows the root has multiplicity 2.

optionExplanations.1: Divisibility by (x-10) is unrelated; the only guaranteed root is x=5.
optionExplanations.2: Divisibility by (x-25) is not implied by a double root at x=5.
optionExplanations.3: P(5) is actually 0 (in fact a double root), so this claim is false.

shortExplanation: With shares 3k:5k:8k, Gamma minus Alfa = 5k = 450 gives k = 90, so Beta minus Alfa = 2k = 180 euros.
solutionSteps: Let the shares be 3k, 5k, 8k for Alfa, Beta, Gamma.
Gamma - Alfa = 8k - 3k = 5k = 450, so k = 90.
Beta - Alfa = 5k - 3k = 2k.
keyConcept: Convert ratio parts to a common unit k using the given difference, then apply k to the requested difference.
commonMistake: Solving for k with the wrong difference (e.g., using 8k = 450) instead of the 5k difference between Gamma and Alfa.

optionExplanations.1: 90 euros equals k itself, not the Beta-Alfa difference of 2k.
optionExplanations.2: 270 euros equals 3k, not the difference between Beta and Alfa.
optionExplanations.3: 450 euros is the Gamma-Alfa difference, not the Beta-Alfa difference.

shortExplanation: The outer radius is 5 cm and the 2 cm wall gives an inner radius of 3 cm, so the steel volume is (4/3)pi(5^3 - 3^3) = 392pi/3 cm^3.
solutionSteps: Read the outer radius from centre to outer edge: 5 cm.
Read the wall thickness: 2 cm, so inner radius = 5 - 2 = 3 cm.
keyConcept: The volume of a spherical shell is the outer sphere volume minus the concentric inner cavity volume.
commonMistake: Using the 2 cm wall as a radius, or subtracting radii before cubing instead of cubing each radius first.

optionExplanations.1: 500pi/3 cm^3 is the full solid sphere of radius 5 with no cavity subtracted.
optionExplanations.3: 32pi/3 cm^3 is (4/3)pi times only the cavity of radius 2, a misread of the dimensions.
optionExplanations.4: 392/3 cm^3 drops the factor pi from the sphere volume formula.

figureExplanation: The shaded ring is the steel: outer radius 5 cm reaches the outer circle, the 2 cm wall marks the shell thickness, leaving an inner cavity of radius 3 cm.

shortExplanation: All means are 5, so variance is driven by spread from 5. Bea's scores (1,1,9,9,5) sit farthest from the mean, giving the largest sum of squared deviations.
solutionSteps: Read each player's five scores from the dot plots.
Ada: 0,4,5,6,10 -> squared deviations 25+1+0+1+25 = 52.
The largest total, 64, belongs to Bea, so Bea has the greatest variance.
keyConcept: With equal means, variance is largest when data cluster at the extremes rather than near the centre.
commonMistake: Judging variance by the range (width) alone; several players span 0-to-10-ish, but placement of the middle points changes the variance.

optionExplanations.0: Ada spans 0 to 10 but has three values at or near the mean, lowering her spread below Bea's.
optionExplanations.2: Cid keeps most scores near 5, giving the smallest variance of all.
optionExplanations.4: Width alone does not equal variance; Bea's mass concentrated at the extremes beats equal-width spreads.

figureExplanation: Bea's dots are stacked far out at about 1 and 9 with one at 5, placing four of five games far from the mean, unlike the more central spreads of the others.
formulaNotes: Variance is proportional to sum of (score - 5)^2 since all n = 5 and mean = 5.

shortExplanation: The vertex on the x-axis at (3,0) gives y = a(x-3)^2, and the y-intercept (0,18) forces a = 2, so b = -6a = -12.
solutionSteps: A double root at the vertex (3, 0) means y = a(x - 3)^2.
Use the y-intercept (0, 18): a(0 - 3)^2 = 9a = 18, so a = 2.
Read off b = -12.
keyConcept: A parabola tangent to the x-axis has a repeated root, so it factors as a(x - r)^2.
commonMistake: Forgetting the factor a when expanding, taking b = -6 (from a single (x-3)^2) instead of -12.

optionExplanations.0: 18 is the constant term c, not the coefficient b.
optionExplanations.1: 12 has the correct magnitude but wrong sign; the vertex at positive x makes b negative.
optionExplanations.2: -6 comes from expanding (x - 3)^2 without the leading coefficient a = 2.

figureExplanation: The curve just touches the x-axis at (3, 0) (the vertex) and rises to (0, 18) on the y-axis; these two points fix a and hence b.

shortExplanation: By Vieta's formulas alpha+beta = 4 and alpha*beta = 12/5, so 1/alpha + 1/beta = (alpha+beta)/(alpha*beta) = 4/(12/5) = 5/3.
solutionSteps: For 5x^2 - 20x + 12 = 0, sum of roots = 20/5 = 4.
Product of roots = 12/5.
1/alpha + 1/beta = (alpha + beta)/(alpha*beta).
keyConcept: The sum of reciprocals of roots equals sum of roots over product of roots, both from Vieta's formulas.
commonMistake: Inverting the ratio to get 3/5, or using the wrong signs for the sum and product of roots.

optionExplanations.1: -5/3 has the wrong sign; both sum (4) and product (12/5) are positive.
optionExplanations.2: 3/5 inverts the correct ratio (sum over product).
optionExplanations.4: 12/5 is the product of roots, not the sum of their reciprocals.

shortExplanation: The solid line through (0,1) and (2,2) is f(x) = x/2 + 1; solving for x gives the inverse f^{-1}(x) = 2x - 2.
solutionSteps: Read two lattice points on the solid line: (0, 1) and (2, 2).
Swap roles: write x = (1/2)y + 1 and solve for y.
keyConcept: The inverse of a linear function is found by swapping x and y and solving; its slope is the reciprocal of the original.
commonMistake: Reflecting the intercept incorrectly and keeping +2 instead of -2, or using the negative-reciprocal slope meant for perpendiculars.

optionExplanations.0: 2x + 2 has the right slope but wrong intercept; the inverse must pass through (1, 0), not (1, 4).
optionExplanations.3: -1/2 x - 1 uses the perpendicular slope, not the reciprocal needed for an inverse.
optionExplanations.4: 1/2 x - 1 keeps the original slope 1/2 instead of inverting it to 2.

figureExplanation: The solid line crosses (0,1) and (2,2); reflecting these across y = x sends them to (1,0) and (2,2), which lie on y = 2x - 2.

shortExplanation: Consecutive differences of a quadratic are linear: 5a+b=17 and 13a+b=41 give a=3, b=2. The difference from pattern 5 to 6 is 11a+b = 35.
solutionSteps: Difference P_{n+1} - P_n = a(2n+1) + b, which is linear in n.
Pattern 2 to 3 (n=2): 5a + b = 17.
Pattern 6 to 7 (n=6): 13a + b = 41.
Subtract: 8a = 24, so a = 3; then b = 17 - 15 = 2.
keyConcept: For a quadratic sequence the first differences form an arithmetic (linear) sequence, so two data points fix them.
commonMistake: Indexing the differences incorrectly (using n rather than the lower pattern number) when setting up the two equations.

optionExplanations.0: 23 would require different a, b than those forced by the two given differences.
optionExplanations.1: 29 skips the correct linear value at n=5.
optionExplanations.3: 41 is the pattern 6-to-7 difference, not the 5-to-6 difference.

shortExplanation: The asymptote x = -3 gives a = 3, so y = log2(x + 3). Setting y = 3 gives x + 3 = 8, so x = 5.
solutionSteps: The vertical asymptote is where x + a = 0; from x = -3, a = 3.
So the curve is y = log2(x + 3).
At P the height is y = 3: 3 = log2(x + 3).
Convert: x + 3 = 2^3 = 8.
Solve x = 5.
keyConcept: For y = log2(x + a), the vertical asymptote is x = -a, and log2(u) = 3 means u = 2^3.
commonMistake: Forgetting the +3 shift and solving 2^3 = x directly to get x = 8.

optionExplanations.0: x = 3 ignores the horizontal shift, as if the asymptote were at x = 0.
optionExplanations.3: x = 8 sets x + 3 = ... but forgets to subtract the shift, using 2^3 = x.
optionExplanations.4: x = 11 corresponds to y = log2(14), well above the given height of 3.

figureExplanation: The red dashed asymptote at x = -3 fixes a = 3, and the blue line y = 3 meets the curve at P where x + 3 = 8.

shortExplanation: The root x=1/2 forces m=6, giving p(x)=2x^3-9x^2+6x-1 = (2x-1)(x^2-4x+1). The quadratic yields x = 2 +/- sqrt(3).
solutionSteps: Solution set: x = 1/2, x = 2 - sqrt(3), x = 2 + sqrt(3).
keyConcept: Use a known root to find the parameter, then factor and solve the remaining quadratic for the other roots.
commonMistake: Miscomputing the discriminant (sqrt(12) vs sqrt(8)) or dropping the factor of 2 when dividing out (2x-1).

optionExplanations.1: 2 +/- sqrt(2) would need discriminant 8; here it is 12, giving sqrt(3).
optionExplanations.2: The root is x = +1/2, not -1/2, from the given data.
optionExplanations.3: Nice-looking rational roots 2 and 4 do not satisfy x^2 - 4x + 1 = 0.

shortExplanation: The line rises 2 for every run of 3, so its slope is 2/3; substituting point (1, 3) gives the y-intercept b = 7/3.
solutionSteps: Read the slope triangle: rise 2 over run 3, so slope m = 2/3.
Write the line as y = (2/3)x + b.
Substitute the marked point (1, 3): 3 = (2/3)(1) + b.
keyConcept: The y-intercept is found by plugging a known point into y = mx + b after reading the slope.
commonMistake: Taking the slope as 3/2 (run over rise) instead of rise over run.

optionExplanations.1: This overshoots; it results from adding rather than subtracting 2/3 from 3.
optionExplanations.2: This is the value 3/2, which comes from inverting the slope to 3/2 and mishandling the intercept.
optionExplanations.4: A negative intercept contradicts the graph, which crosses the y-axis between 2 and 3.

figureExplanation: The dashed slope triangle labelled run 3 and rise 2 fixes m = 2/3, and point B(1, 3) then pins b.

shortExplanation: The first A being the third quiz means the first two are non-A and the third is an A: (6/9)(5/8)(3/7) = 5/28.
solutionSteps: Need positions 1 and 2 to be non-A and position 3 to be A.
P(1st non-A) = 6/9.
P(2nd non-A given one gone) = 5/8.
P(3rd is A) = 3/7.
keyConcept: Sequential without-replacement probability multiplies conditional probabilities in the required order.
commonMistake: Ignoring the without-replacement change in denominators or allowing an A in the first two positions.

optionExplanations.1: 15/28 corresponds to a different event, not two non-A followed by an A.
optionExplanations.2: 1/3 wrongly assumes uniform placement of the first A across positions.
optionExplanations.3: 5/12 does not arise from the correct product 90/504.

shortExplanation: Depth becomes 60*1.45 = 87 cm after the storm, then loses one third to reach 87*(2/3) = 58 cm, a 3.3% decrease from 60 cm.
solutionSteps: Depth tracks volume, so apply the percentage changes to depth directly.
After Tuesday: 60 * 1.45 = 87 cm.
Remove one third: 87 * (2/3) = 58 cm.
Overall factor: 1.45 * (2/3) = 0.9667, i.e., about a 3.3% decrease.
Final depth 58 cm, roughly a 3.3% decrease from 60 cm.
keyConcept: Because cross-section is constant, depth scales with volume, so multiply the successive percentage factors.
commonMistake: Subtracting one third of the original 60 cm instead of one third of the post-storm 87 cm.

optionExplanations.1: 58 cm is correct but the change from 60 to 58 is 3.3%, not 2%.
optionExplanations.2: 60 cm ignores the net loss; the two changes do not cancel.
optionExplanations.4: 72.6 cm fails to remove a third of the increased volume after the storm.

shortExplanation: The corner at (−3, 12) forces a = 3, and solving |2x−6| + |x+3| = 9 on each piece gives x = 0 and x = 4.
solutionSteps: The corner of |x + a| occurs at x = −a; the figure puts it at x = −3, so a = 3.
Check: f(3) = |0| + |6| = 6 and f(−3) = |−12| + |0| = 12, matching the marked corners.
For x < −3: f(x) = −3x + 3 = 9 gives x = −2, which is not < −3, so it is rejected.
Solution set is {0, 4}.
keyConcept: A sum of absolute values is piecewise linear; solve on each interval and keep only roots inside that interval.
commonMistake: Accepting x = −2 from the left-hand piece without checking it lies in that piece's interval.

optionExplanations.0: This keeps the rejected root −2 and drops the valid root 0.
optionExplanations.1: This omits the intersection at x = 0 shown by the left small circle.
optionExplanations.3: This adds a spurious −2 that fails the domain check for its piece.

figureExplanation: The corners (−3, 12) and (3, 6) give a = 3; the two small circles where the graph meets y = 9 sit at x = 0 and x = 4.
formulaNotes: |x + a| has its corner at x = −a.

shortExplanation: The 12 batches plus the new value 7 give 13 numbers; the 7th ordered value is 5, so the median is 5.
solutionSteps: Read the dot plot counts: one 2, two 3s, three 4s, two 5s, two 6s, one 7, one 8 (12 values).
Add the 13th batch value of 7.
The median is the 7th value (middle of 13): that value is 5.
keyConcept: For 13 ordered values the median is the single middle (7th) entry.
commonMistake: Averaging the two central values as if the count were even.

optionExplanations.0: 4.5 is the median of the original 12 batches, before the 13th is added.
optionExplanations.2: 5.5 would require an even count with 5 and 6 straddling the middle.
optionExplanations.4: 7 is just the added value, not the middle of the ordered set.

figureExplanation: Counting stacked dots per column gives the 12 starting values used to build the ordered list.
formulaNotes: Median position for n = 13 is the (n+1)/2 = 7th ordered value.

shortExplanation: The plot is a trapezoid with parallel horizontal sides 9 and 3 and height 6, giving area (1/2)(9+3)(6) = 36 m².
solutionSteps: Parallel side AB runs from x = −3 to x = 6 at y = −2, length 9.
Parallel side DC runs from x = 1 to x = 4 at y = 4, length 3.
The perpendicular distance between them is 4 − (−2) = 6.
keyConcept: A trapezoid's area is half the sum of the parallel sides times the distance between them.
commonMistake: Using a slanted side length as the height instead of the vertical distance between the parallel sides.

optionExplanations.0: 24 uses too small a base or height combination.
optionExplanations.3: 54 doubles a factor, e.g. treats the average base times height without the 1/2.
optionExplanations.4: 72 uses the full sum 12 times 6 without halving.

figureExplanation: The grid gives AB = 9 (bottom) and DC = 3 (top) with a vertical gap of 6 between them.

shortExplanation: Prime positive differences are 2, 3, and 5. Counting ordered pairs gives 8 + 6 + 2 = 16 out of 36, i.e., 4/9.
solutionSteps: Possible positive differences: 0,1,2,3,4,5; primes among them are 2, 3, 5.
Count ordered pairs by difference: d=2 -> 8, d=3 -> 6, d=5 -> 2.
Total favorable = 8 + 6 + 2 = 16.
Probability = 16/36 = 4/9.
keyConcept: Enumerate ordered (red, blue) outcomes by their absolute difference and keep those equal to a prime.
commonMistake: Including difference 1 as prime, or miscounting the number of ordered pairs for each difference value.

optionExplanations.0: 5/9 (20/36) would incorrectly include some non-prime differences.
optionExplanations.2: 13/18 overcounts; only 16 of 36 outcomes give a prime difference.
optionExplanations.3: 7/18 (14/36) undercounts the favorable pairs.

shortExplanation: f is negative for −3 < input < 5, so f(2x−1) < 0 needs −3 < 2x−1 < 5, giving −1 < x < 3.
solutionSteps: From the graph, f(t) < 0 exactly when −3 < t < 5 (the shaded region between the roots).
Set the argument t = 2x − 1 inside this range: −3 < 2x − 1 < 5.
Add 1 throughout: −2 < 2x < 6.
Divide by 2: −1 < x < 3.
keyConcept: For a composite inequality, require the inner expression to fall in the interval where the outer function is negative.
commonMistake: Solving f(x) < 0 directly and reporting −3 < x < 5 without substituting 2x − 1.

optionExplanations.1: −3 < x < 5 ignores the substitution and just copies the roots.
optionExplanations.2: −2 < x < 2 comes from a half-completed transformation.
optionExplanations.4: This is the outside region, where f is positive, not negative.

figureExplanation: The shaded arc between roots −3 and 5 marks where f < 0, defining the interval for the argument 2x − 1.

shortExplanation: OP sits at 45° + 30° = 75° from the positive x-axis, so OQ = cos 75° = (√6 − √2)/4.
solutionSteps: The ray OA makes 45° with the positive x-axis.
OP is a further 30° from OA toward the y-axis, so its angle is 45° + 30° = 75°.
On the unit circle P = (cos 75°, sin 75°); OQ is the horizontal foot, length cos 75°.
keyConcept: The x-coordinate of a unit-circle point equals the cosine of its angle; use the sum formula for 75°.
commonMistake: Adding the angles incorrectly or using the sum formula for sine instead of cosine.

optionExplanations.1: (√6 + √2)/4 is cos 15° (or sin 75°), not cos 75°.
optionExplanations.2: (√2 − √6)/4 is negative, but OQ lies on the positive x-axis.
optionExplanations.4: (√3 − 1)/2 does not match cos 75° numerically.

figureExplanation: The 45° arc to OA plus the 30° arc from OA to OP places P at 75°, whose cosine is the length OQ.
formulaNotes: cos(A+B) = cosA cosB − sinA sinB; cos75° = (√6 − √2)/4.

shortExplanation: The slant height 10 and half-edge 6 give height 8; volume = (1/3)(12²)(8) = 384 cm³.
solutionSteps: Half of the 12 cm base edge is 6 cm.
The slant height, half-edge, and vertical height form a right triangle: 10² = h² + 6².
Solve: h² = 100 − 36 = 64, so h = 8 cm.
Base area = 12² = 144; Volume = (1/3)(144)(8) = 384 cm³.
keyConcept: The slant-to-edge-midpoint, half the base edge, and pyramid height form a right triangle.
commonMistake: Using the slant height 10 directly as the pyramid's vertical height in the volume formula.

optionExplanations.0: 288 results from using height 6 instead of 8.
optionExplanations.3: 576 doubles the correct volume, e.g. using height 12.
optionExplanations.4: 1152 forgets the factor 1/3 and uses base area times height.

figureExplanation: The 10 cm slant to the edge midpoint and the 12 cm base edge give half-edge 6, yielding height 8 by Pythagoras.

shortExplanation: Center C(−2, 1) and radius CP = 5 give (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 25.
solutionSteps: Read C = (−2, 1) and P = (1, 5) from the grid.
Standard form: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² with h = −2, k = 1, r² = 25.
This gives (x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 25.
keyConcept: Standard circle form uses the center (h, k) with sign flips and r² from the distance to a boundary point.
commonMistake: Writing (x − 2)² for a center at x = −2, or leaving r instead of r² on the right side.

optionExplanations.0: (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² flips both center signs the wrong way.
optionExplanations.2: This uses r = 5 as r², giving 5 instead of 25.
optionExplanations.3: This misreads the center as (1, 5), which is actually the point P.

figureExplanation: C is at (−2, 1) and P at (1, 5); the radius CP measures 5, fixing r² = 25.
formulaNotes: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², r = distance from center to P.

shortExplanation: Reaching +2 after 4 jumps needs 3 rights and 1 left; there are C(4,3) = 4 such paths out of 16, giving 1/4.
solutionSteps: Let R rights and L lefts, R + L = 4 and R - L = 2, so R = 3, L = 1.
Number of sequences with exactly 3 rights: C(4,3) = 4.
Total equally likely sequences: 2^4 = 16.
Probability = 4/16 = 1/4.
keyConcept: A signed random walk lands at a position set by the count of right steps; use the binomial count over all 2^n paths.
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide by all 16 outcomes, or solving R and L incorrectly from the position and step-count equations.

optionExplanations.0: 1/16 is the probability of a single specific path, not all four that reach +2.
optionExplanations.2: 5/16 does not correspond to C(4,3)=4 favorable outcomes.
optionExplanations.3: 3/8 (6/16) matches landing at 0, not at +2.

shortExplanation: The lateral surface equals the sector area: (240/360)·π·12² = (2/3)(144)π = 96π cm².
solutionSteps: The unrolled lateral surface is the sector itself, radius 12 cm, angle 240°.
Compute: (2/3)·π·144 = 96π cm².
keyConcept: A cone's lateral surface area equals the area of the sector that forms its net.
commonMistake: Using the full circle area π·12² and ignoring the 240° fraction.

optionExplanations.1: 144π is the full-circle area, not the 240° sector.
optionExplanations.2: 160π does not correspond to any correct fraction of 144π.
optionExplanations.3: 64π would use a 160° angle, not 240°.

figureExplanation: The shaded sector has slant edge 12 cm and central angle 240°, and its area is the cone's lateral surface.

shortExplanation: Since the product of roots is −15 and one root is 5, the other is −3, so f(x) ≤ 0 on −3 ≤ x ≤ 5.
solutionSteps: For f(x) = x² + bx − 15, the product of the roots equals −15.
