One x-intercept is 5, so the other root is −15/5 = −3.
The upward parabola is ≤ 0 between its roots.
Solution: −3 ≤ x ≤ 5.
keyConcept: An upward parabola is non-positive on the closed interval between its two roots.
commonMistake: Reporting the outside region (x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 5), which is where the parabola is positive.

optionExplanations.0: x ≤ −3 or x ≥ 5 is where f is ≥ 0, the opposite region.
optionExplanations.1: −5 ≤ x ≤ 3 swaps the roots to −5 and 3.
optionExplanations.3: x ≤ −5 or x ≥ 3 uses the wrong roots and the wrong region.

figureExplanation: The graph gives the y-intercept −15 and one x-intercept at 5; the product of roots −15 fixes the other root at −3.
formulaNotes: For x² + bx + c, product of roots = c; here −15.

shortExplanation: The focus F(2, 1) is 2 below the vertex V(2, 3), so the directrix is 2 above the vertex at y = 5.
solutionSteps: Vertex V = (2, 3), focus F = (2, 1); the focus lies below the vertex, so the parabola opens downward.
Focal distance p = |3 − 1| = 2.
The directrix is the same distance on the opposite side of the vertex from the focus.
So it sits 2 above the vertex: y = 3 + 2 = 5.
keyConcept: The vertex is midway between focus and directrix, which lie on opposite sides at equal distance.
commonMistake: Placing the directrix on the same side as the focus, giving y = 1.

optionExplanations.1: y = 1 is the focus line, not the directrix.
optionExplanations.2: y = 3 is the vertex's height, not the directrix.
optionExplanations.4: x = 2 is the axis of symmetry, a vertical line, not a horizontal directrix.

figureExplanation: V(2, 3) sits 2 above F(2, 1); the directrix mirrors the focus across the vertex, landing at y = 5.
formulaNotes: Vertex is midpoint of focus and directrix; directrix distance = focal distance.

shortExplanation: P lies in the third quadrant with reference angle 30°, so θ = 210° and sin θ = −1/2.
solutionSteps: P is below the x-axis and left of the y-axis, placing the terminal ray in the third quadrant.
The acute angle with the x-axis is 30°, so the reference angle is 30°.
In the third quadrant sine is negative: sin θ = −sin 30°.
Thus sin θ = −1/2.
keyConcept: Sine equals the y-coordinate on the unit circle, negative in the third quadrant.
commonMistake: Taking sin 30° as +1/2 and ignoring the sign for the third quadrant.

optionExplanations.0: 1/2 ignores that P lies below the x-axis.
optionExplanations.1: −√3/2 is sin of a 60° reference angle, not 30°.
optionExplanations.3: √3/2 is both the wrong sign and the wrong reference angle.

figureExplanation: P sits in the lower-left (third quadrant) with a 30° angle to the negative x-axis, so its y-coordinate sin θ is −1/2.
formulaNotes: sin θ = y-coordinate; third-quadrant sine < 0; sin 30° = 1/2.

shortExplanation: The counts are 3,9,8,5,3,1,0,0,1 for 0..8 seeds, giving mode 1, median 2, mean 65/30 ≈ 2.17, so mean > median > mode. Removing the lone 8-seed pot drops the mean to 57/29 ≈ 1.97 (now below the median), while the median stays 2 and the mode stays 1.
solutionSteps: Mode = value with the tallest bar = 1.
Median = average of the 15th and 16th ordered values; both fall in the '2 seeds' group, so median = 2.
Remove the single 8-seed pot: sum = 57, n = 29, mean = 57/29 ≈ 1.97, which is below the median.
The median (still the 15th value = 2) and the mode (still 1) are unchanged.
keyConcept: In a right-skewed distribution mean > median > mode, and a lone high outlier pulls only the mean.
commonMistake: Assuming one pot out of thirty cannot move the mean enough to matter.

optionExplanations.0: The bars are clearly right-skewed, not symmetric, so the three averages are not equal.
optionExplanations.1: The ordering is reversed: the high tail makes the mean the largest and the mode the smallest.
optionExplanations.2: The mode is set by the tallest bar (1 seed); deleting the 8-seed pot does not change it to 2.

figureExplanation: The tallest bar is at 1 seed (mode), the bulk of pots sit at 1-2 seeds, and a single isolated bar at 8 seeds forms the right tail that inflates the mean.
formulaNotes: mean = (sum of value*frequency)/n; median = middle ordered value(s).

shortExplanation: M is the common midpoint of the diagonals. Using P(-3,-2) and R(5,2), M = ((-3+5)/2, (-2+2)/2) = (1, 0).
solutionSteps: The diagonals of parallelogram PQRS are PR and QS, and they bisect each other at M.
keyConcept: The intersection of a parallelogram's diagonals is the midpoint of each diagonal.
commonMistake: Pairing adjacent vertices (a side) instead of opposite vertices (a diagonal).

optionExplanations.1: (2,0) would require the diagonal endpoints to average to x = 2, but they average to 1.
optionExplanations.3: (4,-0.5) is not the midpoint of either diagonal; it does not lie at the crossing of the dashed lines.
optionExplanations.4: (-2,0.5) sits well to the upper-left of where the diagonals actually cross.

figureExplanation: The dashed diagonals PR and QS cross just to the right of the y-axis at the marked point M ≈ (1, 0).

shortExplanation: Count multiples of 4 or 6 from 1 to 60 using inclusion-exclusion, then divide by 60. There are 20 such numbers, giving probability 1/3.
solutionSteps: Multiples of 4 in 1..60: 60/4 = 15.
Multiples of 6 in 1..60: 60/6 = 10.
Multiples of both (i.e. of 12): 60/12 = 5.
Union = 15 + 10 - 5 = 20 numbers.
Probability = 20/60 = 1/3.
keyConcept: Inclusion-exclusion: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|.
commonMistake: Forgetting to subtract the overlap (multiples of 12), which double-counts them.

optionExplanations.1: 5/12 = 25/60 comes from adding 15 + 10 without subtracting the 5 shared multiples of 12.
optionExplanations.2: 23/60 miscounts the overlap or one of the base counts; the correct union is 20.
optionExplanations.4: 1/12 corresponds only to the 5 multiples of 12, not the full union.

formulaNotes: P = (multiples of 4 + multiples of 6 - multiples of 12)/60 = (15+10-5)/60.

shortExplanation: Group A scores are 1,5,5,5,9 (squared deviations sum 16+0+0+0+16 = 32); Group B scores are 2,2,5,8,8 (sum 9+9+0+9+9 = 36). Group B has the larger total squared deviation and therefore the larger standard deviation.
solutionSteps: Read the dot plots: Group A = {1,5,5,5,9}, Group B = {2,2,5,8,8}, both with mean 5.
Group A squared deviations from 5: 16, 0, 0, 0, 16 → total 32.
Group B squared deviations from 5: 9, 9, 0, 9, 9 → total 36.
Since standard deviation grows with total squared deviation (same n), Group B's is larger.
keyConcept: Standard deviation depends on the sum of squared deviations, not on the range alone.
commonMistake: Judging spread by range (A is wider) instead of by how many points sit far from the mean.

optionExplanations.0: Range favors Group A, but range ignores that Group B has four points far from the mean; total squared deviation decides it.
optionExplanations.3: Group A's extremes are individually farther (4 vs 3), yet its three central points contribute nothing, so its total is smaller.
optionExplanations.4: The population-vs-sample choice scales both groups by the same factor and cannot flip which is larger.

figureExplanation: Group A clusters three dots exactly on the mean of 5 with only two outliers, while Group B places four dots equally at 2 and 8, spreading more mass away from the mean.
formulaNotes: sigma is proportional to sqrt(sum (x - mean)^2); compare the sums of squared deviations.

shortExplanation: The first drop is 18 m; every rebound is climbed and re-fallen, forming a geometric series with ratio 2/3. Total distance = 18 + 2*(36) = 90 m.
solutionSteps: Initial fall = 18 m (down only).
Rebound heights: 18*(2/3)=12, then 8, ... a geometric series with first term 12 and ratio 2/3.
Sum of rebound heights = 12/(1 - 2/3) = 12/(1/3) = 36 m.
Each rebound is traveled twice (up then down): 2*36 = 72 m.
keyConcept: Infinite geometric series sum a/(1-r) for |r|<1, with rebounds counted up and down.
commonMistake: Counting the rebounds only once, or including the initial 18 m in the doubled part.

optionExplanations.0: 72 m is only the doubled rebound distance, omitting the initial 18 m drop.
optionExplanations.1: 108 m comes from doubling the initial fall as well, but the first 18 m is a fall only.
optionExplanations.3: 54 m results from summing rebounds once (36) plus 18, ignoring the return climbs.

shortExplanation: The y-intercept gives c = 7, and minima at x = ±2 force b = -8, so f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2 + 7 and f(2) = 16 - 32 + 7 = -9.
solutionSteps: y-intercept: f(0) = c = 7.
f'(x) = 4x^3 + 2bx = 2x(2x^2 + b); the nonzero minima satisfy 2x^2 + b = 0.
keyConcept: Setting the derivative to zero at the marked minimum locates b; the intercept gives c.
commonMistake: Reading -9 as the y-intercept or forgetting to subtract the -8x^2 term at x = 2.

optionExplanations.0: -16 comes from using only x^4 - 8x^2 (ignoring c = +7) at x = 2.
optionExplanations.2: -5 does not satisfy f(2) = 16 - 32 + 7 for the required b and c.
optionExplanations.3: 3 and 7 are positive, but the marked lowest points lie below the x-axis, so the minimum must be negative.

figureExplanation: The curve crosses the y-axis at (0,7) and dips to its two equal lowest points directly above x = ±2, fixing c and b.
formulaNotes: f(x) = x^4 + bx^2 + c; minimum at x=2 means b = -8, c = f(0) = 7.

shortExplanation: Factor the difference of cubes and the difference of squares, then cancel the common factor 2x-3. The result is (4x^2 + 6x + 9)/(2x + 3).
solutionSteps: 8x^3 - 27 = (2x - 3)(4x^2 + 6x + 9) (difference of cubes).
4x^2 - 9 = (2x - 3)(2x + 3) (difference of squares).
Cancel the common factor (2x - 3).
keyConcept: Difference of cubes a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2); difference of squares a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b).
commonMistake: Getting the middle sign of the quadratic factor wrong (writing 4x^2 - 6x + 9 instead of +6x).

optionExplanations.1: (4x^2 - 6x + 9)/(2x + 3) uses the wrong sum-of-cubes trinomial; here the sign is +6x.
optionExplanations.2: (4x^2 + 6x + 9)/(2x - 3) cancels the wrong factor, leaving 2x-3 in the denominator.
optionExplanations.3: 2x - 3 would require the numerator to factor as (2x-3)^2 times the denominator, which it does not.

shortExplanation: The foci lie on the y-axis at (0,±4), so c = 4 and the major axis is vertical; the x-axis endpoint (3,0) gives b = 3, so a^2 = b^2 + c^2 = 25 and the equation is x^2/9 + y^2/25 = 1.
solutionSteps: Foci at (0,±4) mean the major axis is vertical with c = 4.
The marked axis endpoint (3,0) is a minor-axis vertex, so b = 3, b^2 = 9.
For an ellipse, a^2 = b^2 + c^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.
With the major axis along y, the equation is x^2/9 + y^2/25 = 1.
keyConcept: Foci lie on the major axis, and a^2 = b^2 + c^2 for an ellipse.
commonMistake: Placing the larger denominator under x when the foci (and major axis) are actually vertical.

optionExplanations.1: x^2/25 + y^2/9 = 1 has a horizontal major axis, contradicting foci on the y-axis.
optionExplanations.2: x^2/9 + y^2/16 = 1 gives a^2 = 16, but c = 4 needs a^2 = 25.
optionExplanations.4: x^2/9 + y^2/7 = 1 has a^2 < b^2, which cannot hold with vertical foci.

figureExplanation: The ellipse is taller than it is wide, with both foci on the vertical axis at (0,±4) and its side reaching (3,0).
formulaNotes: vertical ellipse: x^2/b^2 + y^2/a^2 = 1 with a^2 = b^2 + c^2.

shortExplanation: Vertices at (0,±4) give a vertical transverse axis with a = 4; the asymptote through (3,4) has slope a/b = 4/3, so b = 3 and the equation is y^2/16 - x^2/9 = 1.
solutionSteps: Vertices (0,±4) on the y-axis: transverse axis vertical, a = 4, a^2 = 16.
For y^2/a^2 - x^2/b^2 = 1 the asymptotes are y = ±(a/b)x.
The asymptote passes through (3,4), so slope = 4/3 = a/b = 4/b → b = 3, b^2 = 9.
Equation: y^2/16 - x^2/9 = 1.
keyConcept: A vertical hyperbola has y^2 positive, a from the vertices, and asymptote slope a/b.
commonMistake: Swapping the x^2 and y^2 terms, which describes a horizontal hyperbola instead.

optionExplanations.1: y^2/9 - x^2/16 = 1 puts a^2 = 9, but the vertices at (0,±4) require a^2 = 16.
optionExplanations.2: x^2/16 - y^2/9 = 1 is a horizontal hyperbola with vertices on the x-axis, not at (0,±4).
optionExplanations.4: y^2/4 - x^2/3 = 1 gives a = 2, contradicting vertices at y = ±4.

figureExplanation: The two branches open up and down through (0,±4), and the dashed asymptotes pass through the rectangle corner (3,4), fixing slope 4/3.
formulaNotes: vertical hyperbola: y^2/a^2 - x^2/b^2 = 1, asymptotes y = ±(a/b)x.

shortExplanation: The altitude to the base splits it into two 5-13 right triangles, so h = sqrt(13^2 - 5^2) = 12, and the area is (1/2)*10*12 = 60.
solutionSteps: The base is 10, so each half of the base is 5, and the equal sides are 13.
The altitude h satisfies h^2 + 5^2 = 13^2 → h^2 = 169 - 25 = 144 → h = 12.
keyConcept: In an isosceles triangle the altitude to the base bisects it, forming right triangles.
commonMistake: Using a slant side (13) as the height instead of computing the true altitude.

optionExplanations.0: 30 uses h = 6, which is half the actual altitude.
optionExplanations.3: 78 = (1/2)*12*13 mistakenly multiplies the height by a slant side rather than the base.
optionExplanations.4: 120 = (1/2)*10*24 doubles the correct height.

figureExplanation: The dashed wire is the altitude h dropped to the midpoint of the base, shown with a right angle, creating a 5-12-13 right triangle.

shortExplanation: At theta = 0 the value is b ≈ sqrt(3) and at theta = 90 it is a = 1, giving f(theta) = sin theta + sqrt(3) cos theta, whose amplitude 2 peaks at 30° exactly as shown.
solutionSteps: f(0°) = b: the curve starts near 1.73 = sqrt(3), so b = sqrt(3).
f(90°) = a: the curve ends at 1, so a = 1.
Thus f(theta) = sin theta + sqrt(3) cos theta.
Amplitude = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2, and the peak occurs where tan theta = a/b = 1/sqrt(3), i.e. theta = 30°, matching the marked peak of 2.
keyConcept: For a sin theta + b cos theta, f(0) = b, f(90°) = a, amplitude = sqrt(a^2+b^2), peak at tan theta = a/b.
commonMistake: Swapping a and b, i.e. reading the theta = 0 value as the coefficient of sin instead of cos.

optionExplanations.1: sqrt(3) sin theta + cos theta gives f(0) = 1 and f(90°) = sqrt(3), the reverse of the graph, and peaks at 60°.
optionExplanations.2: sin theta + cos theta has amplitude sqrt(2) ≈ 1.41, too small for the peak of 2.
optionExplanations.3: 2 sin theta + 2 cos theta has amplitude 2*sqrt(2) ≈ 2.83 and f(0) = 2, not sqrt(3).

figureExplanation: The curve starts at about 1.73 (sqrt 3) at 0°, rises to a peak of 2 at 30°, then falls to 1 at 90°, pinning b = sqrt(3) and a = 1.
formulaNotes: amplitude R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2); f(0) = b, f(90°) = a.

shortExplanation: The inscribed sphere fixes cylinder radius 6 and height 12, so cylinder volume = 432π and sphere volume = 288π; the region between them is 432π - 288π = 144π cm³.
solutionSteps: Tangency to the wall gives cylinder radius = sphere radius = 6 cm.
Tangency to top and bottom gives cylinder height = sphere diameter = 12 cm.
Cylinder volume = π r^2 h = π*36*12 = 432π.
Sphere volume = (4/3)π r^3 = (4/3)π*216 = 288π.
Inside cylinder but outside sphere = 432π - 288π = 144π cm³.
keyConcept: A sphere inscribed in a cylinder shares its radius and has height equal to the diameter.
commonMistake: Subtracting the cone instead of the sphere, or forgetting height = 2r.

optionExplanations.1: 216π is the cone's volume ((1/3)*432π), not the requested cylinder-minus-sphere region.
optionExplanations.2: 288π is the sphere's own volume, not the leftover space.
optionExplanations.3: 432π is the full cylinder volume before removing the sphere.

figureExplanation: The cross-section shows the circle touching the top, bottom, and both sides of the square, so r = 6 sets both the cylinder radius and half its height; the cone drawn inside is a distractor.
formulaNotes: V_cylinder = π r^2 h, V_sphere = (4/3)π r^3; here h = 2r = 12, r = 6.

shortExplanation: The red segment joins opposite corners through the interior, so it is the space diagonal s*sqrt(3) = 6, giving s^2 = 12 and total surface area 6s^2 = 72 cm².
solutionSteps: The segment runs from a bottom vertex to the opposite top vertex through the cube's interior: it is the space diagonal.
Space diagonal = s*sqrt(3) = 6 → s = 6/sqrt(3), so s^2 = 36/3 = 12.
Surface area of a cube = 6s^2 = 6*12 = 72 cm².
keyConcept: A cube's space diagonal equals s*sqrt(3), and its surface area is 6s^2.
commonMistake: Treating the interior diagonal as a face diagonal (s*sqrt(2)) or as an edge.

optionExplanations.0: 48 uses s^2 = 8, which no correct interpretation of the diagonal produces.
optionExplanations.2: 108 comes from treating 6 as a face diagonal (s*sqrt(2)), giving s^2 = 18.
optionExplanations.3: 216 comes from treating 6 as an edge length (s = 6).

figureExplanation: The red line connects the front-bottom vertex to the far top-back vertex, passing through the cube's interior, so it is the body diagonal, not a face diagonal or edge.
formulaNotes: space diagonal d = s*sqrt(3); surface area = 6s^2.

shortExplanation: Line ℓ through (0,6) and (8,0) is 3x + 4y - 24 = 0; the radius is the distance from C(4,8): |3*4 + 4*8 - 24|/5 = 20/5 = 4.
solutionSteps: Line ℓ through (0,6) and (8,0) has slope -6/8 = -3/4, giving 3x + 4y - 24 = 0.
The radius equals the perpendicular distance from the centre to the tangent line.
= 20/5 = 4, so the radius is 4.
keyConcept: The radius to the point of tangency is the perpendicular distance from the centre to the line.
commonMistake: Forgetting to divide by sqrt(a^2+b^2) when using the point-to-line distance formula.

optionExplanations.0: 0.8 divides by 25 instead of sqrt(25) = 5.
optionExplanations.2: 5 is the distance from C to a marked point like (0,6), not the perpendicular distance to the line.
optionExplanations.3: 8 overshoots; it ignores the /5 normalisation in the distance formula.

figureExplanation: The right-angle mark at T shows CT is perpendicular to ℓ, so the radius is exactly the distance from C(4,8) to the line through (0,6) and (8,0).

shortExplanation: Consider the worst case that still lacks a required type. Pulling every hyacinth, daffodil and crocus (24) leaves no tulip, so the 25th pull guarantees both a tulip and a hyacinth.
solutionSteps: Required: at least one tulip and at least one hyacinth.
Worst case missing a tulip: pull all 12 hyacinth + 7 daffodil + 5 crocus = 24 bulbs, still no tulip.
Worst case missing a hyacinth: pull all 9 tulip + 7 daffodil + 5 crocus = 21 bulbs.
The larger bad case is 24; one more pull (the 25th) must be a tulip.
At 25 pulls both required types are guaranteed.
keyConcept: Pigeonhole / worst-case: take the largest set that avoids the goal, then add one.
commonMistake: Using the smaller (21) missing-hyacinth case, or forgetting daffodils and crocuses can all come out first.

optionExplanations.0: 13 far understates the worst case, since 12 hyacinths alone give no tulip.
optionExplanations.2: 24 is the largest set that can still be missing a tulip, not yet a guarantee.
optionExplanations.4: 26 overshoots; 25 already forces both types.

shortExplanation: Let B take t hours; A takes t+5. Their combined rate 1/t + 1/(t+5) equals 1/6. Solving gives t = 10 hours.
solutionSteps: Let B alone = t hours, so A alone = t + 5 hours.
Combined rate: 1/t + 1/(t+5) = 1/6.
Multiply by 6t(t+5): 6(t+5) + 6t = t(t+5).
Factor (t-10)(t+3)=0, so t = 10 (positive root).
keyConcept: Combined work rates add; time = reciprocal of rate.
commonMistake: Adding times instead of rates, or keeping the negative root t = -3.

optionExplanations.2: 15 hours would make A take 20 hours; together that gives 1/15+1/20 = 7/60, not 1/6.
optionExplanations.3: 6 hours is the joint time, not B's solo time.
optionExplanations.4: 12 hours makes A take 17 hours; combined rate is not 1/6.

shortExplanation: With BC = 30 - 8 - 12 = 10, the angle-bisector theorem gives BD/DC = AB/AC = 8/12 = 2/3, so BD = 10*(2/5) = 4.
solutionSteps: Perimeter 30 with AB = 8 and AC = 12 gives BC = 30 - 8 - 12 = 10.
The angle bisector from A splits BC in the ratio BD/DC = AB/AC = 8/12 = 2/3.
keyConcept: The angle-bisector theorem: the bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.
commonMistake: Splitting BC in the ratio AC/AB instead of AB/AC, or halving it as if D were the midpoint.

optionExplanations.2: BD = 5 treats D as the midpoint of BC, ignoring the unequal sides.
optionExplanations.3: BD = 6 uses the ratio 3/5 (AC:AB reversed) instead of 2/5.
optionExplanations.4: BD = 8 confuses BD with the side AB rather than a fraction of BC.

figureExplanation: The two equal angles alpha at A show AD is the bisector, and the labels AB = 8 and AC = 12 set the division ratio applied to base BC.
formulaNotes: angle-bisector theorem: BD/DC = AB/AC; BD = BC*AB/(AB+AC).

shortExplanation: The rule 'released only if passed' means released implies passed. 'No batch is released unless it has passed' states exactly the same implication.
solutionSteps: Translate: released -> passed the creep test.
'Only if passed' = 'if released, then passed'.
'No batch released unless passed' is the same conditional restated negatively.
Check others are the converse, inverse, a contradiction, or a biconditional.
keyConcept: 'P only if Q' and 'not P unless Q' both mean P -> Q.
commonMistake: Reading 'only if' as a biconditional, or swapping it into the converse 'passed -> released'.

optionExplanations.1: 'Every batch that passed is released' is the converse (passed -> released), not equivalent.
optionExplanations.2: 'At least one released without passing' directly contradicts the rule.
optionExplanations.4: The biconditional adds that passing forces release, which the rule never states.

shortExplanation: The statement is (sterile AND sealed) -> archivable. Its contrapositive negates and swaps: not archivable -> (not sterile OR not sealed), by De Morgan's law.
solutionSteps: Original: (sterile AND sealed) -> may be archived.
Contrapositive of P -> Q is (not Q) -> (not P).
Not Q: may not be archived.
Not P: NOT(sterile AND sealed) = not sterile OR not sealed.
So: if not archivable, then not sterile or not sealed.
keyConcept: Contrapositive negates both sides and reverses; De Morgan turns AND into OR.
commonMistake: Keeping 'AND' after negation instead of switching to 'OR'.

optionExplanations.1: 'not sterile AND not sealed' wrongly keeps AND; De Morgan requires OR.
optionExplanations.2: 'If archivable, then sterile and sealed' is the converse, not the contrapositive.
optionExplanations.3: 'If not sterile or not sealed, then not archivable' is the inverse, not equivalent.

shortExplanation: Using the Fibonacci-type rule, back out the early terms from Week 3 = 10 and Week 5 = 26, then extend to Week 7 = 68.
solutionSteps: Let Week1 = a, Week2 = b. Then Week3 = a + b = 10.
Week4 = b + 10; Week5 = Week3 + Week4 = 10 + (b + 10) = 20 + b = 26, so b = 6, a = 4.
Week4 = 6 + 10 = 16; Week5 = 26 (checks).
Week6 = Week4 + Week5 = 16 + 26 = 42.
Week7 = Week5 + Week6 = 26 + 42 = 68.
keyConcept: Each term is the sum of the two preceding terms (Fibonacci recurrence).
commonMistake: Assuming Week4 = 16 without solving, or jumping straight from 10 and 26 without the intermediate terms.

optionExplanations.0: 42 is Week 6, not Week 7.
optionExplanations.1: 65 does not arise from the correct terms 26 and 42.
optionExplanations.3: 84 doubles Week 6 instead of adding Weeks 5 and 6.

shortExplanation: A palindrome of length 5 has the form c1 c2 c3 c2 c1, so only c1, c2, c3 are free. Adjacency forces c1!=c2 and c2!=c3, giving 5*4*4 = 80.
solutionSteps: Palindrome pattern: positions are c1, c2, c3, c2, c1.
Adjacent-different constraints reduce to c1 != c2 and c2 != c3 (the mirror pairs are automatic).
Choose c1: 5 ways.
Choose c2 (different from c1): 4 ways.
Choose c3 (different from c2): 4 ways. Total = 5*4*4 = 80.
keyConcept: Palindromic symmetry fixes half the cells; only distinct-neighbor constraints on the free cells remain.
commonMistake: Forgetting the palindrome halves the free choices, or missing that c3 need only differ from c2.

optionExplanations.0: 60 undercounts one of the free-cell factors.
optionExplanations.2: 64 = 4^3 wrongly forces c1 to have only 4 choices.
optionExplanations.3: 125 = 5^3 ignores the adjacency constraint entirely.

shortExplanation: Cables form a complete graph, so total cables = C(n,2). Adding 3 servers raises this by 3n+3 = 39, giving n = 12.
solutionSteps: Original cables = C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2.
After adding 3: C(n+3,2) = (n+3)(n+2)/2.
keyConcept: Complete-graph edge count C(n,2); the increase from adding k vertices is a linear expression.
commonMistake: Computing 3 extra edges instead of connecting each new server to all others.

optionExplanations.0: 10 gives an increase of 3*10+3 = 33, not 39.
optionExplanations.1: 11 gives 36, still short of 39.
optionExplanations.3: 13 gives 42, overshooting 39.

shortExplanation: Take the worst case that still lacks one required type. Pulling all non-required (28) plus all glass and metal (18) but no paper gives 46; the 47th pull guarantees a paper item and hence all three.
solutionSteps: Non-required items: 14 plastic + 11 compostable + 3 foam = 28.
Worst case missing paper: 28 + 10 glass + 8 metal = 46 items, still no paper.
Missing metal instead: 28 + 10 + 5 = 43; missing glass: 28 + 8 + 5 = 41.
The largest bad case is 46 (no paper).
One more pull (47) forces a paper item, so all three required types are present.
keyConcept: Worst-case pigeonhole: exhaust everything that avoids the goal, then add one.
commonMistake: Ignoring the plentiful non-required items, or picking a smaller missing-type case.

optionExplanations.0: 19 ignores the 28 non-required plus the abundant glass/metal that can all come first.
optionExplanations.2: 46 is the largest set that can still lack paper, not yet a guarantee.
optionExplanations.3: 51 overshoots; 47 already suffices.

shortExplanation: Following the arrows S -> P -> V -> A chains into the single conditional S -> A: if the tank is sealed, the alarm sounds. The statement true in exactly the same cases is its contrapositive, 'if the alarm does not sound, then the tank is not sealed.'
solutionSteps: Read the legend: S = tank is sealed, P = pressure rises, V = relief valve opens, A = alarm sounds.
Trace the arrows: S -> P, P -> V, V -> A.
Chain them by transitivity to get the entailed conditional linking S and A: S -> A.
A conditional is logically equivalent only to its contrapositive: not-A -> not-S.
Match that to 'If the alarm does not sound, then the tank is not sealed.'
keyConcept: A conditional is logically equivalent to its contrapositive (negate and swap), not to its converse or inverse.
commonMistake: Confusing the converse ('alarm -> sealed') or inverse ('not sealed -> no alarm') with a truly equivalent statement.

optionExplanations.0: 'If the alarm sounds, then the tank is sealed' is the converse A -> S, which is not equivalent to S -> A.
optionExplanations.1: 'If the relief valve does not open, then the tank is not sealed' is the contrapositive of S -> V; it is true in the system but not equivalent to the S-to-A conditional.
optionExplanations.3: 'If the tank is not sealed, then the alarm does not sound' is the inverse not-S -> not-A, which is not equivalent to S -> A.

figureExplanation: The one directed path from S to A runs S -> P -> V -> A, so the only conditional the diagram entails between S and A is S -> A.
formulaNotes: Contrapositive: (X -> Y) is equivalent to (not-Y -> not-X).

shortExplanation: The minute hand points at 8 (40 minutes) and the hour hand sits just past 4, so the time is 4:40. The hour hand is at 140 deg and the minute hand at 240 deg, giving a gap of 100 deg.
solutionSteps: The minute hand points exactly at the numeral 8, so it reads 40 minutes: 8 * 30 = 240 deg from 12.
The hour hand lies between 4 and 5, consistent with 4:40.
Hour-hand angle = 4 * 30 + 40 * 0.5 = 120 + 20 = 140 deg from 12.
Angle between hands = |240 - 140| = 100 deg.
100 deg is already less than 180 deg, so it is the smaller (non-reflex) angle.
keyConcept: Hour-hand angle = 30 * hour + 0.5 * minutes; minute-hand angle = 6 * minutes, both measured from the 12.
commonMistake: Placing the hour hand exactly on 4 (giving 120 deg) instead of advancing it 20 deg for the 40 minutes elapsed.

optionExplanations.1: 90 deg does not correspond to any correct hand placement for 4:40.
optionExplanations.3: 120 deg results from leaving the hour hand exactly on the 4 rather than advancing it toward 5.
optionExplanations.4: 140 deg is the hour hand's own angle from 12, not the gap between the two hands.

figureExplanation: The minute hand tip reaches the numeral 8 and the hour hand tip sits one third of the way from 4 toward 5, marking 4:40; the small arc at the pivot indicates the measured angle.

shortExplanation: First count all orders with Thunder and Storm non-adjacent (3600), then halve for Dragon-before-Phoenix by symmetry, giving 1800.
solutionSteps: Total orders of 7 floats = 7! = 5040.
Orders with Thunder and Storm adjacent = 2 * 6! = 1440.
Non-adjacent orders = 5040 - 1440 = 3600.
Dragon before Phoenix occurs in exactly half of these by symmetry.
keyConcept: Handle the two constraints separately: adjacency by complement, order by symmetry.
commonMistake: Halving before removing adjacent cases, or forgetting the two internal orders of the Thunder-Storm block.

optionExplanations.2: 2160 does not match either intermediate or final count.
optionExplanations.3: 2520 = 7!/2 applies only the Dragon-before-Phoenix rule, ignoring the adjacency ban.
optionExplanations.4: 3600 is the non-adjacent count before applying Dragon-before-Phoenix.

shortExplanation: From P(8,4)=1680 total ordered displays, subtract the 420 in which the Marble Faun is chosen but sits in an interior slot, leaving 1260.
solutionSteps: Unrestricted ordered selections of 4 from 8 = 8*7*6*5 = 1680.
Count displays containing the Marble Faun: 4 slots * P(7,3) = 4*210 = 840.
Of these, Marble Faun at an end (2 end slots): 2 * 210 = 420 (allowed).
Marble Faun in an interior slot (forbidden): 840 - 420 = 420.
Valid displays = 1680 - 420 = 1260.
keyConcept: Subtract forbidden placements of the constrained item from the total permutations.
commonMistake: Forgetting that the Marble Faun need not be chosen at all, or mis-splitting end vs interior slots.

optionExplanations.1: 1680 is the total with no restriction on the Marble Faun.
optionExplanations.2: 1050 does not correspond to a correct case split.
optionExplanations.3: 420 counts only the Marble-Faun-at-end displays, dropping all displays without it.

shortExplanation: Channels equal C(n,2). Requiring C(n+6,2) = 2*C(n,2) yields n^2 - 13n - 30 = 0, so n = 15.
solutionSteps: Channels = C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2.
Factor (n-15)(n+2)=0, giving n = 15.
keyConcept: Complete-graph edge count and setting the new total to double the old.
commonMistake: Doubling n instead of the number of channels, or taking the negative root.

optionExplanations.0: 6 gives 15 -> 66, far from double.
optionExplanations.1: 10 gives 45 -> 120 channels, which is more than double (90 would be double).
optionExplanations.3: 21 gives 210 -> 351, not double.

shortExplanation: With t meaning 'temperature is NOT above 30', not-t means 'temperature IS above 30', and not-s means 'vent is not open'. So not-t -> not-s reads 'if the temperature is above 30 C, then the vent is not open.'
solutionSteps: Read the legend: s = 'the vent is open', t = 'the temperature is NOT above 30 C'.
Negate t: not-t = 'the temperature IS above 30 C' (the two nots cancel).
Negate s: not-s = 'the vent is not open'.
Substitute into the contrapositive not-t -> not-s.
Read it out: 'If the temperature is above 30 C, then the vent is not open.'
keyConcept: When translating a negated proposition, cancel a built-in negative before writing the sentence.
commonMistake: Forgetting that t is already negative, so leaving 'not-t' as 'temperature not above 30' instead of 'above 30'.

optionExplanations.0: 'If the temperature is not above 30, then the vent is open' just restates the original s and t directly, not their negations.
optionExplanations.1: 'If the vent is not open, then the temperature is above 30' reverses antecedent and consequent (not-s -> not-t), the converse of the contrapositive.
optionExplanations.4: 'If the temperature is above 30, then the vent is open' keeps not-t but wrongly uses s instead of not-s.

figureExplanation: The highlighted CONTRAPOSITIVE box shows not-t -> not-s; combining that structure with the legend's meanings of s and t fixes the correct sentence.
formulaNotes: not-(NOT above 30) = above 30; not-(vent open) = vent not open.

shortExplanation: Gem-grade sits inside Quartz-bearing, which sits inside Silicate minerals, so every gem-grade sample is necessarily a silicate mineral. The Fluorescent circle only partially overlaps Silicate minerals, so nothing certain follows about fluorescence.
solutionSteps: Read the nesting: Gem-grade circle is inside Quartz-bearing, which is inside Silicate minerals.
Therefore Gem-grade is a subset of Silicate minerals.
Conclude 'Every gem-grade sample is a silicate mineral' is necessarily true.
Note the Fluorescent circle only crosses the edge of Silicate minerals, so no full-containment claim about fluorescence holds.
keyConcept: In an Euler diagram, a circle fully enclosed by another means 'all of the inner category is in the outer category.'
commonMistake: Reading containment in reverse, e.g. assuming every silicate mineral must be quartz-bearing or gem-grade.

optionExplanations.0: 'Every silicate-mineral sample is quartz-bearing' reverses the nesting; quartz-bearing is only part of the silicate circle.
optionExplanations.2: 'Every fluorescent sample is a silicate mineral' fails because the fluorescent circle sticks out beyond the silicate circle.
optionExplanations.4: 'No silicate-mineral sample is fluorescent' is false since the two circles clearly overlap.

figureExplanation: Three concentric circles (Gem-grade inside Quartz-bearing inside Silicate minerals) force gem-grade to be silicate; the Fluorescent circle only partially overlaps the outer circle.

shortExplanation: Add the three pair-rates to get 2(X+Y+Z), so X+Y+Z = 3/8 per hour; all three together take 8/3 hours = 2 hours 40 minutes.
solutionSteps: Rates: X+Y = 1/3, Y+Z = 1/4, X+Z = 1/6 (jobs per hour).
So X+Y+Z = 3/8 per hour.
Time for all three = 1/(3/8) = 8/3 hours = 2 h 40 min.
keyConcept: Adding all pairwise rates counts each scanner twice, giving twice the combined rate.
commonMistake: Averaging the three times (3,4,6) instead of adding rates.

optionExplanations.0: 1 h 20 min corresponds to rate 3/4, i.e. the summed-pairs total, not the single combined rate.
optionExplanations.2: 4 h uses only one pair's rate, not all three scanners.
optionExplanations.3: 4 h 20 min does not match 8/3 hours.

shortExplanation: Vertex A ('every valve must be sealed') is contradictory to 'some valve can become unsealed'. By the stated law, A is equivalent to the denial of that contradictory, namely 'no valve can ever become unsealed.'
solutionSteps: Identify A: for all valves, it is necessary that the valve is sealed (every valve must be sealed).
Find A's contradictory along the diagonal: D = 'some valve can become unsealed' (there exists a valve that possibly is unsealed).
Apply the law: A is logically equivalent to the negation of its contradictory.
Negate D: 'it is not the case that some valve can become unsealed' = 'no valve can ever become unsealed'.
That negation equals 'for all valves it is necessary to be sealed', which is A.
keyConcept: A proposition equals the denial of its contradictory; negating an existential-possibility gives a universal-necessity of the opposite.
commonMistake: Picking the contradictory itself instead of its denial, or confusing the contrary B with an equivalent.

optionExplanations.0: 'Some valve can become unsealed' is A's contradictory (D); it has the opposite truth value, not the same.
optionExplanations.1: 'Every valve must become unsealed' is the contrary B, which can be false when A is false, so it is not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'Some valve can remain sealed' is the subaltern C, weaker than A and not equivalent to it.

figureExplanation: The dashed diagonal joins A to D as contradictories; denying D (the diagonal partner) yields exactly the universal-necessity claim at A.
formulaNotes: not(exists v: possibly not-Sealed(v)) = for all v: necessarily Sealed(v).

shortExplanation: The rule is pass -> (stable AND intact). Its contrapositive: not(stable AND intact) -> not pass, i.e. unstable OR not intact -> does not pass inspection.
solutionSteps: Original: passes -> (voltage stable AND casing intact).
Contrapositive of P -> Q is (not Q) -> (not P).
Not Q by De Morgan: voltage unstable OR casing not intact.
Not P: does not pass inspection.
So: if unstable or casing not intact, then does not pass inspection.
keyConcept: Contrapositive plus De Morgan (negating AND yields OR).
commonMistake: Writing 'unstable AND not intact', which is a stronger, non-equivalent condition.

optionExplanations.0: 'If stable and intact, then passes' is the converse.
optionExplanations.1: 'unstable and not intact -> does not pass' keeps AND wrongly (should be OR).
optionExplanations.3: 'does not pass -> unstable or not intact' is the inverse, not the contrapositive.

shortExplanation: The inlet fills at 1/2 tank per hour; with both open the net fill is 1/3 per hour, so the drain removes 1/6 per hour and empties a full tank in 6 hours.
solutionSteps: Inlet: 5/8 tank in 1.25 h -> rate = (5/8)/(5/4) = 1/2 tank per hour.
Both open: 5/6 tank in 2.5 h -> net rate = (5/6)/(5/2) = 1/3 tank per hour.
Drain rate = inlet - net = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 tank per hour.
Time to empty full tank = 1/(1/6) = 6 hours.
keyConcept: Net rate = inlet rate - drain rate; solve for the drain rate, then invert.
commonMistake: Subtracting times instead of rates, or forgetting to convert 1 h 15 min and 2 h 30 min to hours.

optionExplanations.0: 2 hours is the inlet's full-fill time, not the drain time.
optionExplanations.1: 2 h 30 min is the both-open fill time to 5/6, not the drain-only empty time.
optionExplanations.3: 5 hours does not match a drain rate of 1/6 per hour.

formulaNotes: drain = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6 per hour; empty time = 6 h.

shortExplanation: Alpha ('all are conductive') is contradictory to delta ('some are not conductive'), so if alpha is false, delta must be true. No other vertex is forced, since alpha being false leaves the contrary and subaltern undetermined.
solutionSteps: Locate alpha ('all are conductive') and its diagonal contradictory delta ('some are not conductive').
Contradictories always have opposite truth values, so alpha false forces delta true.
Check beta (contrary of alpha): two contraries can both be false, so beta is not determined.
Check gamma (subaltern of alpha): alpha being false does not force gamma either way.
Conclude only delta is guaranteed true.
keyConcept: Contradictory pairs on the square always take opposite truth values; contraries and subalterns do not.
commonMistake: Assuming that 'all are conductive' being false makes 'none are conductive' true, but those are only contraries, not contradictories.

optionExplanations.0: The statement at beta ('none are conductive') is only a contrary of alpha, so it can be false too when alpha is false.
optionExplanations.2: The statement at gamma ('some are conductive') is the subaltern; alpha's falsity does not fix gamma's truth value.
optionExplanations.3: Both beta and delta cannot be guaranteed, since beta is undetermined.

figureExplanation: The bold diagonals mark alpha-delta and beta-gamma as contradictory pairs, so falsifying alpha immediately makes delta true while leaving the contrary and subaltern open.

shortExplanation: With labs of sizes n and n+1, same-lab handshakes total C(n,2)+C(n+1,2) = n^2 = 36, so n = 6 and the total attendance is 6 + 7 = 13.
solutionSteps: Let the labs have n and n+1 members.
Set n^2 = 36, so n = 6.
Total attendance = n + (n+1) = 6 + 7 = 13.
keyConcept: Handshakes occur only within a lab; the two consecutive-size sum simplifies to n^2.
commonMistake: Counting cross-lab handshakes, or reporting one lab's size (6 or 7) instead of the total.

optionExplanations.0: 6 is one lab's size, not the total.
optionExplanations.1: 7 is the other lab's size, not the total.
optionExplanations.3: 12 would require equal labs of 6 and 6, contradicting the one-more condition and giving 30 handshakes.

shortExplanation: The diagram shows 9 birds in the waders-only region, so there are waders that are not herons. That makes 'some waders are not herons' necessarily true.
solutionSteps: Read the regions: herons only = 0, both = 14, waders only = 9, neither = 17.
Waders-only = 9 means 9 waders lie outside the heron set.
Therefore 'some waders are not herons' is necessarily true.
Note herons-only = 0, so every heron is also a wader, ruling out heron-only claims.
keyConcept: A nonzero count in an exclusive region establishes an existential ('some ... are not ...') statement.
commonMistake: Trusting the field guide's 'all waders are herons' claim, which the counts directly contradict.

optionExplanations.0: 'Some herons are not waders' is false because the herons-only region is 0.
optionExplanations.3: 'All waders are herons' is false because 9 waders sit outside the heron circle.
optionExplanations.4: 'Some non-waders are herons' is false since herons-only = 0, meaning no heron is a non-wader.

figureExplanation: The waders-only region holds 9 birds and the herons-only region holds 0, so waders extend beyond herons while every heron is also a wader.

shortExplanation: Each game awards exactly 1 point in total, so total points equals the number of games C(n,2) = 210, giving n = 21.
solutionSteps: Every game (win or draw) distributes exactly 1 point total.
So total points = number of games = C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2.
keyConcept: Total points in a round-robin equals the number of games played.
commonMistake: Treating draws as changing the total points, or solving n(n-1)=210 instead of 420.

optionExplanations.1: 15 gives 105 games, far below 210.
optionExplanations.2: 20 gives 20*19/2 = 190 games, not 210.
optionExplanations.4: 22 gives 22*21/2 = 231, too many.

shortExplanation: The rule is (not kept below 8C) -> (not valid). Its contrapositive: valid -> kept below 8C.
solutionSteps: Original: not(kept below 8C) -> not(valid result).
Contrapositive of P -> Q is (not Q) -> (not P).
Not Q = valid result; not P = kept below 8C.
So: if the assay returns a valid result, then the reagent is kept below 8C.
keyConcept: Contrapositive negates and reverses; double negatives cancel to positive statements.
commonMistake: Producing the converse or inverse, or mishandling the double negations.

optionExplanations.1: 'If not valid, then not kept below 8C' just restates the original, not its contrapositive.
optionExplanations.2: 'If kept below 8C, then valid' is the inverse, not equivalent.
optionExplanations.3: 'If valid, then not kept below 8C' reverses the correct temperature condition.

shortExplanation: The circle labels 38 and 29 are the full set totals, so both = 38 + 29 - |A or B| = 17 + neither. With neither required to be at least 4, the smallest overlap is 17 + 4 = 21.
solutionSteps: Read the figure: universe U = 50, set A (passed corrosion) = 38, set B (passed fatigue) = 29, and passed neither >= 4.

Confirm 38 and 29 are full set totals, not left-only and right-only regions: two exclusive regions of 38 and 29 already sum to 67 > 50, which is impossible, so each number counts an entire circle including the overlap.
Apply inclusion-exclusion: |A or B| = |A| + |B| - both = 38 + 29 - both = 67 - both.
Relate to the universe: neither = U - |A or B| = 50 - (67 - both) = both - 17, so both = 17 + neither.
Increasing 'both' increases 'neither' one-for-one, so the smallest overlap comes from the smallest allowed 'neither', which is 4.
Substitute neither = 4: both = 17 + 4 = 21.
Check consistency: both = 21 gives |A or B| = 46 and neither = 4, and 46 + 4 = 50 matches the universe, with 21 <= min(38, 29).
keyConcept: Inclusion-exclusion links the overlap to the 'neither' count: both = |A| + |B| - U + neither, so minimizing the overlap means minimizing 'neither'.
commonMistake: Ignoring the 'at least 4 passed neither' constraint and taking the unconstrained minimum overlap of 17, or misreading 38 and 29 as the exclusive-only regions.

optionExplanations.0: 12 is below the feasible range; it would force neither = 12 - 17 = -5, which is impossible.
optionExplanations.1: 17 would be the overlap only if 'neither' could be 0, but the figure requires at least 4 samples passed neither test.
optionExplanations.3: 9 is smaller than the minimum feasible overlap of 21 and again forces a negative 'neither'.
optionExplanations.4: 4 is the minimum 'passed neither' count read from the figure, not the overlap.

figureExplanation: The Venn diagram gives the universe U = 50, the corrosion-test circle total |A| = 38, the fatigue-test circle total |B| = 29, and a marked note that at least 4 samples passed neither test. The central overlap (both) is the unknown.
formulaNotes: both = |A| + |B| - |A or B|; neither = U - |A or B|; combined: both = |A| + |B| - U + neither = 17 + neither.

shortExplanation: Worst case: pull all 15 filler plus the two largest sulfate stacks (copper 8 + iron 6 = 14) but no zinc, totaling 29; the 30th vial guarantees a zinc and thus all three sulfates.
solutionSteps: Filler vials are not sulfates: 15 can all come out first.
Worst case missing zinc: 15 + 8 copper + 6 iron = 29 vials, still no zinc.
Missing iron: 15 + 8 + 5 = 28; missing copper: 15 + 6 + 5 = 26.
The largest bad case is 29 (no zinc).
The 30th vial must be zinc, completing all three sulfates.
keyConcept: Worst-case pigeonhole: exhaust filler and the two biggest sulfate groups, then add one.
commonMistake: Ignoring the 15 filler vials, or using the smaller missing-copper case.

optionExplanations.1: 24 = 15 + 8 + ... miscounts; the true worst case reaches 29.
optionExplanations.2: 29 is the largest set that can still lack zinc, not yet a guarantee.
optionExplanations.4: 34 overshoots; 30 already suffices.

shortExplanation: Squaring doubles the exponent each generation: 2^3 -> 2^6 -> 2^12 -> 2^24 -> 2^48. Generation 5 has 2^48 sites.
keyConcept: Squaring a power doubles its exponent: (2^k)^2 = 2^(2k).
commonMistake: Adding 3 each time or doubling the base instead of the exponent.

optionExplanations.1: 2^15 comes from adding exponents linearly rather than doubling.
optionExplanations.2: 2^24 is generation 4, one step short.
optionExplanations.4: 2^96 doubles once too many (that would be generation 6).

shortExplanation: The rule is (not magnetic) -> (no iron). Its contrapositive: contains iron -> magnetic.
solutionSteps: Original: not(magnetic) -> not(contains iron).
Contrapositive of P -> Q is (not Q) -> (not P).
Not Q = contains iron; not P = magnetic.
So: if a sample contains iron, then it is magnetic.
keyConcept: Contrapositive negates both parts and swaps them; equivalent to the original.
commonMistake: Stating the converse ('magnetic -> iron') or the inverse instead.

optionExplanations.1: 'If no iron, then not magnetic' restates the original, not the contrapositive.
optionExplanations.2: 'If magnetic, then contains iron' is the converse.
optionExplanations.3: 'If iron, then not magnetic' negates the wrong side.

shortExplanation: From 6! = 720 total arrangements, subtract the 240 with the volatile bottle in an end slot, leaving 480.
solutionSteps: Total arrangements of 6 distinct bottles = 6! = 720.
Volatile bottle in slot 1 or slot 6: 2 * 5! = 240.
Valid arrangements = 720 - 240 = 480.
keyConcept: Total minus forbidden placements of the constrained item.
commonMistake: Placing the volatile bottle in only 4 interior slots but mis-multiplying the remaining arrangements.

optionExplanations.0: 720 is the unrestricted total, ignoring the end-slot ban.
optionExplanations.1: 600 does not match a correct case count.
optionExplanations.3: 240 counts the forbidden end-slot arrangements, the opposite of what is asked.

shortExplanation: The rule is (sterile AND labeled) -> cold room. The guaranteed truth is its contrapositive: not cold room -> not sterile OR not labeled.
solutionSteps: Original: (sterile AND correctly labeled) -> kept in cold room.
The statement that must also hold is the contrapositive.
Contrapositive: not(cold room) -> not(sterile AND labeled).
By De Morgan: not sterile OR not correctly labeled.
So: if not in the cold room, then not sterile or not correctly labeled.
keyConcept: Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent; De Morgan turns AND into OR under negation.
commonMistake: Keeping 'AND' after negation, or choosing the converse/inverse.

optionExplanations.1: 'not sterile AND not labeled' wrongly keeps AND instead of OR.
optionExplanations.2: 'If in cold room, then sterile and labeled' is the converse.
optionExplanations.3: 'If not sterile or not labeled, then not in cold room' is the inverse.

shortExplanation: Only destroying DNA (portion 4) abolishes the permanently inherited trait, so the heritable instructions reside in the nucleic acid, even though the pigment is ultimately made by an enzyme (a protein).
solutionSteps: Note that portions treated with protease, lipase, and amylase still transform the recipients permanently.
Only the portion whose DNA is destroyed fails to confer the heritable trait.
Conclude that the transforming (heritable) material is DNA.
Distinguish the carrier of information (DNA) from the executor of the trait (the pigment enzyme, a protein).
keyConcept: DNA is the transforming principle that carries heritable information; proteins execute the trait but are not what is inherited.
commonMistake: Confusing the molecule that carries the instructions (DNA) with the molecule that performs the function (the enzyme).

optionExplanations.1: DNA is not itself a catalyst that makes pigment; it encodes the enzyme that does.
optionExplanations.2: Destroying the protein did not abolish the inherited trait, so protein is not the transmitted material.
optionExplanations.3: Carbohydrates are not the repository of genetic information; destroying them had no effect.

shortExplanation: Heat removed per gram of a fluid that evaporates completely is governed by its heat of vaporization; water's value (2260 J/g) is by far the largest.
solutionSteps: Identify that the fluid evaporates completely, so the relevant quantity is energy absorbed per gram to convert liquid to vapor.
That energy is the heat of vaporization, not the specific heat (which applies to temperature change within the liquid).
Compare heats of vaporization: water 2260 is much greater than ammonia 1370, ethanol 841, acetone 518.
Water removes the most heat per gram evaporated.
keyConcept: Heat of vaporization sets the energy absorbed per gram during evaporation; water's is exceptionally high due to extensive hydrogen bonding.
commonMistake: Using specific heat instead of heat of vaporization; specific heat governs warming a liquid, not the liquid-to-vapor transition.

optionExplanations.1: Specific heat governs temperature change of the liquid, not the heat absorbed during complete evaporation.
optionExplanations.2: Ammonia's specific heat is irrelevant to evaporative cooling, and its heat of vaporization is lower than water's.
optionExplanations.3: Acetone's low heat of vaporization means it absorbs the least energy per gram, not the most.

formulaNotes: Heat removed per gram evaporated = heat of vaporization (Q = m*L_v).

shortExplanation: A eukaryote with a membrane-bound nucleus, no cell wall, that engulfs food with pseudopodia is an amoeba-like protist, so its assignment to Protista is correct.
solutionSteps: Screen each organism against defining kingdom features.
Presence of a true nucleus rules out Bacteria/Monera regardless of other traits.
No cell wall plus phagocytosis by pseudopodia matches a protozoan (e.g., amoeba).
That organism is correctly placed in Protista.
keyConcept: Kingdom assignment requires matching nuclear presence, wall chemistry, and nutrition together, not a single trait.
commonMistake: Assigning based on one trait alone rather than checking that all features fit the kingdom.

optionExplanations.0: No nuclear envelope plus a peptidoglycan wall defines a bacterium (Monera), not a protist.
optionExplanations.1: A chitin wall with budding and absorptive nutrition describes a yeast (Fungi), not Protista.
optionExplanations.3: A cellulose-walled, multicellular, photosynthetic organism is a plant (Plantae), not Fungi.

shortExplanation: Cell R has a cell wall and a large central vacuole, hallmarks of a plant cell; the absence of chloroplasts is expected in a non-photosynthetic underground storage tissue.
solutionSteps: Read R's features: cell wall present, large central vacuole present, no chloroplast, no centriole.
Recognize that cell wall plus large central vacuole are characteristic plant-cell markers.
Note that storage tissue of a tuber buried underground never photosynthesizes, so lacking chloroplasts is normal.
Conclude R is a plant cell.
keyConcept: Plant cells are identified by a cell wall and a large central vacuole; chloroplasts occur only in photosynthetic tissues.
commonMistake: Assuming any plant cell must contain chloroplasts, when non-green storage cells lack them.

optionExplanations.0: Animal cells have no cell wall or large central vacuole, both of which R possesses.
optionExplanations.2: Centrioles are typical of animal cells, so their presence would not mark plant cells.
optionExplanations.3: The chloroplast is not the sole plant marker; the wall and vacuole also identify plant cells.

shortExplanation: Blocking ER-to-Golgi vesicle formation traps the enzyme in the ER, where it is folded and bears only its core sugars, so it remains inactive because it never reaches the Golgi for terminal glycosylation.
solutionSteps: Recall the secretory route: ribosome/ER synthesis and folding, then vesicle transport to the Golgi for terminal sugar modification, then secretion.
The mutation prevents budding of ER-to-Golgi transport vesicles.
The enzyme is therefore stuck in the ER with core (initial) glycosylation only.
Without Golgi terminal sugars it cannot become catalytically active.
keyConcept: Terminal glycosylation occurs in the Golgi, so cargo that cannot leave the ER stays core-glycosylated and inactive.
commonMistake: Thinking the protein is made in the Golgi, or that ER retention leaves it unfolded in the cytosol.

optionExplanations.1: The Golgi is not where the protein is synthesized, and cargo cannot reach it once vesicles fail to form.
optionExplanations.2: Ribosomes still insert the chain into the ER, where it folds; it is not left unfolded in the cytosol.
optionExplanations.3: With transport blocked the enzyme cannot be secreted at all, let alone at a normal rate.

shortExplanation: Without a spindle, chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down but the sisters cannot align at the equator, so the spindle-assembly checkpoint halts cells at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
solutionSteps: The drug prevents tubulin from polymerizing, so no spindle microtubules form.
Observed state: chromosomes maximally condensed, each with two sister chromatids, no nuclear envelope, scattered rather than aligned.
This is a cell that entered mitosis (envelope broken down, chromosomes condensed) but cannot build a metaphase plate.
The spindle-assembly checkpoint blocks the metaphase-to-anaphase transition until proper attachment, so sisters never separate.
keyConcept: The spindle-assembly checkpoint arrests cells before anaphase when kinetochores are not properly attached to spindle microtubules.
commonMistake: Assuming loss of microtubules blocks nuclear-envelope breakdown or chromosome condensation; both occur normally here.

optionExplanations.1: The envelope is described as absent, so it did break down; the block is not before prometaphase.
optionExplanations.3: Chromatids are still joined at the centromere, so no separation has occurred; the arrest is before anaphase.
optionExplanations.4: Chromosomes are fully condensed, so condensation clearly did occur despite the missing microtubules.

shortExplanation: Same protein length with only one amino acid changed (Glu to Val at residue 3) points to a single base substitution, since the reading frame and all other codons are preserved.
solutionSteps: Wild-type codon 3 is GAG (Glu).
A single base change GAG to GUG gives Val, changing only residue 3.
All other codons and the total length stay the same, ruling out frame shifts.
This is a point substitution (a missense mutation).
keyConcept: A single missense substitution changes one amino acid while leaving reading frame and protein length intact.
commonMistake: Assuming any single-base event is a frameshift; only insertions or deletions shift the frame.

optionExplanations.0: An insertion would shift the frame, altering every downstream residue and likely the length.
optionExplanations.1: A deletion would likewise shift the frame and scramble downstream residues.
optionExplanations.4: Duplicating a codon would add one residue, changing the total length.

formulaNotes: GAG (Glu) -> GUG (Val): a single A->U change at the middle position of codon 3.

shortExplanation: The ribosome positions a tRNA solely by codon-anticodon pairing and does not re-check the attached amino acid, so the cysteine-charged tRNA with an edited anticodon inserts cysteine wherever GCA appears.
solutionSteps: The tRNA still carries cysteine but its anticodon now pairs with GCA.
Ribosomes select aminoacyl-tRNAs by codon-anticodon base pairing only.
There is no proofreading of which amino acid is attached once charging is done.
Therefore cysteine is inserted at every GCA codon.
keyConcept: Translational fidelity for amino-acid identity is set at the aminoacylation step; the ribosome reads only the anticodon.
commonMistake: Believing the ribosome verifies the amino acid against the codon and corrects mismatches.

optionExplanations.1: The ribosome does not swap the amino acid; it cannot correct a mischarged or edited tRNA.
optionExplanations.2: A codon-amino-acid mismatch is not read as a stop signal; translation continues.
optionExplanations.3: An edited anticodon that pairs with GCA still allows the tRNA to enter the A site.

shortExplanation: Digestion would break insulin into amino acids, the same monomers that build enzymes and antibodies, identifying insulin as a protein; hemoglobin is also a protein.
solutionSteps: The clinician says the drug is cleaved into monomers that also build enzymes and antibodies.
Enzymes and antibodies are proteins, whose monomers are amino acids.
So insulin is a protein.
Among the choices, hemoglobin is the protein.
keyConcept: Proteins (insulin, enzymes, antibodies, hemoglobin) are polymers of amino acids.
commonMistake: Grouping insulin with sugars because it lowers blood glucose, ignoring that it is a protein hormone.

optionExplanations.0: Glycogen is a polysaccharide of glucose, not a protein.
optionExplanations.1: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide, not made of amino acids.
optionExplanations.4: Glucose is a monosaccharide, a different class of biomolecule from proteins.

shortExplanation: Organism Z is a multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryote with a cellulose cell wall, which is exactly the profile of Kingdom Plantae.
solutionSteps: Read Z's row: nucleus present, multicellular, photosynthetic, cellulose cell wall.
Photosynthesis plus a cellulose wall plus multicellular eukaryotic organization defines Plantae.
Confirm the other rows do not fit their proposed kingdoms.
Select 'Organism Z belongs to Kingdom Plantae.'
keyConcept: Plantae = multicellular eukaryotes that are photosynthetic and have cellulose cell walls.
commonMistake: Classifying a unicellular eukaryote as an animal instead of a protist, or a chitin-walled organism as a plant.

optionExplanations.0: W has no nucleus and a peptidoglycan wall, so it is a prokaryote (Monera), not a plant.
optionExplanations.1: X is a unicellular eukaryote, placing it in Protista rather than Animalia.
optionExplanations.2: Y is a multicellular absorptive heterotroph with a chitin wall, which describes Fungi, not Plantae.

figureExplanation: The table row for Z lists photosynthetic nutrition and a cellulose cell wall in a multicellular nucleated organism, the defining traits of Plantae.

shortExplanation: Glucose crosses only when protein X is present and the rate saturates at high concentration, showing X is a selective, limited-number transporter for glucose while the bilayer alone blocks glucose and ions.
solutionSteps: Compare sets A and B: O2 and water cross both, K+ crosses neither.
Glucose is negligible in A (bilayer only) but rapid and saturating in B (with protein X).
The dependence on protein X shows glucose entry needs a transporter, not the bilayer.
Saturation at high glucose indicates a finite number of transport proteins.
keyConcept: Facilitated diffusion through a specific carrier is protein-dependent and saturable, unlike simple diffusion.
commonMistake: Attributing glucose entry to the bilayer, when glucose only crosses when protein X is present.

optionExplanations.0: The bilayer alone (set A) gives negligible glucose entry, so the lipid is not the selective route.
optionExplanations.1: A nonspecific pore would also admit K+, but K+ entry stays negligible in set B.
optionExplanations.2: O2 crosses both sets equally, indicating simple diffusion through lipid, not a dedicated protein.

shortExplanation: The acidic (pH ~4.7) degradative organelle that hydrolyzes engulfed material is the lysosome, whose acid hydrolases work best in the low-pH interior maintained by its proton pumps.
solutionSteps: A double-membrane vesicle engulfs the mitochondrion (autophagy).
It fuses with an organelle kept at pH ~4.7 by proton pumps.
Acidic hydrolytic enzymes there break macromolecules into monomers.
This organelle is the lysosome, and its acidic interior is essential for enzyme activity.
keyConcept: Lysosomes contain acid hydrolases that require the low internal pH set by V-type proton pumps.
commonMistake: Confusing the lysosome with the peroxisome; peroxisomes oxidize substrates near neutral pH, not by acid hydrolysis.

optionExplanations.1: Peroxisomes oxidize material near neutral pH and do not maintain a pH ~4.7 hydrolytic interior.
optionExplanations.2: Mitochondria generate ATP but do not hydrolyze engulfed organelles into monomers.
optionExplanations.4: The Golgi sorts and modifies proteins; it is not the acidic degradative compartment.

shortExplanation: Blocking all light stops photosynthetic producers from converting solar energy into chemical energy, cutting off the sole energy input to the food web, so the consumers eventually collapse.
solutionSteps: The sheet blocks all light while still allowing gas exchange at the edges.
Producers can no longer photosynthesize without light.
Photosynthesis is the only route by which usable energy enters this community.
With the energy base gone, animal populations decline and the community collapses.
keyConcept: Producers are the energy gateway of an ecosystem; removing photosynthesis starves the entire food web.
commonMistake: Attributing collapse to oxygen loss or vision, when the fundamental cause is loss of the energy-fixing base.

optionExplanations.0: Decomposers do not require light; the collapse stems from lost energy input, not halted recycling.
optionExplanations.3: Air exchange continues at the edges, so suffocation is not the fundamental cause of collapse.
optionExplanations.4: Not all animals hunt by sight; the deeper cause is the loss of the producer energy base.

shortExplanation: A uniform first brood produced without mating indicates asexual reproduction (clones of the Aa Bb mother), while the 1:1:1:1 second brood after mating with an aa bb male reflects normal meiosis and fertilization.
solutionSteps: First brood without mating and all identical to the mother implies mitotic (asexual) cloning.
The mother is Aa Bb, so clones are all Aa Bb.
After mating, the mother's meiosis yields four gamete types (AB, Ab, aB, ab) by independent assortment.
The aa bb male contributes only ab, giving AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb in a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
keyConcept: Asexual reproduction yields clones of the parent; sexual reproduction with independent assortment yields a 1:1:1:1 test-cross ratio.
commonMistake: Trying to explain the identical first brood by meiosis 'without crossing over,' which still produces variable gametes by independent assortment.

optionExplanations.1: Even without crossing over, meiosis with independent assortment would vary the first brood, not make it uniform.
optionExplanations.2: Self-fertilization in a single female would still segregate alleles, so the first brood would not be uniformly Aa Bb.
optionExplanations.3: New mutations cannot generate an orderly 1:1:1:1 array of four genotypes in the second brood.

shortExplanation: Estrogen is secreted by granulosa cells, rises through the follicular phase, and switches from negative to positive feedback on the pituitary once it stays high, triggering the LH surge and ovulation.
solutionSteps: Identify the granulosa-cell hormone that rises through the follicular phase: estrogen.
At low levels estrogen suppresses gonadotropin release (negative feedback).
Sustained high estrogen reverses to positive feedback on the anterior pituitary.
This positive feedback produces the mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation.
keyConcept: Estrogen exerts concentration-dependent feedback: negative when low, positive when sustained above threshold, driving the ovulatory LH surge.
commonMistake: Naming LH as the switching hormone, when LH is the surge that estrogen's positive feedback produces.

optionExplanations.1: Progesterone dominates the luteal phase and exerts negative feedback, not the pre-ovulatory positive switch.
optionExplanations.2: LH is the pituitary output that surges in response to estrogen, not the granulosa-cell hormone that switches feedback.
optionExplanations.3: FSH is a pituitary gonadotropin, not the granulosa-secreted hormone with this feedback switch.

shortExplanation: Cyanide blocks the final complex, so oxygen can no longer be reduced to water; electron carriers upstream stay reduced and NAD+ cannot be regenerated, stalling respiration.
solutionSteps: Cyanide blocks the last complex of the electron transport chain.
Oxygen, the terminal electron acceptor, is no longer reduced to water.
Electrons back up, keeping the upstream carriers in their reduced state.
Reduced carriers cannot pass electrons on, so NAD+ is not regenerated and the chain stops.
keyConcept: Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor; blocking its reduction backs up the chain and prevents NAD+ regeneration.
commonMistake: Thinking CO2 or FAD serves as the terminal acceptor, or that ATP accepts electrons directly.

optionExplanations.1: CO2 is a product of the citric acid cycle, not the terminal electron acceptor of the chain.
optionExplanations.2: ATP does not accept electrons from cytochrome c; oxidative phosphorylation halts when the chain is blocked.
optionExplanations.3: FAD is an upstream electron carrier, not a substitute terminal acceptor that would sustain water production.

shortExplanation: RNA polymerase II makes messenger RNA, the short-lived template ribosomes translate; blocking its transcription leaves intact ribosomes with no new mRNA to read, so protein synthesis falls.
solutionSteps: RNA polymerase II transcribes protein-coding genes into mRNA.
mRNA is short-lived and must be continually replenished.
Inhibiting Pol II stops new mRNA production while ribosomes and tRNAs remain functional.
Existing mRNAs decay and ribosomes run out of templates, so protein synthesis declines.
keyConcept: mRNA is the transient template linking gene transcription to translation; its supply depends on ongoing RNA polymerase II activity.
commonMistake: Thinking DNA itself travels to ribosomes, or that rRNA/tRNA depletion (other polymerases) causes the drop.

optionExplanations.1: Amino-acid delivery is the job of tRNA, made by RNA polymerase III, which the drug leaves functional.
optionExplanations.2: tRNA carries amino acids and is not made by RNA polymerase II, so its supply is unaffected.
optionExplanations.3: Ribosomal RNA is made by RNA polymerase I, so the ribosomes retain their catalytic RNA.

shortExplanation: The lagging strand exists as fully DNA Okazaki fragments whose only defect is a nick between adjacent pieces, exactly the substrate DNA ligase seals, so ligase is the defective enzyme.
solutionSteps: Unwinding, priming, and synthesis all succeeded (helicase, primase, polymerase III work).
Primers were fully replaced by DNA (polymerase I and RNase H function).
The only remaining defect is a single-strand nick between each adjacent Okazaki fragment.
Sealing such nicks is the specific role of DNA ligase, so ligase is defective.
keyConcept: DNA ligase seals the nicks between adjacent Okazaki fragments after primer replacement, completing the lagging strand.
commonMistake: Blaming polymerase or primase, but synthesis and primer removal already succeeded; only the joining step failed.

optionExplanations.0: Helicase failure would leave the duplex unwound; here both strands were copied.
optionExplanations.1: Primase failure would prevent fragment synthesis; instead fragments formed with primers already replaced.
optionExplanations.2: DNA polymerase III failure would block strand synthesis, yet both leading and lagging strands were made.

shortExplanation: Abnormal forward glide of the tibia (a positive anterior drawer) with fully preserved active extension points to a torn stabilizing ligament, the anterior cruciate, not to the muscle or its tendon.
solutionSteps: Excess forward movement of the tibia means loss of passive restraint, a ligament function.
Preserved voluntary extension against resistance shows the quadriceps muscle and patellar tendon are intact.
Smooth gliding indicates the cartilage and menisci are not the primary problem.
The single structure explaining laxity with intact extension is a knee ligament (the anterior cruciate).
keyConcept: Ligaments provide passive joint stability; their rupture causes laxity without impairing muscle-driven active movement.
commonMistake: Attributing the give-way to muscle damage, which would instead weaken active extension.

optionExplanations.1: A torn patellar tendon would abolish active knee extension, which is preserved here.
optionExplanations.2: Quadriceps damage would weaken active straightening, contradicting the intact extension.
optionExplanations.3: Damaged articular cartilage causes catching and pain, not the clean forward laxity described.

shortExplanation: After the shared pharynx, inhaled air enters the larynx (guarded by the epiglottis) toward the lungs, while swallowed food enters the esophagus toward the stomach.
solutionSteps: The shared crossing segment is the pharynx.
The air route continues into the larynx and then trachea toward the lungs.
A movable flap, the epiglottis, folds over the larynx during swallowing.
The food route continues into the esophagus toward the stomach.
keyConcept: Beyond the shared pharynx, air enters the larynx and food enters the esophagus; the epiglottis diverts food away from the airway.
commonMistake: Swapping the two tubes, sending air into the esophagus or food into the larynx.

optionExplanations.1: This reverses the pathways: air does not enter the esophagus, and food does not enter the larynx.
optionExplanations.2: Air enters the larynx first (then the trachea); the immediate structure past the pharynx is the larynx.
optionExplanations.4: Food enters the esophagus, not the trachea, which is part of the airway.

shortExplanation: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla; the resulting conceptus is then blocked by the scarred isthmus on its way to the uterus and implants in the tube, producing an ectopic (tubal) pregnancy.
solutionSteps: Human fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.
The conceptus must travel through the isthmus toward the uterus.
The scarred, narrowed isthmus obstructs this passage.
Trapped in the tube, the conceptus implants there as a tubal (ectopic) pregnancy.
keyConcept: Fertilization occurs in the ampulla; isthmic obstruction traps the conceptus in the tube, causing ectopic implantation.
commonMistake: Assuming the narrowing blocks fertilization or has no effect, rather than trapping the already-formed conceptus.

optionExplanations.0: Fertilization still occurs in the ampulla before the isthmus; the sperm reached the oocyte, as stated.
optionExplanations.2: Fertilization does not occur in the uterus, so implantation there is not the expected outcome.
optionExplanations.4: The zygote does not reverse through the fimbriae to implant on the ovary; it is trapped in the tube.

shortExplanation: A broad-based ataxic gait, dysmetria (overshooting on finger-to-nose), and inability to perform rapid alternating movements, with normal strength and sensation, are classic signs of a cerebellar lesion.
solutionSteps: List the deficits: wide-based staggering gait, past-pointing, impaired rapid alternating movements.
Note the spared functions: full strength, normal sensation, stable vital signs, intact alertness.
These are coordination deficits without weakness or sensory loss.
This pattern localizes to the cerebellum.
keyConcept: The cerebellum coordinates movement; its damage causes ataxia, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia without weakness or sensory loss.
commonMistake: Attributing incoordination to the motor cortex, whose damage would cause weakness rather than pure ataxia.

optionExplanations.1: A primary motor cortex lesion causes weakness or paralysis, but strength is fully preserved here.
optionExplanations.2: A medulla lesion would disturb breathing and heart rate, which remain steady.
optionExplanations.3: A thalamic lesion typically produces sensory disturbances, but sensation is normal.

shortExplanation: A leukocyte that kills virus-infected and tumor cells on first encounter without prior exposure and independent of MHC-presented antigen is a natural killer (NK) cell of the innate immune system.
solutionSteps: Property 1: induces apoptosis in virus-infected and tumor cells.
Property 2: acts on first encounter without prior immunization, i.e., innate.
Property 3: killing does not require recognizing a specific MHC-presented peptide.
Only the NK cell satisfies all three, especially MHC-independent innate killing.
keyConcept: NK cells are innate lymphocytes that kill stressed cells without antigen priming or MHC-restricted peptide recognition.
commonMistake: Choosing cytotoxic T cells, which require prior antigen exposure and recognize peptide on MHC class I.

optionExplanations.1: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells need prior antigen exposure and recognize peptide presented on MHC.
optionExplanations.2: Plasma cells secrete antibodies; they do not directly kill target cells by inducing apoptosis.
optionExplanations.4: Helper CD4+ T cells coordinate immunity and are MHC-restricted; they do not perform this cytotoxic killing.

shortExplanation: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane (permeable to water but not the solute) from the more dilute toward the more concentrated compartment.
solutionSteps: Define osmosis: passive water movement through a membrane permeable to water but not to solute.
Water moves down its own concentration gradient, from dilute (high water) to concentrated (low water).
Match the option describing exactly this selective-membrane, dilute-to-concentrated flow.
That option is water crossing a solute-impermeable membrane from dilute to concentrated.
keyConcept: Osmosis requires a semipermeable membrane and is the passive flow of water from lower to higher solute concentration.
commonMistake: Calling ATP-driven or pressure-driven water movement osmosis, or reversing the direction of flow.

optionExplanations.0: ATP-driven water movement is active transport, not passive osmosis.
optionExplanations.3: Pressure-driven bulk flow of water and ions through a pore is filtration, not osmosis.
optionExplanations.4: Across a freely permeable membrane there is no osmotic restriction, and flow is stated in the wrong direction.

shortExplanation: A ductless gland secreting a hormone directly into the blood that acts only on distant receptor-bearing target cells is the defining feature of the endocrine system.
solutionSteps: The gland is ductless and releases its product straight into the bloodstream.
The molecule reaches distant cells but affects only those with the matching receptor.
Ductless secretion into blood plus receptor-specific distant action defines endocrine signaling.
Therefore the gland belongs to the endocrine system.
keyConcept: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood, acting selectively on receptor-bearing target cells.
commonMistake: Choosing the circulatory system because blood carries the molecule, when the defining feature is the ductless secreting gland.

optionExplanations.0: The nervous system signals via neurons and synapses, not a ductless gland secreting into blood.
optionExplanations.2: The circulatory system merely transports the hormone; it is not the gland that produces it.
optionExplanations.3: Receptor specificity alone does not make this the immune system; the source is an endocrine gland.

shortExplanation: Carbohydrate (glucose chain), protein (amino acids), and nucleic acid (nucleotides) are true polymers of repeating monomers, whereas a triglyceride is assembled from glycerol plus three fatty acids, not a chain of repeating monomers.
solutionSteps: Sample 1 yields many glucose units, a polysaccharide (polymer).
Sample 2 yields amino acids, a protein (polymer).
Sample 4 yields nucleotides, a nucleic acid (polymer).
Sample 3 yields glycerol plus three fatty acids, a fixed small set of unlike parts, so a triglyceride is not a true polymer.
keyConcept: Polysaccharides, proteins, and nucleic acids are polymers of repeating monomers; lipids are assembled from a small set of unlike components, not repeating monomers.
commonMistake: Calling a triglyceride a polymer simply because hydrolysis breaks it into smaller molecules.

optionExplanations.1: Being hydrolyzable into subunits does not make lipids polymers; a triglyceride is not a repeating-monomer chain.
optionExplanations.2: Nucleotides are not the only monomer type; glucose and amino acids also polymerize.
optionExplanations.3: Nucleic acids (Sample 4) are also polymers, so restricting polymers to carbohydrates and proteins is wrong.

shortExplanation: The enzyme-secreting fungus is the decomposer (saprotroph): it externally digests dead leaf litter and releases small inorganic molecules back to the soil. Removing it directly halts the mineralization of dead organic matter.
solutionSteps: Identify the process asked about: decomposition/mineralization of dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients.
Organism 1 secretes digestive enzymes onto DEAD fallen leaves and absorbs the products — this is saprotrophic decomposition.
Check the others: N-fixer converts atmospheric N2 (not dead matter); caterpillar eats LIVING tissue; alga is a photosynthetic producer; tapeworm feeds on a living host's digested food.
Only the fungus breaks down dead organic matter, so its removal most directly interrupts the recycling of inorganic nutrients.
